They are free from brush and underwood and not the least vestige of their having been cultivated. The country is excellent for grazing and abounds in Buffalo, Deer, Bear &c. It is a matter of Speculation to account for the formation of the Prairies. The eastern side of the Wabash is overflown in the Spring for several miles.

On the 17<sup>th</sup> I was visited by the Magistrates and principal cohabitants of Kaskaskias, welcoming us upon our arrival. Baptiste De Coigne the Chief of the Kaskias Indians paid me a visit in the afternoon and delivered me a much Profession of greatest friendship for the U. States. and presented me with one of the Calumets or Pipes of Peace, which is now sent on. Some of the Pioria Indians likewise visited me. The Kaskaskias, Piorias, Cohokias, and Mitchis tribes compose the Illinois Indians. They are almost extinct at present, not exceeding forty or fifty totol.

Kaskaskias is a handsome little village situated on the river of the same name which empties into the river Mississippi at two Leagues distance from it. It is 105 miles up the Mississippi, from the mouth of the Ohio. The situation is low and unhealthy and subject to inundation. The inhabitants are French, and much of the same class, as at Post Vincennes. Their number 191 old and young men.

Having but overlittle time to spare I left Ensign H<sup>d</sup> Darnell with the Party at Kaskaskias, and on the 18<sup>th</sup> set out accompanied by her [undecipherable] and the Gentlemen of the village for Cohokia. We passed Prairie du Rochen a small village 3 leagues distance from Kaskaskias, where we lodged for the night.

On the 19<sup>th</sup> we passed through St. Phillips, a trifling village 3 leagues distance from Prairie du Rochen and dined at La Belle Fontaine, six leagues farther. La Belle Fontaine is a small stockade inhabited altogether by Americans who have settled themselves there without authority.

It is a beautiful situation, fine fertile lands, no taxation and the inhabitants have abundance to live upon. They were exceedingly alarmed when I informed them of their precarious State respecting a title to their possessions, & have sent on a Petition to Congress by Mr. Tardiveau. On the same day we passed another small stockade Grand Ruisseau inhabited by the same sort of Americans (as those at La Belle Fontaine) and arrived at Cohokia that evening.

Cohokia is a Village nearly of the same size as that of Kaskaskias, and the inhabitants by the same kind of people. Their number 239 old men and young. I was received with the greatest Hospitality by the inhabitants.

There was a decent submission and respect in their behaviour. Cohokia is distant from Kaskaskias, 22 French Leagues which is about 50 miles.

On the 21<sup>st</sup> in consequence of an invitation from Monsieur Cruzat the Spanish Commandant at St. Louis we crossed the Mississippi and were very politely entertained by him. After dinner we returned to Cohokia.

St. Louis (nick-named Paincourt) is much the handsomest and genteelest village I have seen on the Mississippi. It is about 4 miles distant from Cohokia, and five Leagues above it the river Missouri unites with the Mississippi. The inhabitants are of the same sort as before described, excepting that they are more wealthy. About 20 regular Spanish troops are stationed here.

On the 22<sup>nd</sup> I left Cohokia to return to Kaskaskias. Previous to my departure, at the request of the inhabitants I assembled them and gave them advice to place their Militia upon a more respectable footing, than it was, to obey to the decision of their Courts &c, and if there were any turbulent or refractory persons to put them under guard, until Congress should be pleased to order a Government for them.

Exclusive of the intruders already described, there are about thirty more Americans settled on the rich fertile bottoms on the Mississippi, who are likewise petitioned by this conveyance.

On the 23<sup>d</sup> I passed by the ruins of Fort Chartres, which is one league above the Prairie du Rochen and situated on the Mississippi. It was built of Stone and must have been a considerable Fortification formerly, but the part next to the river has been carried away by the floods, and is of no consequence at present. I staid about a quarter of an hour, but had no time to view it minutely as it was all a thicket within. Several iron pieces of Cannon are here at present, and also at the different villages.

This evening I returned to Kaskaskias.

On the 24<sup>th</sup> Monsieur Senes the Spanish Commandant at St. Previeur sent me an invitation to pay him a visit. We crossed the Mississippi accordingly, were politely entertained and after dinner returned to Kaskaskias.

St. Previeur (nicknamed Moiseru) is a village much inferior in every respect, to St. Louis. It is about 4 miles (including the passage of the Mississippi) distance from Kaskaskias. about 8 or 10 Spanish troops are stationed here.

On the 26<sup>th</sup> at the request of the inhabitants (which is enclosed) I assembled them and gave them advice to regulate their Militia and obey their Magistrates &c. until Congress should be pleased to order a Government for them.

I have to remark, that all these people are entirely unacquainted with what Americans call Liberty, Trial by Jury &c, they are strangers to.

A Commandant and a few troops to give them orders is the best form of Government for them, it is what they have been accustomed to.

On the 29<sup>th</sup> I left Kaskaskias after having received every mark of respect and attention from the inhabitants in order to set out for the Post. We marched by a lower route several of the French, and the Kaskaskias Chief and his tribe (about 60 in number) accompanied us. And we arrived safe at Post Vincennes in the afternoon of the 3<sup>d</sup> of September. I make the distance by the lower route to be about 170 miles.

On the 5<sup>th</sup> the Piankeshaw and Weea Indians arrived at the Post from of the Wabash to the number of 120. Every precaution was taken, we had a fortified Camp, two redoubts were thrown up, on our right and left, and the guard extended. The troops were all new clothed and made a truly military appearance. The Indians saluted us by firing several vollies on the Wabash opposite our Camp. Their Salute was returned by a party of ours firing several platoons.

I was determined to impress upon them as much as possible the majesty of the United States, and at the same time they were informed that it was the wish of Congress to live in peace and friendship with them. Likewise to let them know that if they persisted in being Hostile, that a body of troops would march to their towns and sweep them off the face of the Earth.

On the 7<sup>th</sup> I invited them to Camp, and made the enclosed speech to them. The Indians admired the troops I believe they had never seen such a sight before.

On the 8<sup>th</sup> they answered my speech and in strong figurative language, expressing their determination to preserve peace and friendship with the United States as long as the waters flowed &c. They utterly disavowed any knowledge of the murder that had been committed and assured me that enquiry should be made for the prisoners.

They presented me with a number of Calumets and Wampum, which I now have the honor of transmitting, enclosed in a rich otter skin, they will be delivered by Mr. Dubre.

My Dubre has acted as a Volunteer for a considerable time in the Regiment, and has conducted himself with Propriety. If a vacancy should happen in the Connecticut quota I beg leave to recommend him your notice.

On the 9<sup>th</sup> the young Warriors were drinking whiskey and dancing before our tents all the morning to demonstrate their joy.

On the 10<sup>th</sup> I made them several presents from the Commissioners Goods to no great amount.

On the 12<sup>th</sup> the Chief part of them left the Post for their different Villages, on the Wabash, they returned highly satisfied with the treatment they received. Indeed it was a sober hour of fatigue for me, I found it politic to pay the greatest attention to them. They are amazing fond of whiskey and destroyed a considerable quantity of it.

I must you will find this conference with the Indians attended with very little expense, I question whether the whole Whiskey, Provisions, and Presents, will cost the public more than 150 dollars.

Their interpreter is a half French man and married to a Weea squaw, he has very great influence among them. I judged it necessary to pay extra ordinary attention to him.

I have the honor to communicate the receipt of several letters from you, which I shall fully answer by the next conveyance. Particularly one of the 2<sup>d</sup> of August, enclosing me a Brevet Commission of Brigadier General.

After finishing the conference with the Indians and obtaining the enclosed petitions of the inhabitants at Post Vincennes to Congress relinquishing their charter and trusting to the generosity of that Honorable body I judged it expedient to leave a garrison at that Post, as it would have been impolitic, after the parade we had made, to entirely abandon the Country.

Accordingly Major Hamtramck commands there. His command consists of Captain Smiths Company 55 and part of Fergusons Company 40 total 95. I have ordered him to fortify himself and to regulate the Militia who are to join him in case of Hostilities.

You are pleased to ask my opinion of the price of the ration at the Post. I conceive that the Contractors could afford it for the same price here, as at the falls, provided the troops bring it on, otherwise they cannot, as the expense of transportation Hireing of hands &c is considerable.

It was an uncommon sickly season at the Post. In the month of September I had no less than 196 sick present.

Having arranged all matters to my satisfaction, as we had a long and tiresome voyage before as I began to think of Winter Quarters.

Accordingly on the 1<sup>st</sup> of October I marched by land with the well men of Captain Zeigler and Strongs Companies (total 91) for the Rapids of the Ohio. I gave orders to Major Wyllys to command the fleet and to embark for the Rapids the next morning, with the late Captain Finneys and Nevans Companies and the sick of the other Companies, and a brace three pounder.

I omitted mentioning of my taking into our possession some Ordnance and Ammunition (public Property) at Louisville and at the Post. At the former we got a brace six pounders and several swivels, (at the latter from Mr. Dotton two brass three pounders). I thought it best that the public property should be under our own charge.

We marched along what is called Clarks Trace and arrived on the 1<sup>st</sup> October at the Rapids of the Ohio. I was mistaken in a former letter concerning the distance, it is about 130 miles. We saw no Indians nor Signs of Indians. From the Falls to the Post the country is in general hilly, and good wheat land.

Major Wyllys and the Fleet arrived at Clarksville on the 21<sup>st</sup>. On the 23<sup>d</sup> and 24<sup>th</sup> the men were all employed in dragging the Boats over the Falls, a very difficult fatiguing tour of duty the more so as the water was remarkably low.

On the 28<sup>th</sup> I left the falls in the Barge for Muskingum with orders for Captain Zeigler and Strongs and their companies to follow me the next day. On the 13<sup>th</sup> November we arrived at this Post. Captain Zeigler arrived here with the fleet on the 21<sup>st</sup>. We are favored with remarkable fine weather ever since we set out from the Post.

The following are among my arrangements for Winter Quarters:

At Venango. .............. Capt. Hearts. Company.

At Mc Intosh — Part of Capt. Ferguson's Company

Such a large proportion of the Regiment being quartered at Muskingum during the winter will save the public considerable expense, with respect to Provisions.

The water being so exceedingly low detained [strikethrough: detained] Capt. Beatty a long time at Fort Pitt. He did not arrive at his garrison until the 26<sup>th</sup> instant at night. We are all happy to find that he has obtained such a just and honorable settlement for the Regiment, and are much indebted to you for having been pleased to lend him every assistance in the business.

The Bearer Mr. Bartholomew Tardiveau, I believe you will find to be a sensible well informed Gentleman, as well, if not better acquainted with the western Country (Particularly the Illinois) than any one who has been from thence to Congress.

I beg leave to refer you to him for a minute and particular description of it. There has been some impostors before Congress, particularly one Parker a whining canting Methodist as kind of [underline: would be] Governor. He is extremely unpopular at Kaskaskias, and despised by the inhabitants.

I am happy to hear of General St. Clair's appointment as Governor of the Western Territory, as it will add to the dignity and consequence of Congress.

Be pleased to receive the enclosed monthly Returns of the Regiment dated the 1<sup>st</sup> of Sept., 1<sup>st</sup> Oct. & 1<sup>st</sup> of Nov.

You are pleased to ask me intelligence respecting the Military lands from Fort Massac to the mouth of the Ohio, and from thence about twenty (20) miles up the Mississippi. The Country overflows, and is by no means habitable.

I shall have the honor of writing to you again in a short time.

I have the honor to be &c.

Jos. Harmar

The Hon<sup>b</sup>.

It is a mortifying circumstance that while under the sanction of federal authority, negotiations and treaties are holding with the indians that there should be such presumption in the People of Kentucky, as to be forming expeditions against them.

Your letter of August 2nd. was received at the Post, which covered the duplicate letter of July 24<sup>th</sup> and a duplicate of the resolve of Congress of July 21<sup>st</sup>.

I likewise have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 4<sup>th</sup> October enclosing me the resolve of Congress of the 3<sup>rd</sup> October.

expedition to Post Vincennes. At that time and long afterwards I knew of no farther engagement entered into with Mess<sup>rs</sup> Turnball, Marmie & C<sup>o</sup> by the board of Treasury for the supply. From either inability, or inattention previous to that upon their part which I sufficiently experienced by having been obliged to expend nearly £100 in Specia from my private funds for the support of this Garrison, otherwise to have abandoned it. From these facts I presume you will judge, that there are sufficient inducements for me to place no farther dependance upon them. I was actuated by this principle only, that the expedition should not be retarded. Kentucky abounded in provisions, to be procured cheap and speedily which determined me upon the steps which I have taken. The new Contractors have paid the bills drawn by Mr Broadshaw, as they were refused payment by Mr Marmie.

You have been pleased to approve of my conduct in the order of March from the Ohio to Post Vincennes, which is highly pleasing. It shall ever by my study to merit your approbation.

I hope before this letter reaches you that Mr Tardiveau has arrived, by whom I wrote a minute and particular account of all my transactions until the 24<sup>th</sup> ult. A duplicate was not sent, as I esteemed it as safe and speedy conveyance. The circumstances of the French at Post Vincennes giving up their Charter and trusting to the generosity of Congress I believe will have a good effect. Yours of the 28 Ult. has come to hand for which I return you my most hearty thanks — But find you do not exactly understand what I yet want from M<sup>r</sup> Phillips. The securities which you mentioned being with M<sup>r</sup> Walcott were allowed to me when I was in New York last, what I want of him is a sheet of Paper whereon are a number of names who signed orders on him to receive their securities which securities I gave him which orders I now want as my voucher for the delivery of them to him and which is in attention I left in his hands after I had delivered him all the securities and which he now wickedly detains — or my idea which you received are the names of the Persons the securities belonged to, which by comparing with the account of M<sup>r</sup> Walcott you will find to be all different persons — Now what I want you to do is to write to him and put him in mind that he has received such a number of securities which he must account for and that he is liable to an arrest from the [undecipherable] if he does not do it — It seems that he has not delivered them all to the owners, but if he will deliver up the Paper I mentioned it will be sufficient for me — you mentioned Major Patten he signed the order I have a Letter from him wherein he mentions signing the order.

Tallon to which I have to observe that when I received the securities Capt. J. Howell Jr.

[Copy of a letter from Brigadier Harmar to the Secretary at War.]

Fort Harmar January 10<sup>th</sup> 1788.

Sir,

I had the honor of addressing you on the 24<sup>th</sup> of November by Mr. Bartholomew Tardiveau and on the 19<sup>th</sup> of December last, by Lieutenant Kersey, which I hope have safe arrivd. I now have the acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 26<sup>th</sup> of October with the following enclosures, — Viz:

1st.     A duplicate of your letter of the 16<sup>th</sup> of October.

2nd.     Resolve of Congress of the 13<sup>th</sup> October respecting certain person and conferring a certain John Sullivan.

3d.     Resolve of Congress of the 22<sup>d</sup> of October empowering the Governor of the Western Territory to hold a treaty with the Indians, if in his judgement the public

good requires it.

4 th.     Resolve of Congress of the 22<sup>d</sup> of October reserving certain tracts of lands therein described in order to satisfy the claims of the late Army.

5th.     Resolve of Congress of the 9<sup>th</sup> of October for continuing the present Corps for three years longer.

Agreeably to your directions I have sent orders to the Officers commanding at the several Posts to put his troops forfaitely upon their guard, in order to avoid surprises, as from the intelligence you have transmitted me, there may be a possibility of the Indians confederating under Brant, and committing hostilities.

I am in hopes that the general treaty which the Governor of the Western Territory means to hold in the Spring, will pacify the savages, and settle all differences.

The information which you are pleased to make me,

of respecting the lands referred to satisfy the claims of the late Army, I shall give according to the best of my knowledge.

The million of acres which is to be bounded south by the Ohio Company Purchase, I believe will be found to be excellent land; especially if it should take in the lands on the Muskingum, and its branches which I am led to suppose will be the case, from all accounts the Muskingum river continues more to the Eastward than is laid down in Captain Hutchins's maps; if so, the tract reserved for the late Army will be very valuable.

Having never been personally present at the mouth of the Ohio, it is out of my power to give further information respecting the lands thereabout, than what was rendered in my letter of the 24<sup>th</sup> November last. Viz:

From Fort Massac to the mouth of the Ohio and from thence about twenty miles up the

Mississippi, the country overflows and is by no means habitable.

This information proceeds from Mr. Tardiveau. The commercial situation (as you partly observe) is fine indeed. It is a great misfortune that it is so subject to inundation. I beg leave to refer you to Mr. Tardiveau for more particular intelligence upon this subject. It is my opinion that a million of acres adjoining the other million on the Muskingum would take in excellent land, and comprehend a very valuable tract of country.

I have also the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 14<sup>th</sup> of November last, with its several enclosures. viz:

1st.     A duplicate of your letter of the 26<sup>th</sup> of October last, with its Enclosures.

2nd.     Copy of a letter from John Sullivan to Major William Brown, dated Charlestown 24<sup>th</sup> Sep<sup>t</sup>. 1787.

3<sup>d</sup>.     Resolve of Congress of the 26<sup>th</sup> of October respecting furnishing the Governor of the Western Territory with Troops.

4th.     Resolve of Congress of the 29<sup>th</sup> October associating the Superintendent with the Governor in case of a treaty.

5th.     The Act of New Jersey, appointing its Officers agreeably to the resolve of Congress of the 3rd of October last.

On the 6<sup>th</sup> of last month, I wrote to Major Wyllys at the rapids of the Ohio, and enclosed him a copy of the inflammatory letter written by Mr. Sullivan to His Excellency the Spanish Minister, and informed him that if said Sullivan should be found in the Federal Territory, I had orders to seize and confine him. It is the universal sentiment of the inhabitants westward of the Alleghany mountains, that they ought to enjoy the free navigation of the Mississippi; but I very much question whether the

Kentucky, Cumberland people, and those below will have the audacity, to attempt to seize upon the Natches and New Orleans. Such an enterprise would certainly be a disgrace to the United States. I know of no cannon and the necessary apparatus, which they have in their possession, to carry on such an expedition. I shall transmit a duplicate of your letter of the 14<sup>th</sup> of November and a copy of Sullivan's letter to Major Brown, to Major Wyllys (as soon as the weather permits) which strict orders to watch closely and know their designs. I shall likewise give him directions to send an Officer and two or three confidential persons to Franklie and Kentucky under pretence of exploring the Country, in order that I may be made acquainted with their intended manœuvres. It appears to me that this matter will not be so serious as is imagined but rather an evidence of the mutinous disposition of Sullivan and an insignificant banditti.

Sullivan was the principal ring-leader in the

mutiny of the Pennsylvania line during the late war, and it is high time to put an end of his career.

If he can be apprehended in Franklie, our out of the Federal Territory I should suppose myself justifiable in giving orders for that purpose.

We have had a remarkable spell of hard weather since Christmas. The Thermometer has been 16 degrees below the 0. point. The river is now fast bound with ice and according to custom, we have only twelve days meat and flour on hand through the neglect of the Contractors. The men have nearly 40 days Whiskey due them.

As soon as the weather will permit I shall send Major Wyllys the necessary orders respecting Sullivan and his adherents.

If from the intelligence which I have given you respecting the inundation of the lands at the mouth of the Ohio, it should be judged adviseable to fix upon some other tract of country to satisfy

the claims of the late Army, whenever Congress may be pleased to fixat upon said tract, I shall (agreeably to your directions) Notion an adequate body of troops in the vicinity thereof, in order that the surveyors may be protected in the execution of their business.

I am anxiously waiting for the arrival of the second suit of Clothing for the three Companies and shall expect the third suit for the other companies early in March. Captain McDougys company which is at the Post suffers much for want of woolen overalls.

I observe that the overalls are to be all blue. I am sorry that it was out of your power to have white cloth procured. White overalls in my opinion more military.

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 22nd of November last, enclosing me duplicates of yours of the 14<sup>th</sup> of November.

Captain Rümeys resignation which was offered on the 10<sup>th</sup> November (after having received the formality of the approbation of Congress) will cause promotion for Lieutenant Ashton and Ensign Bear. The Enclosed list is the order which I wish to take place in appointing the Officers for the quota of Pennsylvania, I have written to the Supreme Executive Council upon this subject.

A considerable length of time certainly elapsed between by letters of the 17<sup>th</sup> of August and the 24<sup>th</sup> of November, but beg you to attribute it to no other cause than awaiting for Mr. Tardiveaus arrival. I was obliged at last to embark at the rapids of the Ohio for this Post without him. I sincerely hope that he has long since safe arrived, as also Lieutenant Kersey, by whom I had the honor of addressing you.

Duplicates of these, my two last letters were not sent on.

I have written to the posts below

(but it will be a considerable time before an answer can be had) to know what prospects there are of reengaging the men of the six old Companies, and to use all possible diligence to effect the object.

Captain Hart has been written to upon the same subject. There are three old companies at this Post, the men have been sounded, and I am in hopes, we shall be able to retain 40 or 50 of them; but this is merely conjecture. The three Companies raised in 1786, having more than a year to serve, I shall make no proposals to them upon this head. In order to commence the business in time, Captain Smith and Lieutenant Kersey have been dispatched from hence to their respective States, for the purpose of recruiting. About the beginning of next month I shall dispatch Lieutenant Potts and Ensign Jeffers, a good Serjeant, and two trusty men to Connecticut; likewise Captain Bradford as Subaltern and two non-commissioned officers to the State of New York,

and an Officer and Non Commissioned Officer to the State of Pennsylvania, to expedite the business. It shall be my object to manœuvre with the old Soldiers in order to re-enlist them; One of them is worth half a dozen recruits, as they have a knowledge of the Country and have acquired the habits of a Soldier.

There will be a necessity of appointing another Captain to command the company which is to be composed of the fractional parts from Connecticut, New York and New Jersey. Whosoever may answer a good purpose for one of the States, (whichever you may be pleased to call upon) to furnish the Captain immediately, who by being employed in recruiting, would be anxious for his own sake, to speedily raise his company & join the Corps.

I pray you to let seniority take place; the eldest Subaltern from the state which is called upon ought to be Captain. If the men upon

the expiration of their time incline to go home, which I believe out of novelty will generally be the case, especially the Connecticut quota, the recruiting Officers being on the spot, will in a short time be able to reengage them, as I am convinced they will soon be fond of the life of a citizen.

I have received no letters from the Posts below since we left them. If anything material should have happened, the Commanding Officers are ordered to send me immediate intelligence thereof by Express. Consequently I take it for granted, that at the rapids of the Ohio and at Post Vincennes, all is well.

The muster of the Field & Staff and of the four Companies at this Post, is made from the 1<sup>st</sup> of January 1787, to the 31<sup>st</sup> of December 1787, inclusive. The troops were mustered by Major Doughty. By his conveyance I enclose the

Rolls to Lieutenant Beatty. It will be some time before the troops at the other Posts can be mustered and the rolls forwarded.

Be pleased to receive the following Enclosures.

viz:

1st.     Monthly return of the regiment dated 1st instant.

2nd.     Return of the Ordnance and Military Stores on hand at the several posts dated the 1st inst.

3d.     Return of Quartermaster's Stores on hand at the several Posts dated the 1st instant.

4th.     Estimate of Military Stores wanting for the service of the United States in the Western department, dated the 1st instant.

5th.     Copy of Captain Harts letter to me dated December 5<sup>th</sup> 1787, which will show the state of affairs in that quarter.

6th.     Address of the French inhabitants at the Illinois, dated August 3<sup>d</sup> 1787. It was intended to have been transmitted

by Mr. Tardiveau.

7th.     Prices of the articles at Post Vincennes. The prices are enormous, and the Officers and the Officers stationed there are in a very disagreeable situation, with respect to Subsistence money.

I beg leave to observe that Post McIntosh is by no means tenable. The small party stationed there at present I propose to order to Post Pitt, in order to receive Stores, clothing &c. and the Officer commanding there may forward them, also any dispatches which may carrier from the War Office.

It should have been evacuated last Spring, but for the orders I received from you countermanding the same. I shall direct Major Doughty to proceed there early in the Spring, and to dismantle it.

The Post is built of hewn timber, it will be easy to raft it to this Post, where it will be of

service. I shall not give these orders until I have your sanction for so doing. If a communication should be wanting to Lake Erie, a Block House for the reception of stores can instantly be built near the Big Beaver.

The Boats are entirely unfit for another expedition, ascending the Wabash last Summer, returning in the fall, and being dragged over the rapids of the Ohio (the water was so low) have wrecked them almost to pieces.

I beg leave to know your particular Orders respecting the waiters of the Officers.

I am entitled to four anchor armes.

Whether are they, being soldiers, entitled to draw rations or not? If Every Officer was to find his servant, and the public to make him compensation for the same, it would be for the benefit of the service, as the Officers Waiters reduce the effective strength of the regiment

materially.

I have the honor to be Sir,

With perfect esteem and respect,

Your Most hmbl and ob<sup>t</sup> Servt.

Jos Harmar,

Lt. Col. Com<sup>d</sup>. 1<sup>st</sup> U.S. Reg.

Office of Army Accounts
New York, March 28<sup>th</sup> 1786.

Sir

Your letters of the 8 & 21 inst the former covering sundry papers of your late brother were duly received.

I have been some days endeavouring to form a statement of Capt Jones's account which is now inclosed, but for want of the original papers cannot bring it to a close with any degree of precision — The Last Muster Roll which I find of his company is taken 26 May 1777 and contains only forty men, in the return which you have transmitted there appears four men who are not included on this muster, which induces me to suppose that the muster roll now before me is not the first that was taken — Several queries arise which if they can be answered with any degree of certainty I am still of opinion that I shall be enabled to close the account.

They are as follows (viz.)

1<sup>st</sup> When did Capt Jones commence recruiting & when did he cease; did he draw rations while on the recruiting service?

2<sup>d</sup> When did he leave Philadelphia with his company to join head quarters?

3<sup>d</sup> Was he a recruiting serjeant that was not a soldier? what monies did he advance him & how long was the serjeant a recruiting?

4<sup>th</sup> Was he a Drummer, Fifer, or which of them, to assist in recruiting, who were not soldiers? & how long did they recruit?

5<sup>th</sup> Did he supply his recruits with Cockades & how many of them?

6<sup>th</sup> From what time did the men commence drawing provisions?

7<sup>th</sup> Did the men join the main army by detachments or did Capt Jones march with the whole of them?

8<sup>th</sup> Have you any memorandums or accounts for monies advanced by Capt Jones for the subsisting of his provisions to provisions being drawn?

The first & second queries I should suppose Mrs Jones can answer, the rest I must leave to your own Memory or to such Memorandums as may still be procured.

In the account you have transmitted I observe you make

a large balance due the Estate of your brother. I am sorry you have thus stated the account as it has in all probability induced Mrs Jones to suppose that such a balance is due & gave her a hope that it would be received, whereas by my statement you will find that every allowing every thing that is possible for a public officer to do that a very small balance if any will arise — You have charged the United States with Capt Jones's Pay from the 1<sup>st</sup> of August 1778 to the 14<sup>th</sup> April 1780. I have considered the pay as given without advertising to his depreciations being made good to him by the State of Pennsylvania; neither have you considered that pay has been drawn for him in his company rolls not only for part of this time but that is has been regularly paid by Mr Belcher who acted as deputy Barrack Master in Philadelphia which must be considered in full as the act of Congress does not admit of an officers receiving pay in 2 capacities.

You have also charged for five retainer rations from the 8<sup>th</sup> November 1776 to April 8<sup>th</sup> 1780. This is also a wrong charge for in the first place an officer is not entitled to rations while recruiting or subsistance if he receives [strikethrough: rations] rations.

2<sup>dly</sup> The act of Congress have long since [strikethrough: foreclosed] any claim for rations prior to the army settlements.

3<sup>dly</sup> All officers who had rations due them prior the 1<sup>st</sup> June 1778 were required by a general orders to present their accounts to the paymaster General for settlement, and such as applied were paid; this you may recollect happened at Valley Forge — if your brother was there he must also been of the number who were paid.

4<sup>thly</sup> His rations from the 1 June 1778 to 14 April 1780 I have taken up and settled with the 4<sup>th</sup> Reg<sup>t</sup> of Artillery — The balance of [undecipherable] still appears due, which sum is retained in this office until a settlement of this account takes place. You will see it credited in the account now transmitted — From the foregoing you will be convinced of the impropriety of the charge for pay & rations.

There being no receipt for the money charged against Capt Thomas Barr it cannot be admitted —

New Yorke, May 2<sup>d</sup> 1793

Sir

I have the honor to lay before you the Treaties concluded, in pursuance of the instructions received from Congress on the twenty sixth of October 1792 and second of July 1792, with several of the Indian nations in January last— That they were not presented at an earlier period was owing in part to my own indisposition — to the severity of the Winter which rendered the communication

by the Ohio, for a long time impracticable— and to the circumstance that the last Congress did not assemble after it was in my power to have sent them forward.

With the treaties I beg leave to submit the minutes of the proceedings at the different meetings after the Nations were assembled, and I have added to them, by way of appendix, all the letters and messages that passed between them and me prior to their assembling— These were communicated to the Secretary at War from time to time, and tho' they will, no doubt, be submitted by him to your consideration, I thought it best, as they form a considerable part of the transactions, to annex them in that way, that the whole might be seen together.

By the instructions of July the second, I was directed to endeavour at extending the northern boundary, as far north as the completion of the forty first degree of North Lattitude— Besides that it would have been extremely difficult to have made the Indians comprehend how that was to be ascertained, I found that any attempts to extend the limits at that time would be very ill received, if not defeat entirely the settling a peace with them; it was therefore not proposed, and the boundaries remain as settled at the former Treaties except the rectifying an Error about the portage at the Miamis Village.

The negotiation was both tedious and tiresome, and for a long time had an unpromising aspect, but it came at last to as favorable an issue as could have been expected— and I trust will be attended with consequences friendly to the frontier parts of the United States— There are however several nations on the Wabash, and the Rivers which empty themselves into it, that are all dispersed, and from whom there is reason to suspect that a part of the Frontier of Virginia, and the settlements forming on the Miamis, will meet annoyance— indeed that they have not been disturbed during the Winter was not expected, either by me or the Chiefs of the Nations who met me at Fort Harmar. The Wyandots did appoint persons to go to them and inform them of the result of the Treaty, and insist upon their desisting from further Hostilities which may have some effect in preserving the late tranquility.

The claim of the Wyandot Nation to the lands reserved to the Shawanese was strongly insisted upon by them and to be made an Article of the Treaty— to that I could not consent: but to satisfy them, and that it might be kept in remembrance, it is inserted at the bottom of it, by way of memorandum. It seems this is a claim that

has always been held up, and the reason it was so much insisted on at this time, they said was, that they were sure that the Shawanoes, and Cherokees incorporated with them would continue to give us trouble— That it could not be expected to be borne with much longer, that they would be driven out of the Country, and then it would be claimed and held by the United States by right of conquest— they further added that, if the Shawanese continue their depredations, they would, themselves drive them off— They also pressed that a Fort should be taken by the United States at the Miami Villages as the surest means to overawe the Nations on the Wabash— It is certainly well situated for that purpose, and would command the greatest part of the Indian trade— As it was very uncertain whether Congress might approve of such a measure, as a Post so far as I find would with difficulty be supplied, and we in no readiness to carry it into execution if it should be approved, I desired them to consider well whether it could be done without a contest with the Indians who live there— and whether, in that case, there was not danger of they themselves being involved thro' the ungovernahleness of their young men— They acknowledged that they thought there was danger of both, but promised to send some of their principal men to the Miamis and prepare them for receiving a garrison peaceably, and to

give me notice in the Spring.

The reason why the Treaties were made separately with the six Nations and the Wyandots and other westerly tribes was a jealousy that subsisted between them, and which I was not willing to lessen by appearing to consider them as one people— they do not so consider themselves, and I am persuaded their general confederacy is entirely fictitious, indeed it would not be very difficult if circumstances required it to set them at deadly variance.

The great lengths of time that elapsed between the appointed periods for the meeting, and that at which the Indians assembled, during which, numbers of them were constantly going and coming, has increased the expences in the article of provisions considerably, the utmost possible economy however, was used tho' the whole of the business, and in transacting it, I flatter myself with meeting the approbation of Congress.

With the utmost Respect,
I have the honor to be,
Sir,
Your most obedient
and
Humble Servants
A<sup>r</sup> St Clair

The President of the United States.

War Office, June 3. 1793

Sir

Your letters of the 20th and 30 ultimo have been received —

I am exceedingly desirous that your compliment of men should be recruited as soon as possible, and therefore I am sorry that your prospects are less flattering than when you first commenced the recruiting Service.

Company books of the Larger kind are forwarded by Captain Bradford for the whole regiment. Any temporary arrangement therefore will answer your purpose until your arrival on the frontiers.

When you march an arrangement must be made for the accommodation of some form for Brigadier General Harmar. It is not however probable that he can possibly require a whole waggon for his own use.

As to any of your Soldiers folding their arrearage of pay, I cannot countenance the measure. The men ought to be checked in any such improper desires. They have lately received three months pay, and they will from time to time receive their arrearages. They are supplied with rations and clothing, and they ought not to be suffered to sell their arrearages for less than its proper value. Especially as all necessaries are furnished them. They will receive another months pay previous to their departure. I presume that their reasons will have equal influence on your conduct as an officer whose reputation is deservedly established.

I am
Sir
Your humble Serv<sup>t</sup>
Knox

Captain David Ziegler

My dear Sir

The proposed constitution seems to be as well received as could have been conjectured by the most sanguine. The opposition is now complete in itself and subject to a thousand misrepresentations. It is not surprising that it has had its enemies. Mankind are infinitely diversified in their situations and faculties, and being constrained by local circumstances to view the same objects through different mediums and with different apparatuses it is no wonder that their conceptions and opinions should be different. Happy indeed is it for the public and I hope for posterity that so many states have already agreed to it and that none have rejected excepting Rhode Island. 39337:
[Extract of a letter from Brigadier Harmar dated Fort Harmar    June 15, 1788.]

I had the honor of addressing you last on the 26<sup>th</sup> of April from Fort Pitt since which I have to acknowledge the receipt of your letters of the 11<sup>th</sup> and 21<sup>st</sup> April.

On the 27<sup>th</sup> April I left Fort Pitt in the Barge and after six days extreme hard labor in ascending the rapid river Alleghany arrived at Captain Abart's works on French Creek.

Captain Abart with his small command has done an immense deal of work there. His garrison was found to be in excellent order. There are a number of Seneca and Munsy tribes continually in his neighbourhood who conduct themselves very peaceably. Indeed I know of no officer who manages the Indians better than Captain Abart.

The Senecas in particular place great confidence in him, he is a great favorite among them.

After strongly impressing him with the necessity of the utmost vigilance at his Post in order to guard against surprize, as he is out of all manner of Support, and therefore must depend upon nothing for his security but his own alertness & attention I left him on the morning of the 4<sup>th</sup> May & the same evening returned to Fort Pitt. The distance by water I suppose to be about 160 miles, by land about 80.

There is no sort of comparison between the Ohio and the Alleghany rivers as to the current the latter being so much more rapid than the former. The country on both sides of the river from Fort Pitt to French Creek is very rugged and mountainous. I have the honor to enclose you a map of the country from Venango to Lake Erie.

On the 23<sup>d</sup> May General M'Clair arrived at Fort Pitt but as the Indians will be late at assembling to the treaty, & as he had some private affairs to attend to at Ligonier he thought proper to return there & informed me that he would be at Fort Pitt about the 25<sup>th</sup> of this month, it was therefore inconvenient for me to wait so long a time for his return. I left Fort Pitt in the afternoon of the 28<sup>th</sup> May & the next night arrived at this Post. Major Doughty now proceeds in the Barge and will have the honor to receive the Governor and accompany him down. On the 13<sup>th</sup> instant a large boat of the Contractors laden with Provisions for the Treaty set out from hence for the falls of the Muskingum, it is absolutely necessary they should be expeditious in their movements as the Muskingum river will soon be so low that it will be impossible for loaded boats to ascend it. Agreeably to the Governors request I have granted an escort of a Sub. Sergt. Corpl. & 20 Privates for this boat load of Provisions and have given the officer orders to build a Council room for the Savages, at the falls of the Muskingum.

It gives me great satisfaction to learn by your letter of the 11<sup>th</sup> April that Kin Pardivean has at length delivered my dispatches of the 24<sup>th</sup> November and that every unfavorable impression which you had received concerning him are entirely effaced. I must confess his tardiness upon this occasion appeared to me very suspicious. I am happy to observe that my conduct in making the tour to the Mississippi and visiting the several villages on the American and Spanish side has met with the approbation of Congress and yourself which is highly satisfactory.

The Provisions which I took with me to Post Vincennes was transported at the public expence and not at the expence of the Contractors. The Provisions which came to the Rapids by orders of Mess. Turnbull, Marnis & Co. arrived too late, and was therefore not received.

Mr. Britt intended to proceed to Post Vincennes with that Cargo, & there to dispose of it. He was unfortunate, in passing the mouth of the Wabash at the night & was oblig'd to proceed to Kaskaskias for a market, where he deposited his cargo.

From the 19<sup>th</sup> of December to this day three hundred and eight Boats, six thousand three hundred & twenty Souls, two thousand eight hundred and twenty four Horses, five hundred & fifteen Cows, six hundred Sheep, mixed Hogs, and one hundred and fifty Waggons, have passed this garrison bound for Limestone and the Rapids. The emigration is almost incredible. It is to be observed that no boats passed until the 10<sup>th</sup> March, on account of the severity of the winter and the river being shut.

Respecting the million of Acres, reserved by Congress at the mouth of the Ohio for the bounty Lands to the late Army you are pleased to observe the post-scripts of Major Ayllys letter dated at the Rapids, the 18<sup>th</sup> of May a copy of which is enclosed which is very favourable as to its Excellence. This intelligence was given to Major Ayllys by General Obanks who has himself travelled through that part of the country and would willingly have accepted the grant for his regiment there. Major Hamtranch denies the Lands on the Illinois river or the Wabash, but I believe the intelligence transmitted by Major Ayllys is to be depended upon and would therefore give it as in my opinion that we should not hesitate to accept the Lands, described in the Resolve of Congress beginning at the mouth of the Ohio &c.

The surveying of this tract of country however must necessarily be deferred until the result of the grand treaty is known and the temper of the savages perfectly ascertained.

In my letter of the 19<sup>th</sup> March I had the honor to inform you, that I had transmitted printed instructions to Major Ayllys to know the designs of the people below, accordingly Lieutenant Armstrong was dispatched for this purpose to the State of Franklin as they call it. So pleased to receive a copy of his report addressed to Major Ayllys. His Expences while on this service amounted to 92 dollars, which I have paid him out of the contingent money.

Major Doughty now takes off with him as Subaltern and 15 Privates in order to carry into execution the resolve of Congress of the 27 March 1788 respecting dismantling and demolishing Fort McIntosh, and he has my orders to erect a block house, in its vicinity. He will reconnoitre for an eligible position at or near the forks, which is about five miles from the mouth of the Big Beaver.

It is a long time since I was at the falls, if I recollect right it will be some difficulty in finding a proper position there, in which case the Blockhouse will be erected somewhere near the upper boarding about two miles up the Beaver.

I am sorry that the Legislature of New York have not yet passed the necessary Acts for raising their quota of Troops and reappointing their Officers. Pennsylvania has reappointed their Officers and State Commissions have some time since been forwarded to me by Council and a copy of the list of Officers reappointed by Connecticut will (agreeably to your instructions) be forwarded to Major Ayllys.

Lieutenant Sloan whom I detached from hence on the 19<sup>th</sup> March, returned from Post Vincennes and brought off with him from the rapids the remainder of the Commissioners goods. He returned on the 29<sup>th</sup> ultimo and the goods are all safely deposited at this Post ready for the ensuing Treaty.

It is with pain that I have to observe that some rascally vagabond Wabash Indians had the insolence to attack the party on their return from Post Vincennes to the Rapids and killed two of his men. The fire was instantly returned from the troops, but as the number of the Savages was uncertain the officer acted prudently in not landing.

They have an immense advantage in attacking boats ascending the river and indeed there can be no possible security unless our parties are strong enough to afford a good guard, on the shore. Be pleased to receive the enclosed copy of Lieutenant Sloans report, of his passage.

Major Hamtranch informs me that the Officers at the Post, have requested him to represent, their situation to me respecting their Subsistence. The place is indeed very extravagant if they were permitted to draw, a ration besides their Subsistence the Officers could be satisfied. I beg leave to represent this matter for your consideration.

I sincerely hope that the recruiting Officers are use all possible diligence in procuring good men and marching them quickly to the frontiers. Captain Ashton has been very fortunate at the Rapids, he has recruited almost the whole of his company 57 hearty rugged fellows. Major Hamtranch has made no progress in reorganizing Captain Smiths company. at the present time the following number of men are recruited.

Connecticut - - -    38
New York             46
Pennsylvania         88
Total                171

Major Doughty has my directions to hire at Fort Pitt (if practicable) two or three armorers as we have but one in the Corps & he is at the Rapids for the purpose of keeping the spare Arms & accoutrements in the best order possible.

If they are none to be had Major Doughty will do himself the honor of writing to you from Fort Pitt.

I shall be happy to hear that money can be obtained for the transportation of the Ordnance Stores, Medicines & Quarter masters Store and that they be forwarded as soon as possible, as we are in want of them, particularly the medicine.

After the conclusion of the Treaty if the Governor of the Western Territory should decline to go to the Illinois country he shall be furnished with an escort agreeably to your orders.

When the result of the Treaty is known I shall give you my ideas fully concerning a different arrangement of the Posts. I have apprehension that the information you have received concerning the navigation of Big Beaver Creek may not be altogether proper. A certain evidence of its not being navigable is that Mr. Duncan, & those who have been accustomed to send flour &c to Detroit have always sent it from [undecipherable] from McIntosh if the navigation had been practicable they would have sent it by land to Cuyahoga.

Lieutenant Beatty arrived at Fort Pitt on the 17<sup>th</sup> alto on the 20<sup>th</sup> ordered him to Venango to pay Captain Abarts command. He arrived here on the 8<sup>th</sup> inst. & is now engaged in paying his garrison. The sum of money which he brought on with him is very handsome & both Officers and Soldiers are much pleased & express great gratitude to you for your exertions in our behalf.

Colonel Otney who is kind enough to be the bearer of this letter will inform you of the progress made in cultivation by the Ohio Company. The respectable characters who are Engaged in this purchase by their industry & perseverance will most undoubtedly change the Wilderness into a paradise.

Gentlemen

The Assistant Commissioner to whom was referred the Petition of Joseph Spencer late a Major General in the service of the United States begs leave to report.

That in the Month of November 1777 Gen<sup>l</sup> Spencer received of M<sup>r</sup> Hancock Deputy Master General the sum of 13533 dollars for the use of the department in which he then commanded, it appears that by a letter from Jonathan Boul Est. Commissioner that the Sum of 13382 ¾ dollars of this money was paid to Peter Philips Deputy Commissary General, which leaves a balance of 3000 ¾ dollars to be accounted for by General Spencer.

That on the 10<sup>th</sup> June 1775 Congress granted the Additional pay of one hundred and sixty six dollars to a Major General commanding a separate department.

That General Spencer claims this additional pay from the 1<sup>st</sup> January 1777 to the 1<sup>st</sup> April 1779 which time he says he commanded the Army stationed at Rhode Island and its Vicinity, by order of the late commander in Chief.

That this claim being admitted (which the Assistant Commissioner is of opinion is proper) his pay for this service will amount to 2830 ¾ dollars which will still leave a balance due the United States of 176 9/16 dollars, cast at the rate of exchange by the Army Scale to 88 9/16 dollars due.

That General Spencer voluntarily acknowledges that the Monies remaining in his hands was by him returned in March or April 1779 to the Loan Office of the State of Connecticut

for which he received Loan Office Certificates to the amount of 800 dollars Specie.

And by the tenor of his petition the Assistant Commissioner is led to believe that General Spencer considers himself entitled to the additional pay on Specie allowed by the aforesaid act of Congress and that the Monies remaining in his hands should be reduced to Specie Value.

To this your Assistant Commissioner begs leave to object, the following reasons viz

1<sup>st</sup> That on this principal the petitioner would become a Creditor of the United States and in lieu of refunding the balance aforementioned would be entitled to the sum of 1749 ¾ dollars Specie the difference between the Monies remaining in his hands and the pay due.

2. That it appears by the Books of this Office that on or about this day he retired from service he was paid the full balance of his pay as Major General.

3. That as he conceived himself entitled to the Extra pay allowed by the aforesaid Act of Congress, he had it in his power to apply that pay to the Monies remaining in his hands and to refund to the United States the balance found due.

4<sup>th</sup> That in lieu of receiving the sum of 800 ¾ dollars (the last payment made him as Major General) he should, or might only have received 1779 ¾ dollars.

5<sup>th</sup> That Major General Spencer having resigned his Commission previous to the 1<sup>st</sup> April 1779 is precluded from any benefit arising on depreciation of pay.

The Assistant Commissioner is therefore of opinion that the petitioner should account for the balance due & that in consequence of the United States paying interest on

By the United States in Congress Assembled
August 12<sup>th</sup> 1788

Resolved That the Executives of Virginia and Pennsylvania be requested to give orders to the Militia of their respective frontiers to hold themselves in readiness to unite with the federal troops in such operations as the Governor of the Western Territory may judge necessary for the protection of the Inhabitants; and that on application of the said Governor, the said executives be requested to give orders that parts of their said Militia not exceeding one thousand for Virginia and five hundred for Pennsylvania be embodied; and take such positions as the Commanding Officer of the Federal Troops shall direct for acting in conjunction with the said federal troops in protecting and defending the frontiers against any hostilities commenced or meditated by the Indians, and in making such expeditions should they continue hostile as the said Governor shall direct for repelling such hostilities. That the Militia which shall be called into actual Service of the United States for the defence of the frontier inhabitants or the purposes of any expedition, shall be paid supported and equipped by the States from which the same may be respectively called, and that such State be credited for the same out of the existing Specie requisitions, so far as such expenditures shall be for pay and rations, which are to be computed on the Federal Establishments for Similar fermices; provided that no charge for such Service shall be valid unless Supported by musters made by an Officer of the Federal Troop, agreeably to the orders of the Commanding Officer.

That the said Governor be informed that the foregoing Resolution having been taken by Congress on an apprehension that a War may be inevitable, he is to consider it, as their earnest desire that all hostile measures be avoided. unless rendered indispensible to the safety and protection of the Citizens of the United States.

RESOLVED That the Commissioners for Indian Treaties be instructed in the farther purchases of Indian rights to lands to extend the same as far as to them shall appear for the advantage of the United States, upon considering all circumstances any former instructions prescribing certain limits notwithstanding.

By the United States in Congrefs

A PROCLAMATION.

WHEREAS the United States in Congrefs affembled, by their Commiffioners duly appointed and authorifed, did on the Twenty-eighth Day of November, One Thoufand Seven Hundred and Eighty-five, at Hopewell, on the Keowee, conclude Articles of a Treaty with all the Cherokees, and among other things ftipulated and engaged by Article fourth, "That the Boundary allotted to the Cherokees for their Hunting Grounds, between the faid Indians and the Citizens of the United States, within the limits of the United States of America, is and fhall be the following, viz: 'Beginning at the mouth of Duck river on the Tenefee; thence running north-eaft to the ridge dividing the waters running into Cumberland from thofe running into the Tenefee; thence eaftwardly along the faid ridge to a north-eaft line to be run, which fhall ftrike the river Cumberland, forty miles above Nafhville; thence along the faid line to the river; thence up the faid river to the ford where the Kentucky road croffes the river; thence to Campbell's line near to Cumberland Gap; thence to the mouth of Claud's Creek on Holftein; thence to the Chimney-Top Mountain; thence to Cany Creek, near the mouth of Big Lime Stone on Nolichucky; thence a foutherly courfe fix miles to a mountain; thence fouth to the North-Carolina line; thence along the South-Carolina Indian Boundary, and along the fame fouthward over the top of the the Oconee Mountain, till it fhall ftrike Tugalos river; thence a direct line to the top of the Currohoe Mountain; thence to the head of the fouth fork of the Oconee river." And by Article fifth, that "if any Citizen of the United States, or other perfon not being an Indian, fhould attempt to fettle on any of the lands weftward or fouthward of the faid Boundary, which were allotted to the Indians for their Hunting Grounds, or having fettled previoufly to concluding the faid Treaty, and not removing from the fame within fix months after the ratification of the faid Treaty, fuch perfon fhould forfeit the protection of the United States, and that the Indians might punifh him or not as they pleafe; provided, that the faid fifth Article fhould not extend to the People fettled between the fork of French Broad and Holftein rivers, whofe fituation fhould be tranfmitted to the United States in Congrefs affembled for their decifion thereon, which the Indians agreed to abide by." AND WHEREAS it has been reprefented to Congrefs, that feveral diforderily Perfons fettled on the Frontiers of North-Carolina, in the vicinity of Chota, have, in open violation of the faid Treaty, made intruſions upon the faid Indian Hunting Grounds, and committed many unprovoked outrages upon the faid Cherokees, who by the faid Treaty have put themfelves under the protection of the United States, which proceedings are highly injurious and difrefpectful to the authority of the Union, and it being the firm determination of Congrefs to protect the faid Cherokees in their rights, according to the true intent and meaning of the faid Treaty; THE UNITED STATES IN CONGRESS ASSEMBLED, have therefore thought fit to iffue, and they DO hereby iffue this their PROCLAMATION, ftrictly forbidding all fuch unwarrantable intruſions, and hoftile proceedings againft the faid Cherokees; and enjoining all thofe who have fettled upon the faid Hunting Grounds of the faid Cherokees, to depart with their Families and Effects without lofs of time, as they fhall anfwer their difobedience to the injunctions and prohibitions expreffed in this Refolution at their peril: Provided, that this Proclamation fhall not be conftued as requiring the removal of the People fettled between the fork of French Broad and Holftein rivers, referred to in the faid Treaty: Provided alfo, that nothing contained in this Proclamation fhall be confidered as affecting the Territorial Claims of the State of North-Carolina.

*DONE in Congrefs, this Firft Day of September, in the Year of our Lord One Thoufand Seven Hundred and Eighty-eight, and of our Sovereignty and Independence the Thirteenth.*

CYRUS GRIFFIN, Prefident.

CHARLES THOMSON, Secretary.

Norwich, 8<sup>th</sup> Sep<sup>t</sup> 1801

Dear Sir —

The other day when I was at N York, my Son there was accidently meeting with unexpected Disappointments, and being in great haste, I returned home. By your attention to my application, by way of Correspondence, I have no notion that you would wish to destroy me as an individual, unpaid, but that you would wish otherwise, that I be Compensated and rewarded —

At the request of Gov<sup>r</sup>. Trumbull and Council I commenced in public service of the United States, immediately after the battle of Bunker Hill, attended the wounded there, & Continued through all the burdens of the War — In 1777 April 11<sup>th</sup> was appointed Surg<sup>n</sup>. Gen<sup>l</sup>. of the Military Hospitals of Congress, & in that Character served till the arrangement of the Hospital department Oct<sup>r</sup>. 7<sup>th</sup> 1780 when I was appointed as Physician & Surgeon, not having the rank and Standing as heretofore, (no wrong) reduced & derangy &c, but at the pleasure of Congress, however the Circumstances, and State of Hospital affairs were such that I continued in actual Service to the 18<sup>th</sup> June 1781 when I declined to private practice as P<sup>r</sup> Doc<sup>tr</sup>. Cochran's certificate — entitled to have & receive the same pay, amount of Commutation and emoluments as other Citizens so deranged. — As to my letter of the 1<sup>st</sup> June 1781 to Doc<sup>tr</sup>. Cochran it never entered my heart any such thing as resignation, as any thing looking like it, there is nothing more contained in that letter than an abso-

lute refusal of that appointment, and as the all wise protecting God would have it neither Congress nor the Board of War ever noticed Doc<sup>t</sup>. Cochran's report it was a misunderstanding of his, and by his wrongly applied in his letter of the 5<sup>th</sup> July. On his return of August 1<sup>st</sup> 1781 — Congress and the Board treated it as such (un noticed) continuing me as one of the fifteen Surgeons (appointed by them) till 7<sup>th</sup> January 1782 — If the Board of War, or Congress had ever acted on P<sup>r</sup> report, any way, or appointed any one in my stead, perhaps something might have been said on the subject, but as they never did, there is an end, allowing they had acted on report it could not have appeared against me, Sam invited by their doings, as a deranged, retired officer, not only so, but from their continuing me from the beginning to the end, in that sense, (in every other sense settled) there is no going from it, providence has ordered otherwise if the Journals are compleat. —

Take my letter of J. B. of June to Doctor Cochran (which is the letter referr'd to) read it over and over again; make the most of it, you possibly can, you will find no resignation there, or any where else, things of this nature ought to be explicit, particular so; its not in the power of the head of any Department to make reports & returns of the officers relative to resignation without being properly Authorised, Doctor Cochran had no Design to injure me, I dont blame him, I esteem him as a Gentleman of Him and a friend, his conduct will suf-

fer me to say there was nothing [strikethrough: more] in that letter than a refusal of that appointment, wrote in spirit, I was rested and mortified, knowing that I was deranged, not by my Desire, or wish, but that I was at the pleasure of Congress, & that I had a right to retire, being entitled to all the emoluments mentioned heretofore. What a curiosity it is to talk of resignation, and how that I had forfeited every thing in that Channel, when I served the whole war, or near its close, what had I to resign, I had neither Commission nor Warrant, nor never had received any, on that appointment —

You will take this matter, with your care & Deliberate order as you would be done by, pray Don't put [undecipherable] to Congress, by way of petition, why am I Deserving of all this trouble, you cant but be satisfied, you are every way authorized to close with me, & every Voucher necessary, if after all this, there be any hesitation, apply the question, they shall be answered and explained. Dear Sir pray favor the securities and Warr<sup>t</sup>. me with your correspondance

Your friend and
Hum<sup>l</sup>. Serv<sup>t</sup>.
P. Turner —

M<sup>r</sup>. Howell, Commissioner

Sir,

Prince Negroe enlisted into the Continental Service in the year 1777 during the War and belonged to the Second Connecticut Regiment and served faithfully untill by sickness lost one eye and was by other infirmities, brought on him while in the service rendered incapable to do camp duty & was transfered in to the Corps of Invalids and sent to New London to do Garrison duty, where he was left without any Officer to direct him in his duty, and he applied to Col. John Durkee who was at that time at Norwich and commanding officer in that quarter, who gave him liberty to go home and remain untill further orders, where he remained untill Peace took place and received no Orders nor discharge. — He is an honest inoffensive ignorant person & is justly entitled to some aid from the country that has had his Services. I have taken pains & made myself acquainted with the above affairs & facts & can say they are true. I want from your office certificates of his transfer to the Corps of Invalids & what return was made of him afterwards, & whatever else may appear in your office necessary to enable him to give to the Board proper to have him, a proper & fair consideration of his case.

I have no interest in this affair but a compassionate feeling for a poor Soldier & if consistent with right wish him that reward his services & Sufferings intitle him to receive — the time to apply for relief will soon expire therefore I am obliged to urge for an answer as soon as possible. the bearer of this I have requested to call & take it

Sam<sup>d</sup>

The indisposition of M<sup>r</sup> Knox will not permit him at present to continue his correspondence, tho I am in hopes that his complaint, which is more painful than dangerous, will in the course of a few days be so far removed as to enable him in some degree again to attend to it. — Your letter to him of the 25<sup>th</sup> ultimo, enclosing an estimate of expences for the intended march of Lieutenant Pratt, has been received — I have the honor to inform you that due attention has been and will be had to its contents.

Lieutenant Pratt is not yet arrived — he is hourly expected — Orders for his immediate embarkation at West Point were forwarded to him from the War-Office the 25<sup>th</sup> and 27<sup>th</sup> ultimo, and further instructions he must have received by Captain Price, who, in all probability reached that garrison the 30<sup>th</sup> —

There appears to be no difficulty in the business — Discretion and Economy shall attend this object.

As soon as Lieutenant Pratt arrives he shall immediately be ordered to sail for New Brunswick, where he will receive his final instructions — I myself will also repair thither to muster and inspect his men, and see that they march from thence without delay.

The 400 suits of Uniform-clothing, which you were pleased to direct, should be minutely inspected by me, and afterwards properly packed in boxes, and sent to New Brunswick — These directions have been strictly attended to — The clothing is contained in 24 boxes, well made and secured, and properly marked, and the vessel that has it on board sailed this morning — Proper care will be taken of the clothing, when it arrives at New Brunswick, and that it goes forward with Lieutenant Pratt.

We have found it necessary to apply to M<sup>r</sup> Hill for ten new tents — They are made, and of good materials.

Ensign Luse has been ordered to repair to New Brunswick, and to be ready to march

Comptrollers Office

Hartford Novem<sup>r</sup> 3, 1788.

Sir,

I have received your favour of the 22<sup>d</sup> of Oct<sup>r</sup> last relative to the depreciation accounts of this State and finds that your construction of the Act of Congress of the 10<sup>th</sup> of April 1780 is such as I expected, though I have no doubt but that claims upon the Union as equitable as those of Connecticut will be finally admitted —

I now enclose copies of sundry Acts of the General Assembly and Governor & Council of Safety, to enable you to form an idea of the engagements entered into by this State, to their Levy of the Army, and of the mode by which they have been fulfilled — By these Acts you will perceive that immediately, upon raising the Army, the State undertook to supply cloathing and refreshments at specie prices which were delivered by State Commissaries appointted for that purpose and that the families of officers and soldiers were also furnished with supplies at a stated price upon depositing a sum in nominal money equal to the specie value of the supplies which they were entitled to receive — The expenditures for these purposes reduced by the same

would greatly exceed the sum which availed to the credit of the State in the settlement of the Army Accounts — But as the expenditures were made in consequence of a system which had never been authorized by any Act of Congress and had been by mutual consent of Committees from the State and the Army fully adjusted — I imagined that those accounts could not with fairness and & propriety be exhibited — If you judge differently, I will not decline the task of stating them, because I am sensible that the examination of those accounts will evince that the State have lost great sums by their mode of supplying the Army, although their system was as œconomical as the situation of our affairs would then permit —

The receipts for the balances which were found due upon an adjustment are in this Office but as they are filed in the order in which the applications were made for the securities, a different arrangement will be necessary to enable you to compare them with the accounts — When this proper arrangement can be made they shall be transmitted if requested —

I have the honour to be, with great respect your ob<sup>t</sup> & humble Serv<sup>t</sup>

Joseph Howell Jr<sup>y</sup>  
Commissy Army Acts<sup>t</sup>    [signature: Oliver Wolcott]

Freind & Brother

We received your Talk likewise the Resolves of Congress dated 1 Sep 1788 likewise a Copy of a Letter from the Governor of North Carolina to you and the proclamation from Congress, all which affords us much satisfaction that we have on your and our friends who tells us the truth and endeavours to do us Justice it likewise gives us much satisfaction to hear from Congress and Virginia

Brother

You have opened our Eye and likewise our hearts the Talks we receive from you pleases us much that Congress is determined to have our hunting Grounds open so that our young men may hunt and will also to purchase Goods of our traders to Cloath our selves and furnishen our hunts; Grounds was very severely viewed gives us the greatest satisfaction that it will be soon enlarged as appears by the proclamation from Congress it likewise gives us much satisfaction that we have a view of returning from the Woods where we have been drove and once more sitting again in our old Towns which we wished to do When we are certain that the white people have quited our hunting Grounds —

Brother

It affords us much satisfaction that a friendly sick will soon take place you informs us if you have wrot to the Governor of North Carolina to fix a time and place for that purpose as at that time we will talk over all matters and smoke the pipe of friendship.

The headman and Warriors from the middle towns was on their way to Ustinare but being informed that it was good Talks and that white Birds and Tobacco was sent from Ustinare to all the Towns in the Nation they went back fearing that some of their Young men might go out again and as one of the head men are determined to put a stop to all Hostility and for the time to come live like Brothers and friends as long as the sun shines and water runs

The following Talk comes from the Little Turkey —

Freind & Brother

Your talk I have heard which gives us the greatest satisfaction likewise all our beloved men in my part of the Nation it is a Talk from you our great beloved Brother who thou informed is appointed by Congress to see Justice done us we have now heard from our beloved Brothers from New York likewise Virginia which now opens our Eye and hearts for they are the men that we must abide by your Talks are good and your friendship we look on ensures for the good and your land, I have seen the Resolves of Congress likewise the proclamation for all the white people Settled on our hunting Grounds to go of without —

loss of time.

Freind & Brother

I have the satisfaction to inform you that Alexander McGilvery chief of the Creek Nation has taken your Talks likewise the Talks of from Congress and Virginia and means to hold them fast and when they meet will take his white Brothers by the hand as well and Those live in peace and friendship as long as the Grass grows and the water runs —

A Copy of this Talk you will please to send to Congress and Virginia it will be the more better every thing can be sifted to your entire satisfaction — because some of your beloved men are out hunting as for the present it is impossible for us to send them to Ustinare at this time because they are scattered through the Nation but they shall be restored to their friends as soon as possible we shall have them all collected together Orders are given out that they may be with that my people should not be restied upon hereafter for us their prisoners all they will be oblige to acquaint their friends and hope they will make themselves easy for a short time.
