Sir

Your polite and obliging letter of the 9<sup>th</sup> Ulto is now before me; I observe your desire is, to be informed of the whole process of raising and fitting Hemp for use: I shall readily inform you of my own method in the cultivation of this usefull plant, and shall be happy if you are gratified, and any person benefited thereby. —

The Soil I chuse for raising Hemp, is a light rich mould, as free from Stones or gravel as possible, and not any way impregnated with Clay; Care is taken to have the Soil thoroughly manured & once well ploughed in the fall of the year. In the Spring the soil is ploughed two or three times more, and as often harrowed with an Iron toothed harrow, in order to seperate the particles of Earth, and leave it as light as possible; then a light Brush harrow is drawn by one horse over the ground, by which means is is leveled so as to receive the seed equally; after which it is marked out for sowing in the same manner that Barley [undecipherable: Boats?] are generally sown, calculated if the soil is very good at three bushels per Acre, if but middling good at two and half bushels per Acre; the seed is always harrowed in [immediately after sowing] with a fine Iron toothed harrow, and nothing is suffered to pass over it afterwards, lest by treading or otherwise it might be injured. — The Seed must be of the last years growth, and will be benefitted by laying in the Cellar a few weeks previous to its being sowed. —

In general I sow my Seed about the middle of May, (being governed by the season) a little sooner or later will do — my Hemp is commonly fit to pull by the 8<sup>th</sup> or 10<sup>th</sup> of August; which is known by the male Hemp becoming whitish just at the time when the Farina passes off; this is easily discovered by its smoaking when agitated by the wind, or jarred by a Stick. ——

After the Hemp is pulled, it is Spread on the ground where it grew, about one Inch thick, and what that will not receive is carried off to other ground, and after laying two or three days, is turned with a small pole about Six feet long; then receiving one or two days more dew, it is bound into Bundles of about fifteen or eighteen inches in Circumference, and immediately housed from wil[d] untill convenient time offers to put it into [the] water for Rotting, which is done as soon as other business will admit. —— There being a small Stream of water that runs through my Farm, I have erected a Dam which enables me to flow a pond about five or six feet high, wherein the Hemp is laid (much in the same manner that Flax is laid for Rotting) and after covering it with Straw to [keep it down, the plank] [bottoms] being placed thereon, the Dam gate is shut down, and the Hemp being overflowed Remains till it is properly Retted, which is done in six or seven days, if put in the latter end of August or beginning of September — The weather being generally warm at that Season of the Year. If put into the water the latter end of September or beginning of October, I have let it lay Twelve days. — If the latter end of October or beginning of November, Twenty days, unless the weather should be uncommon warm for the Season, In that case I have found it necessary to be Removed Sooner — but have made a point of attending to the heat or cold of the weather; as when the water is warm the Hemp will get a proper Rot much sooner than when it is otherways. —

My practice has been to draw the Water from the Hemp Twenty four hours before the taking it up, leaving the weight on the Hemp, in order that it may be well drained, as in that case it is much better handled; then it is Removed to a dry piece of ground and Spread about two inches thick, and after Remaining a week or ten days in that Situation, it is turned over; and in eight or ten days after taken up, tyed in Bundles & Removed into the Barn; where it Remains till I have leisure time to break & swingle it out, for which purpose I have always found clear cold weather to be the best. —— My Hemp is broke & swingled much in the same manner that Flax is done, excepting that the first breaking is done in a coarser break the teeth or flatts being nearly four Inches apart; then a common Flax break answers well, being carefully Swingled it is fit for use. — A man that understands the breaking & Swingling Hemp, will clean one 50 ℔ per day. ——

My practice for raising Seed hath been to set apart some of my best grown Hemp for that purpose, then pull up the male & female Hemp for about 18 Inches in width so that a man may pass through, leaving the other Hemp in beds about Six feet in width, that two men (one on each Side) may reach in their hands and pull up all the male, without injuring the Seed bearing Hemp; this process is performed when the general pulling is done in August — the female Hemp must Stand till the Seed is fully ripe, which is known by its turning brown; in wet weather I have been obliged to let it Stand till the middle of October before it was fit to pull — after it is pulled it must be tied up in Bundles like the other Hemp, and carefully leyd up against a fence, or if that is not convenient it may be layed on the ground and after one or two days Sun it may be beat out in the same manner that Flax Seed is beat out, striking it lightly, then expose the other Side to the Sun one or two days, after which give it a thorough batting, and spread the Seed with all the leaves &c in a dry place for some time, then thresh it with a light flail, or rub it by hand, either way, till the Seed is all out, and after re-winnowing, put it in a dry place for sowing the next year. —— The Seed bearing Hemp requires a few days longer to rot than the other, owing to the thickness of the Bark and the greater quantity of glutinous Substance occasioned by its longer Standing.

You wish to know what manure is best, I have always preferred the old to the new, more especially if horse or cow dung, tho new will do, and much the better if ploughed in, in the fall.

With respect to the quantity of Hemp Raised on an acre of ground — it varies from Six to Twelve Hundred weight; much depending on the quality of the Soil and the manner of preparing it. — I have the last Season tryed the experiment of Raising Hemp on a piece of dyked Marsh, the Salt water having been kept out better than one Year, I had a small part dug carefully, & manured with some old Dung that was well mixt with Sand, the Hemp grew to full height and proved to be of the best kind: this encouragement has occasioned my preparing a larger piece for further tryal the next year. —— You enquire the expence of Cultivating an acre of Hemp &c this is not in my power at present to ascertain, great part of the business being done at leisure [when] the time could be best Spared. I would just observe that I can raise two or three Acres yearly on my small Farm without interferring much with other Business. —— The price of Hemp here is Fifty five pounds, ₤ Ton, the Bounty given by the State to encourage the Culture of this usefull plant is Twelve pounds, making in the whole better than Two Hundred & Twenty Dollars p̃ Ton — The high price of Hemp together with the Bounty, bids fair to establish its growth here; and I am fully Satisfied from my own experience, that at the present day no branch of Agriculture (where land is found Suitable) can be carried on to so great advantage as that of Raising Hemp, and I have no doubt that our Farmers will soon be convinced of the truth of this Observation — it having been found by experience both in Europe and America that the growing of Hemp rather enriches the Soil than otherways, this also will have its weight. —— Several experiments will be made on Cultivating and cleaning Hemp the next year; if any advantage accrues therefrom, I shall do myself the honor of communicating it to you as early as possible, in the mean time believe me to be with great esteem —— Your —

39811:
[David Sales Esq<sup>r</sup>

Thomaston 3 April
1789

To Major General Henry Knox
New York]

David Sales.          Thomaston April 3<sup>d</sup> 1789

Worthy Sir,                                                   27.

I have your favour of the 10<sup>th</sup> January per Capt. Nose; am well pleased, that an Establishment is making at the Fort and Blockthouse Farm, and hope it will answer the Expectations of all concerned. I have, with others, assisted Capt. Nose in procuring such Fencing Stuff as was thought necessary for securing the Improvements the present Year. Likewise, have informed People of their now having an opportunity of discharging their Debts to him as your Agent, according to their Wishes expressed.

I have permitted Capt. Nose to take a Copy of your Letter to me of the 4<sup>th</sup> Octo. last; he seems to be a Man of a good Disposition and Genius: I shall endeavour to assist him in all Matters that appear to me likely to promote your Interest, in which I expect his is also included.

I have had some Conversation with Waterman Thomas Esq; and with Jacob Ludwig Esq; concerning the affairs at Waldoborough, and expect further to pursue the matter in the Course of this Month; but find neither the Germans, nor the People in Thomaston have quite given up their Hope and Expectation of a Decision of the General Court in their favour on the Petitions preferred, which are committed, with Col<sup>o</sup>. Saltonstall's Petition, to a joint Committee, and referred to the next Session; therefore a further Time seems to be necessary to convince their Minds of some of the utility of their coming to a settlement with you; others there are who seem heartily to desire a Settlement, but postpone it through fear of being censured by their Neighbours.

I have made enquiry concerning the Sales of Lands in Warren for the Payment of Taxes, and find there is no danger from that Quarter, as the Assessments and Sales were none of them conducted conformably to Law, so as to give the Purchasers a Title, should they be disposed to contend for it.

I have made Agreements with several Persons and given them Permission to occupy Lots, some in Warren, Waldsborough, and lower St Georges, now Cushing, but find most of the Land is claimed by some Person; however apprehend there will be no great difficulty in disposing of the Land for valuable Considerations, when those Persons that have agreed are accommodated; but among them I expect there will be claims clashing on one another. I shall now attend to that Business with diligence, having been much confined at home through the Winter by Sickness in my Family.

Many Persons here, sensible of your Benevolence, have desired to be remembered to you with Gratitude.

I am Worthy Sir,
your sincere, obedient,
and humb. Servant
David Willis

Henry Knox Esquire
New York

39814:
New Yorks 11<sup>th</sup> April 1789

Madam!

Being this day at the Board of Treasury M<sup>r</sup> Osgood stated some circumstances relative to Bills of Exchange drawn in favor of your late Husband Colonel Palfrey in December 1780. and which it is highly proper for you to be informed of, in order that you may take the necessary steps to obtain that compensation which on the present aspect of the affair seems to be your due.

The whole amount of the Bills of Exchange which Colonel Palfrey received from the public as a Balance due him was 3.200 dollars.—

These Bills were issued from the Office of Thomas Smith Loan Officer of Pennsylvania on the 14<sup>th</sup> of December 1780 on B. Franklin Esq<sup>r</sup> at Paris and were of the following Denominations. To wit,

Two of 1000 dollars. each
Two of 400. dols  1<sup>st</sup>
Two of 200.      2<sup>d</sup>. —

One of the 400 dollar Bills were endorsed by M<sup>r</sup> Palfrey to Jonathan Nesbitt & Co of Philadelphia and accepted by B Franklin in Paris the 3 of May 1781.

One of the 200 Bills were also endorsed W<sup>m</sup> Palfrey to the same and accepted in Paris the 19<sup>th</sup> of March

March 1781 — The Alienation of these two Bills were undoubtedly proper, and Col<sup>o</sup> Palfrey probably received a full compensation for them.

But the others, to wit — two of 1000 dollars each, one of 400. and one of 200 all being the 3<sup>d</sup> of the felts and amounting to 2 600 dollars were endorsed as follows

"Pay to Cuming & M<sup>c</sup>Carty or order for account of W<sup>m</sup> Palfrey & Self as W<sup>m</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Carty and C<sup>o</sup>     2 Omit 3 Sept<sup>r</sup> 1781

(Signed) Wm M<sup>c</sup>Carty

Accepted 10<sup>th</sup> Sept<sup>r</sup> 1781 B Franklin"

Now — W<sup>m</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Carty became possessed of the said Bills does not appear, or whether any business was transacted between him and your Husband.

As the said Bills were not endorsed by your Husband, it is presumed that as he was going to France he might have remitted the thirds of each Jett to M<sup>r</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Carty knowing they could not be legally paid without his own Signature.

It is to be particularly observed that the Bills which your Husband actually endorsed were accepted the one on the 3 of February and the other on the 19<sup>th</sup> of March 1781 whel[e]as those presented by M<sup>r</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Carty were not accepted

until the 10<sup>th</sup> of September following and were all the thirds of the felts — But it is clear that the said Bills ought not to have been paid but on the actual endorsement of William Palfrey or his legal Representatives — and it appears probable that you as Executrix or Administratrix will have good grounds for an action for the recovery of the amount of 2.600 dollars.

It will be a matter requiring due consideration against whom you bring your Suit. If you bring it against the United States and recover, it is possible you may be paid in Certificates and besides the United States are in possession of the very bills which have been paid by them — Whether it would be better to bring the action against the Prayer of the Bills I cannot say — W<sup>m</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Carty if my information be true has been unfortunate and is unable to pay — so so nothing would be gained by bringing the action against him.

As the original felts consisted of four bills of the same tenor and date you may perhaps have one for which the publick is still liable — But these are only suggestions of which your Lawyers will fully consider — The Bills paid are in possession of the Board of Treasury who I presume would on your application previously to any Suit being instituted deliver authentic copies with the endorsements and acceptances.

I sincerely hope Madam that this information

may be of substantial Service to you and your father's children. If I can render you any further assistance I will cheerfully do it.

I am Madam

Your most Obedient
Humble Servant

Knox

M<sup>rs</sup> Palfrey

The Speech of Colonel George Morgan to the Delawares, Shawnees & Cherokees at his first Meeting them at New Madrid the [blank] day of April 1789.

My Loving Children

Monsieur L'Aurimier & Monsieur Nouvrain, have already informed you of the order of Don Manuel Peris his Majesty's Governor at the Illinois, who I am & the Business I have come here report. They have just now told you that I am sent here by the King of Spain to settle a Number of People whom you now see here & many others who will soon be here, on Six Lands from Cape S<sup>t</sup> Comme to the River S<sup>t</sup> Thomas & from thence back or Westward two Degrees of Longitude or about [three] days March West from the Missisippi—

[margin notation: Nations. The good Friends the Delawares, who have accompanied me to this Place will tell you all the News from your Five Men up the Ohio River & of the Lakes. They will tell you of the Business they came here for.]

As I have now become your Father & all those who accompany me have become Subjects to the King of Spain, I will now tell you my Mind freely to which I desire you will listen with Attention.

I have not come here to drive you the Delawares, Shawnees & Cherokees away from here. On the contrary I wish you all to sit down near to me that I may be useful to you & to your Women & Children, I protect you & them from your Enemies should any offer to injure you.

I see that you have seated yourselves in this Country to make Corn & to hunt for the Support of your Women & Children. For this you are indebted to his Majesty the good King of Spain, & you may depend that you will continue to enjoy this favour so long as you continue to deserve it.

I will survey your [Corn field &] sufficient Lands to your Use wherever you have Settled. I you fill have liberty to hunt. I will use the Game in this Country. Whilst you do this live in Peace & take good Care of your Women & Children. I & my People will improve the Land & plant Corn, Wheat, Tobacco & so that you may buy our Provisions & the Merchandize we bring here in exchange for your Beaver, Deer Skins &c. for I do not mean to allow any White Men to hunt or chase away the Game. When I am hungry I may kill & eat, but I will not allow any White Men to hunt [time] for the sake of Skins or Furs.

On your Part, my Children, you must take good Care of your Women & Children & live in Peace with all Nations. Should any come here to Strike you I will take the Tomahawk from them.

There is one thing I shall be particularly insist upon. It is that you charge your Men to be civil to all my People & not on any Account to Steal a Horse from them [nor take] any of their Property. I will promise that my People here be kind to yours & not take any of your Prop[erty.]

As I mean to kindle a Council Fire at this Place, I desire you to appoint some wise Men to assist one in taking Care of it, that your Women & Children may live without Fear & that we may forever keep a clear Fire for all Nations to come & smoke their Pipes at.

"An Indian War disagreeable at all times would be peculiarly distressing in the present embarrassed state of the Public Finances therefore it must be avoided if possible consistently with the interest and dignity of the United States.

I should be happy to concur in any proper mode in order that the warrants might distributed with the greatest facility — But the rules established on this point appear to be necessary, in order to guard as well the individuals, as the public from injury.

Boston July 23: 1789.

O Sir,

I have received the letter you did me the honor to write me the 15.<sup>th</sup> Instant, the apology you condescended to make for not answering mine of the 20.<sup>th</sup> of May afforded me the most sensible pleasure, as it convinced me I was not mistaken when I addressed myself to you.

When first I addressed myself to you on this subject, I hoped some within your province might be added; — I am extreme-ly obliged to you for the interest you take in my concerns, and should I hear of any particular place, I shall again take the freedom of applying to you. I am apprehensive that my distance from the Seat of Government will prevent my obtaining information in time.

I beg Sir you will forgive the trouble I am to you — But the Military look to you as their patron. I am

Sir

With the sincerest attachment
Your much obliged Servant

Constant Freeman j:<sup>r</sup>

Article 3<sup>d</sup>. The Creek Nation shall deliver as soon as practicable, to the Commanding Officer of the Troops of the United States, stationed at the Rock landing on the Oconee River, all citizens of the United States, white inhabitants or negroes, who are now prisoners in any part of the said Nation. And if any such prisoners or Negroes should not be so delivered, on or before the first day of June ensuing, the Governor of Georgia may empower three persons to repair to the said Nation in order to claim and receive such prisoners and negroes.

Article 4<sup>th</sup>. The boundary between the Citizens of the United States and the Creek Nation, is and shall be from where the old line Strikes the river Savannah thence up the said river to a place on the most northern branch of the same, commonly called the Keowee where a North east line, to be drawn from the top of the Oconee Mountain shall intersect; thence along the said line in a South west direction to Tugelo river; thence to the top of the Currahee mountains; thence to the head or Source of the main South branch of the Oconee River called the Appalachee; thence down the middle of the said main South branch and river Oconee to its confluence with the Oakmulge, which form the river Altamaha; and thence down the middle of the said Altamaha to the old line on the said river, and thence along the said old line to the River S<sup>t</sup> Mary's.

And in order to preclude forever, all disputes relatively to the head or Source of the main South branch of the River Oconee, at the place where it shall be intersected by the line aforesaid from the Currahee mountains, the same shall be ascertained by an able Surveyor on the part of the United States, who shall be assisted by three old Citizens of Georgia, who may be appointed by the Governor of the said State, and three old Creek chiefs to be appointed by the said Nation and the said Surveyor, Citizens and Chiefs shall assemble for this purpose, on the first day of October, one thousand Seven hundred and ninety one, at the [Rock] landing on the said River Oconee, and thence proceed to ascertain the said head or Source of the main South branch of the said River, at the place where it shall be intersected by the line aforesaid to be drawn from the Currahee Mountain. And in order that the said boundary shall be rendered distinct and well known, it [shall] be marked by a line of [posts or trees?] at least twenty feet wide, and trees [to be] chopped on each side from the said Currahee Mountain to the head or Source of the said main South branch of the Oconee River and thence along the margin of the said main South branch and River Oconee for the distance of twenty miles or as much farther as may be necessary to mark distinctly the said boundary. And in order to extinguish forever, all claims of the Creek Nation or any part thereof, to any of the land lying to the northward and eastward of the boundary herein described, it is hereby agreed in addition to the considerations heretofore made for the said land, that the United States will cause certain valuable Indian goods now in the State of Georgia, to be delivered to the said Creek Nation, and the said United States will also cause the Sum of one thousand and five hundred dollars to be paid annually to the said Creek Nation. And the Under signed Kings, Chiefs and Warriors, do hereby for themselves and the whole Creek Nation, their heirs and descendants, for the considerations abovementioned, release, quit claim; relinquish; and cede all the Land to the northward and eastward of the boundary herein described.

Article 5<sup>th</sup>. The United States [guarantee] by guarantee, to the Creek Nation all their Lands within the limits of the United States to the Westward and Southward of the boundary described in the preceding Article.

Article 6<sup>th</sup>. If any citizen of the United States or other person not being an Indian, shall attempt to settle on any of the Creek's lands, such person shall forfeit the protection of the United States and the Creeks may punish him or not as they please.

Article 7<sup>th</sup>. No citizen or inhabitant of the United States shall attempt to hunt or destroy the game on the Creek Lands. Nor shall any such citizen or inhabitant go into the Creek Country without a passport first obtained from the Governor of some one of the United States, or the Officer of the Troops of the United States commanding at the nearest post on the frontiers, or such other person as the President of the United States may from time to time, authorize to grant the same.

Article 8<sup>th</sup>. If any Creek Indian or Indians, or person, residing among them, or who shall take refuge in their Nation, shall commit a robbery or murder or other capital crime on any of the citizens or inhabitants of the United States, the Creek nation, or town or tribe, to which such offender or offenders may belong, shall be bound to deliver him or them up to be punished according to the laws of the United States.

Article 9<sup>th</sup>. If any citizen or inhabitant of the United States, or of either of the territorial districts of the United States, shall go into any town, settlement, or territory belonging to the Creek Nation of Indians, and shall there commit any crime upon or trespass against the person or property of any peaceable and friendly Indian or Indians, which if committed within the jurisdiction of any State or within the jurisdiction of either of the said districts, against a citizen or white inhabitant thereof, would be punishable by the Laws of such State or district; Such offender or offenders shall be subject to the same punishment, and shall be proceeded against in the same manner, as if the offence had been committed within the jurisdiction of the State or district to which he or they may belong against a citizen or white inhabitant thereof.

Article 10<sup>th</sup>. In cases of violence on the persons or property of the individuals of either party, neither retaliation nor reprisal shall be committed by the other until satisfaction shall have been demanded of the party of which the Aggressor is and shall have been refused.

Article 11<sup>th</sup>. The Creek [Nation shall] give notice to the [Governor of the United States] of any designs which they may know, or have reason to [believe are being] formed in any neighbouring tribe, or by any person whatsoever, against the peace and interests of the United States.

Article 12<sup>th</sup>. That the Creek Nation may be led to a greater degree of civilization and to become Herdsmen, and Cultivators instead of remaining in a State of Hunters the United States will from time to time furnish gratuitously the said Nation with useful domestic animals and implements of husbandry. And further, to assist the said Nation to so desirable a pursuit, and at the same time to establish a certain mode of communication, the United States will find such and so many persons to reside in said Nation as they may judge proper, and not exceeding four in number, who shall qualify themselves to act as interpreters. These persons shall have lands assigned them by the Creeks for cultivation for themselves and their Successors in office, but they shall be precluded exercising any kind of traffic.

Article 13<sup>th</sup>. All animosities for past grievances shall henceforth cease, and the contracting parties will carry the foregoing Treaty into full execution with all good faith and Sincerity.

Article 14<sup>th</sup>. This Treaty shall take effect and be obligatory on the contracting parties as soon as the same shall have been ratified by the President of the United States with the advice and consent of the Senate of the United States.

In Witness of all and every thing herein determined between the United States of America and the whole Creek Nations, the parties have hereunto set their hands and Seals in the City of New York within the United States, on this Seventh day of August one thousand Seven hundred and ninety.

About the 10<sup>th</sup> instant two men were fired on by a party of Indians, but no damage sustained only one of the horks the men rode was killed; the Indians took the faddle & bridle, and the night following they ftole eleven horks; our men pursued them, next day came up with them and retook all the horks together with said faddle & bridle, and killed two (one of which was a white mans). On Sunday the 16<sup>th</sup> fix negroes were taken by a party of Indians in ambuscade about three quarters of a mile from my house, they carried them about one quarter of a mile, where they were surprized by the noise of some people hiding near them, they tomahawked four, two of which died; two were left for dead which is now in a hopeful way of recovery the other two made their escape while they were running during the reift. The day following the party was seen twice and the evening or night of the fixteenth they ftole some horks from Captain Buford; we pursued them as quick as possible with about forty men to the Ohio, about twenty five miles below the mouth of Big Miami, where twenty fix volunteers croffed the Ohio after them, we came to a large camp of them early in the morning of the 20<sup>th</sup> about twelve miles from the Ohio, we divided our party and attacked them oppofite, on each fide, they fought us a long time in that pofition, until they got their women & children out of the way, and then give back to a thick place of high weeds & bufhes, where they hid very cloft; we immediately drove up about forty of their horks, and made our retreat acrofs the Ohio, we left three men & two wounded; The Indians wounded one of our men as we returned. Thus they are going on from time to time in this country.

J N B

Ensign Armstrong having marched with his party as far down as opposite Wheeling, which is about twenty from hence, measuring the course of the river, and executing his orders (excepting a few indulgences granted on account of the weather) returned on the 12<sup>th</sup> ulto.

In answer to which I thought it most expedient to grant them one Month from the 21<sup>st</sup> ulto to remove themselves, at the expiration of which time, parties will be detached to drive off all settlers within the distance of one hundred and fifty miles from this garrison, which in my present situation is all that is practicable.

I would therefore (before I proceed farther in the business) beg to know the pleasure of your Excellency, and your particular orders upon the subject.

37308:
Fort M<sup>c</sup>Intosh, June 1, 1785

Sir:

The Wyandot and Delaware Nations have brought in their prisoners (fifteen in number) agreeable to the treaty, and the Hostages left in my possession are now dismissed. These nations are friendly. The Shawanese make great professions of peace. The Cherokees are hostile, and have killed and scalped seven people near the Mouth of the Scioto, about three hundred and seventy miles from hence.—

Speeches have been continually sending by the British from Detroit to the Indians, since the treaty, and I have good intelligence that several traders have been among them, using all means to make them entertain a bad opinion of the Americans. One Simon Girty, I am informed, has been at Sandusky for that purpose.

Your most Ardent Servant,

Jos. Harmar.—

Speech of the United Indian Nations, at their Confederate Council held near the Mouth of the Detroit River between the 28<sup>th</sup> Nov and 18<sup>th</sup> Dec 1786.

Present — The Five Nations, the Hurons, Delawares, Shawanees, Ottawas, Chippewas, Puttawatimies, Twixt-fires, Cherokees & the Wabash Confederates.

To the Congress of the United States of America.

Brethren of the Thirteen United States of America,

It is now more than three Years since Peace was made between the King of Great Britain and you, but we the Indians, were disappointed finding ourselves not included in that Peace according to our Expectations, for we thought that its Conclusion would have promoted a Friendship between the United States & Indians, & that we might enjoy the Happiness which formerly subsisted between us and our Brothers — We have received two very agreeable Messages from the Northern United States we also received a Message from the King whose war we were engaged in, desiring us to remain Quiet, which we accordingly complied with —

During the truce of this Tranquility we were deliberating the best method to form a lasting Reconciliation with the Thirteen United States. Pleased at the same time we thought that we were entering upon a Reconciliation & Friendship with a Set of People from on the same Continent with ourselves certain that the Quarrel that was between us was not of our own Making.

In the Course of our Councils, we imagined we felt approaches to the Presi-dent that would promote a Lasting Peace between us. Brothers —

We Still are of the Same Opinion as to the Means which may tend to Reconcile us to each other & we are sorry to find altho we had the Best Thoughts in our Minds during the before mentioned Period, Mischief has nevertheless happened between You & us. And Especially as Lands & Matters are often the Subject of our [undecipherable] with you, a matter of the greatest Importance & of General Concern to us, in this Case we hold it indispensable, necessary that any Cession of our Lands should be made in the most Public a Manner & by the United Voice of the Confederacy, holding all Partial Treaties as void and of No Effect.

Brothers — We think it is now [undecipherable] to You that the [undecipherable] which since the Peace between us has not lasted, & that the [undecipherable] good has [undecipherable] by much, having Managed [undecipherable] being [undecipherable] in our own [undecipherable], you [undecipherable] your Council, [undecipherable] where you thought proper without Consulting us. At which you [undecipherable] deferred & Treaties & have strictly rejected our Plan of having a General Conference with the different Nations, altho Confederacy had this happened we have

38524:
War Office, 12.<sup>th</sup> Feb<sup>y</sup> 1787.

Sir,

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your Excellency's two favors of December 9.<sup>th</sup> 18 and 30th.

The board of treasury have not yet been able to form any efficient plan for providing for the establishment of the troops in all respects. No contracts for clothing or rations are yet made — These materially depend on some plans which are submitted to Congress for their approbation and direction.

There having been no Congress since October until very lately, and not one of nine States until this day, the subject could not be discussed in Congress. I hope however that the matter will soon be determined, when I shall be able to write fully to Captain Watts respecting his horses, accoutriments and the other necessary supplies.

I have the pleasure to apure your Excellency that the formidable Insurrection in Massachussetts is in a fair train of being effectually and speedily suppressed. General Lincoln informs me that he marched at 8 o'clock in the evening of the 3.<sup>d</sup> instant with his force consisting of upwards of 3000 troops of all descriptions, and after a fatiguing march of 30 miles without halting but for a few moments part of it through a violent storm of snow after which succeeded a severe cold so that most of his men were frozen in different places and degrees he completely surprized the insurgents at Petersham at 9 o'clock Sunday morning the 4.<sup>th</sup> and almost entirely dispersed them — took 150 prisoners; the rest fled in every direction. The leaders have escaped to New Hampshire and other States.

I have the honor to be, with the greatest respect, Your Excellency's
Most obed. humble Serv.<sup>t</sup>
H Knox —

His Excellency
Governor Randolph

[address leaf: His Excellency / The Governor / of the Commonwealth / of the State / of Virginia]
38788:
Camp at the Rapids of the Ohio.
June 15<sup>th</sup> 1787.

Sir

I had the honor of addressing you last on the 4<sup>th</sup> instant. We arrived here on the 11<sup>th</sup>. Considering the immense expence which the public would sustain by Hiring Packhorses, and indeed the uncertainty of procuring them and the delay attending it, these circumstances have induced me to determine upon going to Post St. Vincient by water, I am making arrangements respecting provisions and propose taking my cattle in Kentucky Boats to the mouth of the Wabash, and shall then order them drove along the margin of the river. Ascending the Wabash and driving the cattle will be attended with some difficulty.

This arrangement will be infinitely less expensive than marching by land from Lence directly to the Post. Upon a calculation it would require twenty Pack-horses which could not be hird under half a dollar each per day.

I expect Captain Ferguson will arrive about the 20<sup>th</sup> of the month, and I am in hopes to leave this immediately after his arrival.

When we reach the Post I shall constantly proceed to carry the orders of Congress into effect.

The Commission goods are here. As it is more than probable that I shall have frequent conferences with the Indians I propose taking them along with me, and beg as the Superintendant of Indian Affairs will be absent that you will be pleased to authorize me to distribute some of them in case of necessity.

Judge Symmes formerly a member of Congress is here, and has it in contemplation to establish a settlement on the Wabash.

I think it my duty to transmit you the enclosed proposals of his in order that you may be acquainted with his intentions.

You may be assured Sir that the advancement of federal measures shall be my constant object, and I hope for the countenance and support of Congress on the occasion.

I have the honor to be
Sir &c.

Jos. Harmar
L. Col. Comt 1<sup>st</sup> U.S. Reg.

His Honorable
Major Genl Knox
Sec<sup>y</sup> at War
38814:
[Copy of a letter from Lieutenant Colonel Josiah Harman dated Camp on the Kentucke shore just below the Rapids, July 4, 1787]

Sir

I had the honor of addressing you on the 19<sup>th</sup> March, on the 10<sup>th</sup> April, on the 14<sup>th</sup> May, and on the 7<sup>th</sup> and 15<sup>th</sup> alt<sup>o</sup>. which I hope have been received.

A duplicate of my last was forwarded by the way of Danville through the Wilderness to Richmond which must be the conveyance in future for my letters — As the people are as intimidated by a boat bound for Pittsburg being fired upon by a party of Indians near the Great Magnis that they will not for some time venture up the river.

I had given some of my letters in charge to the owner of this boat, but they were returned to me at the Rapids.

Since my last I have obtained more full information of the Country and have thought it most advisable, as it will save a vast expence to the public to make my operations chiefly by water— I have had all my keel boats repaired and put in tolerable order and have run the public to no further expence than about ten dollars for my Kentucke boats—

Last night I detached Captain Zeigler with 66 men in eight Kentucke boats, two large keel boats one small keel boat and two Canoes laden with flour, Cattle, Whiskey &c. (being three months provisions for three hundred men) with orders to halt at what is called the Landing and Carrying place a few miles on this side of green river called in Hutchins map Buffalo river — Tomorrow morning early I shall move with the troops and the remainder of the fleet and shall overtake Captain Zeigler.

I propose to march by land from this Carrying place to Post Vincennes the distance I am well informed is no more than fifty miles.

The Cattle and eighteen horses will be drove along.— The flour Baggage &c. will be under a strong guard round the Outback river which at this season of the year will be attended with considerable difficulty.— I have sent intelligence to Colonel Le Pragneau Major Beaveron the principal inhabitants at the Post to inform them of this movement.— Be pleased to receive the enclosed copy of my letter to these gentlemen.

Captain Ferguson did not arrive until the evening of the 3<sup>d</sup> instant in the old Contractors boats laden with provisions. I place no dependance on supplies from them; neither did I know of any further engagement of them to supply the troops but immediately upon my arrival at the Rapids in order to expedite the movement gave orders to Mr. Bradshaw the issuing Commissary here to exert himself and furnish the necessary provisions.

Having considerable credit in the Kentucke Country he exerted himself and furnished the provisions accordingly.— He has drawn Bills on the Contractors for the flour which he purchased.

I sincerely hope these Bills may be duly honored, for if his credit fails my resources will be materially injured.— Had this arrangement not been made my operations might probably have been retarded until the month of September—

The old Contractors were bound to deliver the provisions by the first of this month so as not to clash with the new Contract.— As it did not arrive until the 3<sup>d</sup> instant I have refused to receipt for it to Mr. Britt and will have nothing to do with it.

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 7<sup>th</sup> of May & Major Doughty with the pleasing intelligence of 500 dollars having arrived, being one months pay for the troops and three months Subsistence for the Officers.— I have also received your letter of the 17<sup>th</sup> May, with the sum of 1000. dollars Contingent money (Captain Bradford's expences and the discount to be deducted) which shall be administered in the most oeconomical manner.

Agreeably to your orders I have received for the full sum of 1000 dollars and now make said receipt in duplicate of the same shall be forwarded to the War Officer Reins one to Major Doughty.

I have undertaken to enlist for one year four men, with a promise of the same pay rations &c. as a regular soldier receives.

These men will be extremely useful the one is a Canadian interpreter who understands the different dialects of the Outback Indians, to this man I have promised something extra.—

The other three are good woodsmen and will serve as expresses to carry dispatches to and from the Post to the Rapids. Two of them are also and acquainted with the navigation of the Outback river. I trust this will meet with your approbation as it is done upon an oeconomical principle and will certainly be a saving to the public.

Captain Ferguson informs me that he took on board Regain the fellow who murdered an Indian with a design to remove him from McIntosh to Muskingum— but being in irons he started in his sleep and fell overboard and was drowned below Wheeling.— It would have been better to have him executed in presence of the Indians.

I am informed there are a number of British traders on the Outback above Post Vincennes. I hope to have the honor of addressing my next letter to you from that Post, when I shall immediately proceed to expel the usurpers of the public lands and likewise reconnoitre those British traders who are the real cause I believe of all the Indian disturbances.

I have the honor to make you a monthly return of the regiment, dated the 1<sup>st</sup> instant. I shall deliver out any few of the Commissioners goods and have not unless there should be an absolute necessity for it until I receive your sanction for so doing.

Eight of the Chickasaw Nation have been with me for this week past. Their business is to have a trade with the Americans.

These & the Chickasaws have been treated with and are very friendly to the United States.

I have given them eight Anch coats and a few trifles and shall take them down with me tomorrow as far as an go by water and then dismiss them with a Speech and some small presents to the Pianings, the Mountain Chief and the Choctaw Chief.

I have left an Officer with a command of 25 sick and invalids, to garrison the Post at the Rapids of the Ohio.— The chief duty of this Officer is to forward any dispatches which may arrive from the War Office to me immediately at Post Vincennes by land.

Be pleased to order your letters directed to his charge.
38869:
[Copy of a letter from Brigadier General Josiah Harmar dated Camp at Post Vincennes. August 7, 1787.]

Sir,

I had the honor of addressing you last on the 4<sup>th</sup> ulto. from Camp on the Kentucky River just below the rapids of the Ohio.

On the 6<sup>th</sup> ultimo L<sup>t</sup>. Leighton with a party and an adequate number of boats was detached from thence with the provisions. On the 8<sup>th</sup> we embarked and the remainder of the fleet and arrived on the morning of the 10<sup>th</sup> at the Rocks, on the landing and crossing place, called also the Delaware Ab-town about eight miles above Green river and one hundred and eighty miles below the rapids. In the afternoon of the same day Detached Major Hamtramck with a party of one hundred men to convoy the whole fleet from the landing to the mouth of the Wabash and then to ascend the river to Fort Vincennes. On the morning of the 11<sup>th</sup> with the residue of the Troops I took up the enclosed order of march and our cattle in the center in very narrow [undecipherable] and the men being obliged to carry fifteen (days) flour upon their backs rendered it very fatiguing. [Undecipherable] north [undecipherable] from the landing and camping [undecipherable] the woods. Have struck the river in fifty miles distance from the Ohio, but we were obliged to oblique for the sake of water. On the 16<sup>th</sup> we forded the White river (a considerable stream) about fifteen miles below the forks and arrived at Post Vincennes on the [undecipherable] at noon. From the Ohio where we set out to the White river was as very difficult march the country being full of thickets and swarms of [undecipherable] but afterwards we marched through fine open woods and large prairies or natural meadows and encamped on the banks of the Wabash. On the 18<sup>th</sup> we were visited by Colonel Le Gras the Magistrate and the principal French inhabitants advancing to us upon our arrivals. Their behaviour was most respectfully submissive. In the afternoon of the same day finding the Wabash river so low and difficult to ascend I detached a Sergeant and twenty men in three Barges and four [undecipherable] to meet Major Hamtramck and lighten the fleet.

Post Vincennes is a very considerable village situated upon the Wabash about one hundred and twenty miles from the mouth, it contains near four hundred houses (Log and Bark) out houses, barns &c. The number of the inhabitants about 900 (Male) French and about 400 (Souls) Americains. Monsieur Vincennes the French Officer from whom it derives its name [undecipherable] informed [undecipherable] and commenced the settlement eight years ago.

On the 20<sup>th</sup> I called upon Colonel Le Gras for a sight of the French grants and all other papers respecting the original settlers. The papers were produced but I declined having a translation of them until the arrival of Mr. Bartholemi Tardivean, a French gentleman who was with Major Hamtramck in the fleet, well acquainted with the inhabitants, and the footing they held their lands upon. I expected his arrival every day. Major Hamtramck did not arrive with the boats until the 20<sup>th</sup> having been eleven days on very severe fatiguing duty ascending the Wabash.

I was obliged to leave Ensign [undecipherable] Suydam with a party with the clothing all the Whiskey and chief part of the flour at the mouth of the Wabash the water being so shoal that the boats could not ascend the river.

On the 26<sup>th</sup> Detached Lieutenant Armstrong-strong with a party of forty-two fresh men in several [undecipherable] to join Ensign Suydam and assist in bringing up the provisions and our new clothing which was left behind at the mouth of the river.

On the 27<sup>th</sup> the Resolve of Congress respecting the claimants on the public lands together with my orders were published in English and French which amazed the inhabitants exceedingly particularly those who style themselves Americans. A copy of said resolve and the orders relation thereto I take myself the honor to enclose.

On the 28<sup>th</sup> Eight Piankeshaw Indians arrived from the Terre Haute up the Wabash in consequence of Col. Le Gras's information to them of the Troops coming to the Post. On the 29<sup>th</sup> I had a conference with them and presented them with thirteen strings of wampum and assured them of the friendly disposition of the United States and advised them not to listen to what any bad people might say to the contrary.

I sent a message by these Indians to all the Chiefs of the different tribes on the Wabash inviting them to assemble here and hear what I had to say to them. Three Indians were also [undecipherable]; they presented me with a Calumet. I gave them some small presents and they set off on the 21<sup>st</sup> to deliver my message to the different Chiefs. The French inhabitants at the same time sent a speech to them a copy of which I have the honor to enclose.

On the 5<sup>th</sup> instant Lieutenant Armstrong and Ensign Suydam arrived with the new Clothing &c. from the mouth of the Wabash after a very fatiguing dangerous passage. Several parties of Indians were hovering about the Wabash, they waylaid a Canoe on the 25<sup>th</sup> ulto which had fallen in the rear of what is called the long rapids on board of which were some flour and Whiskey, [undecipherable] belonging to our guides they killed one of Captain Leighton's company and a Frenchman and took prisoners one of the men whom I had enlisted for one year. Informed the Indians of this circumstance and to tell their chief that if they did not desist they would certainly draw upon them the vengeance of the United States. They disclaimed in strong terms any knowledge of this murder.

I humbly conceive that the great objects I have to attend to will be to prevent illegal encroachments on the public lands to secure happiness to the inhabitants and to protect private property from arbitrary invasion and to remove if possible differences, fear and jealousy from the mind of the Indians. To these points I shall bend my attention.

I have been lately employed with the aid of Mr. Tardivean in order to make a discrimination between the lands legally obtained and those that have been encroached upon without sufficient authority. The French inhabitants are about framing an humble petition to Congress and will I believe give up their charters and trust to Congress for what lands that Honorable body may please to grant them. Such American inhabitants as have settled under the French charters are also framing a petition to Congress praying for relief and they will be recommended by the French.

As there are no Indians out of the village I shall wait for these petitions and send them to the War Office and although the first of September is the going period for them to depart as I cannot yet possibly ascertain who are actually intruders, I shall not proceed there, until their petitions are sent on and their fate determined and I receive orders from Congress or the War Office upon the subject.

Both parties will appoint Mr. Bartholomeus Tardivean as their Agent. He will go to Congress in the course of next month.

As the Indian chiefs (if they come at all) will not be here in less than a month I propose to take a La Batterie guard and to proceed to Kaskaskias in company with Mr. Tardivean the next day after tomorrow in order that I may be enabled to see a statement of affairs in that part of the United States.

This movement of the troops will have a peculiar good effect. It will deter several people from Kentucky and other parts from taking off the public lands. A door was opened very fast for intrusions from that quarter. Many of General Clarke's militia on their march towards the Vermillion town had cast their eyes on choice land and I am informed had made what they called Tomahawk rights.

I am pleased to receive the following enclosures, viz.

No. 1  Col. Le Gras's answer on behalf of the inhabitants at Post Vincennes to Col. Harmar's letter of the 19<sup>th</sup> June.

2  The address of the French inhabitants at Post Vincennes to Colonel Harmar.

3  The address of the American inhabitants at Post Vincennes to Colonel Harmar.

4  The Recommendations of the French inhabitants to Col. Harmar in favor of the American inhabitants.

The petitions of both the French and American inhabitants to Congress. I have not yet received. They shall be forwarded by Mr. Tardivean.

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 1<sup>st</sup> June enclosing the Contract of Mr. O'Hara and the Board of Treasury for the supply of the Troops &c. x x x x

39191:
Fort Harmar March 9. 1788

Sir:- Mr David Zeisberger, missionary of the Moravian Indians, has written to me requesting an exchange of the Corn at McIntosh for an equivalent in powder, linen &c, which request I shall grant, as we are in want of the corn for the public houses. The distance those Indians are from McIntosh, prevents their bringing it from thence. On the 14<sup>th</sup> Ultimo I received a message from Captain Pipe, the Chief of the Delawares, who was hunting about fifty miles from hence, up the Muskingum, with thirty or forty of his nation. I answered his message, and on the 28<sup>th</sup> detached Ensign McDowell, with a party of a Sergeant and fifteen privates, to view his [strikethrough: situation] situation, and sent him a message and a string of Wampum - the messages are enclosed. On the 6<sup>th</sup> instant Ensign McDowell, with his party, returned, after having been treated with the utmost friendship and hospitality by the Indians at their hunting encampment. Yesterday old Captain Pipe, with seven of his Young men, arrived at the garrison, and are now with me. Their object is to dispose of their skins to the Contractor. He is a manly old fellow, and much more of a gentleman than the generality of these frontier people.

I have the honor to be &c
Jos. Harmar

The Honable Major Genral Knox, Secretary at War.
39258:
Fort Pitt, April 26, 1785.

Sir, I have now an opportunity to transmit, and shall embrace the liberty to inform you of my order to visit Captain Heart's post. — I left Muskingum on the 6<sup>th</sup> inst, and on the 9<sup>th</sup> met General Putnam and part of the Ohio Company. Be assured, Sir, that every assistance and protection that is in my power, shall be rendered to the Concern. — I make not the least doubt, but a flourishing settlement will soon take place, as they are industrious, and quite a different set of people from those frontier men. — I waited with great impatience for the arrival of General Putnam, and it must have afforded me peculiar pleasure to have been personally present with him, but Major Doughty, who commands during my absence will agreably to your orders [undecipherable: afford] him every assistance. — Mr. Nicholson, the Interpreter, and M<sup>c</sup>Curdy who resides at this place, returned from Kentucky on the 13<sup>th</sup> instant. His intelligence is that the Indians will be late in assembling to the treaty, and that it is their determination to insist peremptorily, on the Ohio river as the boundary. — I do not think that full powers and ought to be given to the Commissioners to cede to the Indians the lands which, in the repose of fact the interest and property of North river of Captain Hearts work. — Please direct Captain Heart to make out a map of the country from Mango to Scioto, which I shall shortly have the honor of transmitting to you. —

I have the honor to be &c

Jos. Harmar.

39436:
Fort Harmar July 28. 1788.

Sir,

I have the Honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 4<sup>th</sup> instant enclosing dispatches from Congress to the People of Kentucky.

On the 17<sup>th</sup> instants they were forwarded from hence, by Mr Andrew Hare who inform'd me that he would take the most particular care that they shall be safely delivered.

The Grand Treaty will be deferred for some time. At the request of the Granor I ordered a Subattern — Sergeant, Corporal, & twenty Privates as an Escort for the Granors, and to build a Council Room for the Savages, at the falls of the Muskingum. Regardless of all faith and Honor, a party of the Ottaways & Chippewas attacked this party on the morning of the 13<sup>th</sup> Inst. and killed two, one is missing,

and two wounded, one very badly. the loss of the Indians are two killed on the spot, one wounded and five taken Prisoners who are now in Confinement and under heavy irons at this Garrison. I sincerely hope that the new Government will soon begin to operate, in order that we may be enabled to sweep these perfidious Villians off the face of the Earth.

In consequence of this treacherous proceeding, the Governor and myself were both of opinion that the party and Granions should be removed to this Post accordingly the Officer returned on the morning of the 20<sup>th</sup>.

The Governor has sent a printed message to the different nations who are assembled and Councilling at the Maway on Miami River demanding satisfaction for this gross insult offered to the United States.

an answer to his message may be expected in the course of ten or twelve days.

I have the Honor to be Sir

Humble Serv<sup>t</sup>.

Dear Sir

I am much obliged by your very polite favor of the 9<sup>th</sup> August in answer to my letter of the 15<sup>th</sup> June, the Military arrangements then suggested, appears now to be necessary, as the Commissioners have not been able to succeed in holding a treaty with the Indians, without even deigning to return an answer to the talk delivered by [undecipherable], which gives just presumption to apprehend an immediate & serious war, in fact they have already commenced Hostilities on the frontiers of this State, as appears by an express from a Col. Irvine of the Militia, on the 13<sup>th</sup> Instant who says "the Indians have burnt down Hamp's fort in Washington County, & some houses" — Best reason for their refusing to treat, may possibly be accounted for, by the following circumstance, as McGilvry was on his way with the Indians to the rock landing, he was overtaken by an express from New Orleans, with the ratification of a treaty commenced some time since, between the Spanish & Creek Nations, & lately confirmed by Charles the [undecipherable] the present King of Spain, guaranteeing to the Indians all the lands

they possess or Claim on the East side of the Mississippi, this instrument of writing M<sup>r</sup> Gibson one of the late Commissioners, assures me, he both seen & read, being handed to him by McGilvry for that purpose.

I believe I told you on the 15<sup>th</sup> June that I was decidedly of Opinion, we never should have a permanent peace with the Creek Nation (who are numerous & insolent) until they were made to experience our superiority in the Field, & an Army stationed for the protection of the Southern States, not only against the incursions of the Indians, but also against the ideal Claims of the Spaniards. Their late Conduct verifies this Opinion, & points out the indispensible necessity of compelling the Creeks to treat upon our own terms in the Heart of their Country, which I pledge myself to effect, at the head of Four Battalions of Infantry of Six hundred effectives each, two Regiments of Cavalry of Three Hundred & Seventy pieces, & Two Hundred & fifty Artillery — properly Officered & well appointed, which is as large an Operating force, as can be conveniently supplied with provision &c<sup>a</sup> a draft of Militia in addition to this force may be necessary for the purposes of keeping open the Communication between the [undecipherable] from which we draw our supplies

& the Indian Nation, & for the defence of Proper deposits & places of Arms in case of a serious Operation; I expect shortly to obtain an accurate account of the Number & Gun men which can be opposed to us, from a M<sup>r</sup> McGilvry, a relation of the Indian McGilvry (formerly a resident now a rich planter near this place) I [undecipherable] had a list of the towns & number of fighting men in each, but it is mislaid, however I recollect that the aggregate of the Upper & lower Creeks, was somewhere about 6000 the Chocktaws 5000 the Cherokees, 1500 & the Cussews 800 Gun men.

We have nothing to apprehend I believe but from the Creeks, on the contrary we may probably have the assistance of the Chocktaws & Cherokees if necessary, as they have heretofore been enemies to the Creeks & frequently at war with them; but should a general confederacy take place, they can not support themselves but for a very short time in doing — & should they collect upon the spur of the Occasion, it may be the happy means of hasting a speedy conclusion to the war, as their Numbers, will only serve to confuse, & render them an easy prey, to our Cavalry after being routed by the Infantry & Artillery, in an open Wood & Champagne Country, such as that proposed by the Creek Nation for the northeast is.

I shall be much obliged by the earliest information, should a Military Arrangement be thought necessary, & also for your Interest with His Excellency the President, in obtaining me the Command of or in the Expedition

I am endeavouring to collect the best information, & in the most [undecipherable] manner that Circumstances will admit, in order to facilitate an effectual Operation, should such a measure be adopted.

Interim I have the honor to be
with the sincerest Esteem

Your Most Ob<sup>t</sup>
Daring
Humble Ser<sup>t</sup>

Anty Wayne

The Judiciary System is so defective that it will doubtless undergo much alteration in the next Session of Congress.

The Revolution in France is as singular, as it is important to the cause of liberty. It is perhaps the first instance in the History of Nations of a King & his people Uniting to extend the Rights of the latter in abridging the powers and privileges of the Nobles. The common tendency of Revolutions founded in a force amongst the people, of Oppression from the Nobility, has ever been to an implicit surrender of every thing into the hands of the Sovereign. to say nothing of Ancient Precedents, the modern, nay recent, Revolutions in Denmark & Sweden terminated thus: there is in France a Spirit never before known in the old world; and my pride suggests that it was imbibed from America; and I am completely gratified in being, that a Son of America did, in the extremity of Confusion, "mount the Whirlwind & direct the Storm."

The Commissioners are decidedly of opinion, that the failure of a Treaty at this time with the Creek Nation was the attributable only to three principal: Chief Alex. M'Galloway. 1<sup>st</sup> From the repeated declarations and apparent good disposition of all the Kings, Head Men and Warriors to establish representation and peace with the United States.

2<sup>nd</sup> From the proposed Boundary being offered to the good honor of the Nation, only as the Basis of possible Negotiation.

3<sup>d</sup> From the deception and precipitate return of M<sup>r</sup>. M'Galloway, without stating his objections to the draught of a Treaty either verbally or in writing.

4<sup>th</sup> From many enquiries concerning this Man, and from M<sup>r</sup>. M'Galloway's own declarations. That without obtaining a full equivalent for the sacrifice, he would not announce the class conversion which he had formed with the Spanish Government in the hour of distress, a conversion honorable and lucrative to himself, and advantageous to the Creek Nation.

5<sup>th</sup> From his frequent intimations that no Treaty could be favoured with the Commissioners unless of full and each —

point should be appointed to him upon the Alteration to River M<sup>t</sup>. Many; and,

6<sup>th</sup> From the most positive refusal to acknowledge the Creek Nation to be within the limits or under the protection of the United States, although in express contradiction to a former Letter written by him on the 3<sup>rd</sup> of September 1785, to General Pickens.

The Commissioners beg leave further to report.

That after the most accurate investigation in their powers, to make, after consulting the best Documents, and having recourse to as creditable Depositions, they are unable to discover, but that the Treaty of Augusta in the year 1783, the Treaty of Galphintstown in the year 1785, and the Treaty of Shoulderbone in the year 1786, were all of them conducted with as full and well-apparent good faith, and under standing of the Business, as Indean Treaties have usually been conducted, or perhaps can be, where one of the contracting Parties is destitute of the benefits of enlightened Society. That the Lands in question from the Hunting Grounds, have been ceded by them to the State of Georgia, for considerable compensation, and were possessed and cultivated for some years, without any Claims or molestation by any part of the Creek Nation.

As M<sup>r</sup>. M'Galloway and all the other Chiefs, Head Men & Warriors, have given many strong claims in their Talks, and by writing that no further Hostilities or —

Depredations shall be committed with the part of their Nation, and as the Governor of Georgia by signing Proclamations, seconded by other Spiritual measures, will prevent the Commission of Hostilities & Depredations upon the Creek Nation on the part of Georgia. The Commissioners in the best of their Judgement Expose.

That all animosities with the Creek Nation should henceforth cease.

That some Person should be dispatched to the said Nation with the ultimate Draught of a Treaty, to establish perpetual Peace and Amity. That when such a Draught of a Treaty shall be properly executed by the leading men of the Nation, all the Presents intended for the Indians, and appearing in the State of Georgia should be distributed among them. That if the Indians shall refuse to execute such Draught of a Treaty, the Commissioners humbly Submit.

That the Arms of the Union should be called forth for the Protection of the people of Georgia, in the peaceable and just possession of their Lands, and in case the Creeks shall commit further Hostilities and Depredations upon the Citizens of the United States, that the Creek Nation ought to be deemed the Enemies of the United States and punished accordingly.

War Office Nov<sup>r</sup> 24<sup>th</sup> 1789

Sir

By order of the President of the United States, I have the honor to inform you that the Commissioners for treating with the Creek Nation have returned and reported the progress and issue of their mission

The actual state in which the subject is suspended, impresses the President of the United States with great anxiety— He is exceedingly desirous that a War at this period should be avoided if it can be effected consistently with the interest and dignity of the United States— He is aware of the expence of blood and Treasure of a War with the Creeks and of the embarrassment it would occasion to the Government. And above all he is solicitous that the event should not be brought on by the conduct of the Citizens of the United States. The Commissioners have reported that your honor issued a proclamation forbidding all hostilities on the part of the Citizens of Georgia— The

President of the United States is persuaded that you will take every necessary step to enforce your proclamation

If the Creeks should contrary to their declarations to the Commissioners, commit unprovoked depredations on the persons or property of the Citizens of Georgia, the punishment which may be inflicted on their nation in consequence thereof will receive the approbation of all unprejudiced men.

The President of the United States has further directed me to assure you that were there any considerable body of regular troops at his disposal, that he should immediately order it to be stationed on the frontiers of Georgia, as well to protect its Citizens, as to exhibit to the Creeks our power to punish if necessary— But all the troops in the public service are necessarily employed on the North-Western frontiers, excepting the few hereafter described—

The company of troops which escorted the Commissioners were directed to return, because their engagements with the public were nearly expiring— This company, and some few other troops in similar circumstances are about to be discharged— They will be replaced by recruits to compleat the existing establishment— These recruits will amount to about two hundred men— As soon as one company shall be recruited it will be ordered to Georgia, and the remainder will follow as soon as possible.

This arrangement appears to be the only one which can with propriety be adopted during the recess of Congress, unless the hostile conduct of the Creeks should render it absolutely necessary to call out the Militia for the protection of Georgia— But the expence to the public and distress to individuals involved in such a measure would render it adviseable only in case of extreme exigency.

I have the honor to be
Sir
Your Most Ob<sup>t</sup> Hble Ser
H Knox Sec<sup>y</sup> of War

Wilmington 7<sup>th</sup> Dec<sup>r</sup> 1789

Sir,

I received your favors of 28<sup>th</sup> September and 10<sup>th</sup> October last, together with sundry Papers respecting the depreciation of the Pay Accounts of the Delaware Regiment, and immediately laid them before the General Assembly of this State then in Session; but the Session being near a close, nothing conclusive was determined on them.

As I was principally concerned in making a settlement of the Depreciation Accounts, the two other Gentlemen were in the appointment, I feel myself under obligations to justify them as far as truth will support me.

The Muster rolls came into our hands in a very imperfect State— many were missing, having as the officers alledged been captured at the battle of Camden. From the documents furnished me I formed a list of the Regiment as perfect as we could. This we submitted to the Officers, who, on some business of their own were assembled at Dover. They made notes on our list distinguishing those who were entitled from those who were not, and particularly Noting desertion. some who had been returned as deserters afterwards joined the Regiment and were pardoned. This list I have still in my possession, and have referred to it, in order to furnish an answer to your remarks.

"Patrick Burke" has no note affixed to his name. Cap<sup>t</sup> John Wilson applied personally in his favor, and declared he was entitled to a certificate. He lives in Kent County, and has been confined in the County Gaol for debt since the Certificate was granted him. No mention was ever made of his desertion.

"John Cullen" has no note affixed to his name by the officers, nor was any mention ever made of his desertion.

"James Cane" is noted to be dead. His parents and friends lived within five miles of Dover. No mention was ever made of his desertion.

"William Dixon"
"Daniel Dailey" no notes against their names, and no mention has ever been made of their desertion.

"John King"
"Peter Records" Notes that they were discharged, but no mention was ever made of their desertion.

"Thomas Donaldson"— Certificates instead of his belonging to Spencer's Regiment.

"James Kimmy"
"James Kinney" mention'd as persons, both were paid.

"John Vineyard" a note that he was discharged or finding two men in his room. He was mustered as a non commissioned officer to the 1<sup>st</sup> August 1780, and found the substitutes in 1781.

The Certificates remaining unapplied for were delivered to the President of the State under a Law passed in Delaware the 24<sup>th</sup> Year of the reign of King George the V<sup>th</sup> entitled "An act for "the better settling Intestates estates," in which is the following clause, viz<sup>t</sup> "And all the Goods, chattels & "Personal estate whatsoever of such persons dying intestate "and without wife or kindred, shall go to the Governor "and Commander in Chief of this Government, for the time "being, and to his heirs and assigns forever. But if "any of the said Intestates Relations shall appear and "make good their claim or claims to such intestates "personal estate within seven years after the decease "of the intestate they shall be restored thereunto"

Of the Certificates put into his hands only two have been delivered out, viz<sup>t</sup> John Hatfields, for £63:21:0, now in the possession of Peter Lawlor, and Samuel Merediths for £19:9:2 now in the possession of Nehemiah Tilton Esq<sup>r</sup>

It was never expected that these accounts could be settled without errors. Probably as many have been made against the soldiers as against the United States. The greatest care was taken to do justice, and if, for want of better evidence, something less was done, it would seem hard that the State should suffer on this account.

With respect to the Certificate issued to Gennathan Harney in lieu of all claims, it was the opinion of the General Assembly that they had made an advantageous bargain. The Speaker had neglected to give a certificate agreeable to the inclosed Resolution. Harney died. His relations applied for it, and the Auditors for settling the depreciations were directed to issue one for the sum agreed upon, in the same manner as those for depreciation were issued. This was done and charged in that amount, on a persuasion that the United States would allow it. I have not yet been able to lay my hands upon the Petition to ascertain his claims, or I should not doubt but they would appear fully equal to the sum allowed him.

I now forward sundry recruiting accounts, viz<sup>t</sup> Cap<sup>t</sup> Enoch Anderson, Cap<sup>t</sup> Peter Jaquett, Cap<sup>t</sup> Charles Pope, Cap<sup>t</sup> John Learmonths, Lieu<sup>t</sup> Caleb Browns, and Lieu<sup>t</sup> Elijah Skillington. If any of these are included in accounts already forwarded you will not allow them— if not, you will be pleased to pass them to the Credit of the State and transmit an account for settlement with the officers, most of whom are indebted to the State.

I am Sir,

Your most Obedient
and humble Serv<sup>t</sup>

Eleaz<sup>r</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Comb

To Joseph Howell Jun<sup>r</sup> Esq<sup>r</sup>

You mention that in case the Game should be required a regiment of choice men could be raised in Holston Valley on short notice — Will you please to inform me in what time a regiment of 360 Non commissioned Officers and privates could be raised at that place after the appointment of the Officers had been made? Whether the said regiment could be raised on the continental establishment of pay clothing and rations agreeably to the Schedule herein annexed? and to serve during three years against the Indians unless sooner discharged?

I shall also be obliged by precise answers to the following queries.

1<sup>st</sup> If M<sup>c</sup>Gillivray has sent messages to the Creeks or other nations to find out the exact purport thereof, and the answers of the Cherokees thereto

2<sup>dly</sup> If a War should ensue with the Creeks what side would the Cherokees take as a nation, would they join them against the United States? Or, whether any, or what part of the Cherokees would join the Arms of the United States?

3<sup>dly</sup> What is the distance of the nearest Settlements of Holstein to the Cherokee towns particularly Chota? Have the Cherokees returned to that town?

4<sup>thly</sup> What kind of navigation is it for boats, and the depth and rapidity of the water from Holstein and Chota down the Tennessee to the Muscle Shoals and what is the distance?

5<sup>thly</sup> What is the distance from the Holstein Settlements to Miro and Nashrills settlements on the Cumberland River?

6<sup>thly</sup> The distance from Nashville and Miro Settlements to the Muscle Shoals?

7<sup>thly</sup> What nation of Indians are those who commit depredations on the said Settlements? What are the number of Settlers at Nashville and Miro, and the Cumberland lines generally?

8<sup>thly</sup> What is the distance from Lexington in Kentucky to the nearest upper Creek towns?

John Tracy

my dear Sir

I am very sorry to have occasion to give any my friends trouble or anxiety for me or my family, particularly you, whose time is so fully occupied. — my Father has so left my Childrens Estate, that I see no prospect then twelve months of prosecuting my intention of settleing in the Western Country; this is a very great mortification to me. their real Estate if disposed off must be for real Estate of equal value, to be determined by three persons appointed by the Judge of Probate, could I effect an exchange; their personal property would sell for such a trifle at present, that it would not answer the purpose of settleing myself, without distressing them very much, and perviaps more than they can bear — my friends tell me if I can support myself, a year or two here, they have no doubt the times will be better for me, and then if I feel a disposition to settle I can purchase an Estate in that Country under Cultivation, upon this view my prospect is very slender — into Trade unless their is a Statute of Bankruptey takes place. I received your favors of the 25 September and 16<sup>th</sup> October last together with sundry Papers respecting the Depreciation of the Pay Accounts of the Delaware Regiment, and immediately laid them before the General Assembly of this State who was then in Session, but being about to rise, nothing conclusive was determined on them.

As I was principally concerned in making a Settlement of the Depreciation accounts, the two other Gentlemen were in the appointment, I feel myself under obligations to justify them as far as truth will support me.

The Muster Rolls came into our hands in a very imperfect State many were missing, having, as the officers alleged, been captured at the battle of Camden. From the documents furnished me formed a list of the Regiment as perfect as we could — this we submitted to the officers, who, on some business of their own, were assembled at Dover. They made notes on our list, distinguishing those who were intitled from those who were not — and particularly noting Deserters. Some who had been returned as Deserters afterwards joined the Regiment and were pardoned. This list is still in my possession, and have referred to it in order to furnish an answer to your accounts.

"Patrick Burke" has no notes affixed to his name. Cap<sup>t</sup> John Wilson applied personally in his favor, and declared he was intitled to a Certificate.
