Recruiting INSTRUCTIONS
For Captain Bezaleel Howe
of the Infantry
in the Service of the United States.

SIR,

You are immediately to commence the recruiting service in the State of New York. The principal rendezvous will be at West Point

Your recruits will be furnished by his Contractor with rations, barracks, barrack utensils, straw and fuel; and also with such necessary medicinal assistance as they may require.

The recruiting service in [strikethrough: undecipherable], both as it respects the individuals recruited and the public at large—that is, recruits are unwarily and unworthily entangled, contrary to their intentions: Such men generally desert the service, at some critical moment, or serve grudgingly, and set bad examples to others; or, undesirable persons are engaged, who are constitutionally defective and unfit for the hardships incident to a military life.

Although a recruiting officer may require peculiar talents to obtain uncommon success, yet it is in the power of every officer to conduct himself with candor, integrity and industry.

In order therefore to avoid the errors of this business, the following instructions are to serve as the general rules and principles of your conduct:

1<sup>st</sup>. The recruits are to be inlisted for three years, unless sooner discharged.

2<sup>d</sup>. Each recruit is to receive a bounty of Eight Dollars;—but no part of this sum is to be advanced until the recruit shall have been fairly inlisted and sworn before a Magistrate, according to the form herein prescribed, and then only the said sum is to be advanced in such proportions as the judgment of the recruiting officer shall dictate, until experience shall in some degree have ascertained the fidelity of the recruits. Any money advanced contrary to this direction, will be at the risque of the recruiting officer.

3<sup>d</sup>. Every recruiting officer will be allowed the sum of Two Dollars, for the trouble and expence of inlisting each recruit;—provided however, that such allowance will not be made for any recruit who shall desert before he shall march from the rendezvous of the troops in the State where he shall have been recruited.

4<sup>th</sup>. The utmost fairness is to be used by the recruiting officers, in engaging their recruits; no individual therefore is to be inlisted in a state of intoxication, or be sworn until after he shall have been inlisted for the space of twenty-four hours.

5<sup>th</sup>. Each recruit (musicians excepted) must be five feet and five inches in heighth, without shoes;—he must also be healthy, robust, and sound in his limbs and body, in all respects; and to ascertain which he must be thoroughly examined, previously to inlistment, by a Physician or Surgeon;—but if, notwithstanding this direction, a recruit should have any secret disease at the time of his inlistment, the expence of his cure, if retained in service, shall be deducted from his pay.

6<sup>th</sup>. Each recruit, before he is sworn, is to have distinctly read to him the rules and articles of war against mutiny and desertion, and relative to the administration of justice; and also the Act of Congress of the 30<sup>th</sup> of April 1790, establishing the rations, clothing, and compensation in cases of disability; and the Act of the 5<sup>th</sup> March 1792, establishing the pay: after which he is to take the following oath, before a Magistrate, to wit:

"I A. B. do solemnly swear (or affirm, as the case may be) to bear true allegiance to the United States of America, and to serve them honestly and faithfully against all their enemies or opposers whomsoever, and to observe and to obey the orders of the President of the United States of America, and the orders of the officers appointed over me according to the articles of war."

7<sup>th</sup>. Each recruit (musicians excepted) must be above eighteen and under forty-five years of age.

8<sup>th</sup>. No negro, mulatto, or Indian, to be recruited.

9<sup>th</sup>. All the recruits, if possible, to be natives of fair conduct; or foreigners of good characters for sobriety and fidelity, and who have been some years in the country. Any recruiting officer inlisting a vagrant, or transient person, who shall desert before marching from the place of rendezvous, shall reimburse out of his pay the loss sustained by such desertion.—It is therefore Important that the officers be attentive on this point, as a compliance with this order will be rigidly exacted. The public interests will be better served by a small army of brave, robust, and faithful soldiers, than by a multitude of vagabonds.

10<sup>th</sup>. As soon as the recruits shall be assembled at the rendezvous, they are to be taught, by gentle methods, regularity of conduct, as it shall respect cleanliness of their persons, diet and rooms, and also due subordination, and they are to be exercised at least four hours in every day, in the attitudes and other first principles of a soldier.

11<sup>th</sup>. The commanding officer at each place of rendezvous must make out, on every Saturday, a return of the number of recruits under his command, and of the number joined during the course of the week; and transmit the same to the War-Office by the next post; and also such information as he may possess, of any officers under his command out on the recruiting service.

12<sup>th</sup>. You, or the commanding officer at — West Point rendezvous are to sign returns for the issues of all rations, and other necessary supplies for the troops, made on each Saturday; the daily returns made in the week are to be taken up, and one general return to be made, and signed for the rations received in the course of the week, noticing the daily issues.

13<sup>th</sup>. No allowance is to be made for the expences of a recruit, until he shall join at the rendezvous, the bounty being considered as adequate for that object.

These instructions are to regulate the conduct of the field officers and all others therein concerned, but they are more particularly given to you as captain or commanding officer of the company to be raised in — State of New York — and you are to give copies hereof to your subalterns, and all others under your orders.

The recruits will be mustered and critically inspected as soon as possible after the company shall be completed, and any deviation from these instructions will be noticed.

The clothing, arms and accoutrements for your recruits will be furnished at — West Point

It is expected that you will exert yourself in the highest degree in obtaining your proportion of the company about to be raised.—Any remarkable deficiency arising from want of due industry, on your part, will be reported to the President of the United States, and such conduct may be considered by him as a just cause for withholding your commission, in pursuance of the power vested in him by law.

The establishment of the troops, the articles of war, and blank inlistments are herewith transmitted.

Sir

M<sup>r</sup> Shaw with the Bloody fellow and the other Cherokees who left Philadelphia with him are within ten miles of this place and will be here in the morning all well and have been treated generally with kindness and civility and in some places with much attention — They have however been several times alarmed, from hearing of the observations and threats of fooling unthinking people who in all probability had no serious intention of carrying their threats into execution —

War department
April 22<sup>d</sup> 1792

Sir,

I have the pleasure to inform you that the President of the United States, appoint you a temporary Deputy Agent, to the five Nations of Indians until further directions, at the rate of five hundred dollars P<sup>r</sup> annum.

It will be necessary that you should take the oaths which are herein enclosed before a Magistrate, and transmit the same to me.

I herewith transmit you by the hands of Doctor Israel Allen the sum of four hundred dollars.

The main object of placing this sum on your hands at present is to enable you to make a suitable provision for Captain Joseph Brant who it is expected will shortly make a visit to this City and to request that you would either accompany him to this City, that you would otherwise provide for his journey in a manner perfectly agreeable to him, and that you would give me due notice of his approach at least five days previously to his arrival here.

In the mean time I observe it is the firm determination of the President of the United States that the utmost fairness and kindness Shall be exhibited to the Indian tribes with the United States. —

That it is not only his desire to be at peace with all the Indians tribes, but to be their guardians and protectors against all injustice. —

You will please to observe that a due accounting of all monies or goods placed in your hands will be rigidly expected, and that you must always produce vouchers for every dollar expended.

I am

Sir
with great respect
your very hum<sup>l</sup> Ser<sup>t</sup>
Knox

Sec<sup>y</sup> of War

General Israel Chapin

I Israel Chapin, do solemnly swear to bear true allegiance to the United States of America, and that I will faithfully discharge the duties of temporary deputy agent to the Five Nations of Indians, and that I will not directly or indirectly be concerned in any Indian trade. —

April 24 1793

Sir

I had the honor to receive your letter of the 12 instant and to submit it to the President of the United States.

While it is acknowledged that the frontier Citizens ought to be effectually protected against actual danger it is to be observed that it is difficult and perhaps impracticable to guard against all possible dangers of straggling Indians. The measures therefore adopted on the part of the Executive of directing general [undecipherable] to the scene of apprehended danger is highly judicious in order to judge of the real state of things.

It had been hoped that the proposed treaty with the Indians North of the Ohio would have entirely restrained their depredations until the results should have been known. And although this will probably be the case as it may respect any invasion by considerable bodies of Indians yet the principles of Government among the Savage tribes are too little understood & their manners of living too dispersed to expect that every individual Indian will obey what is understood to have been the injunction of their towns — inhabiting any wanton form attacking on our frontier.

The President of the United States has particularly directed me to inform your Excellency that the proposed treaty will be held at this town [undecipherable] to commence about the first of June next. That among the continuance of the Treaty it is of the highest importance to the success thereof as well as the safety of the Commissioners that all hostile incursions of the White Inhabitants into or near to the Indian Country North of the Ohio should be absolutely prohibited until after the Treaty be closed.

The Commanding General of the Troops has been directed to issue a proclamation to this effect and the President requests that you would be pleased to take such measures on the part of your frontier [undecipherable] as shall in your Judgment be most effectual to prevent a measure which might be attended with highly pernicious consequences.

I have the honor to be &
Signed H Knox

His Excellency
The Governor of Virginia

Dear Sir,

Sunday noon I was honored with yours of the 12<sup>th</sup> inst — in which you have given me the arrangement of the general officers. It is far from my wishes to occasion any needless delay in giving my answer. But [undecipherable] as I am, so remote from the seat of government, it is out of my power to avail myself of such information as is necessary for me to form an opinion in my own mind. I shall therefore take the liberty of delaying an answer to the official letter & the Secretary of war till I can be favored with an answer hereto. I may perhaps mistake the point of propriety, but I conceive no person can give me the needful information but you, & whatever you may think fit to communicate confidentially, will find a safe repository within my own breast.

Three things occur to me as pre-requisites to a statement of the general question of acceptance or non-acceptance, in my own mind. All of them are interesting — the [undecipherable] to my honour. They are whether the order of appointment [viz:] Morgan, [undecipherable]: & Brooks as exhibited in your letter be conformable to the relative rank of the appointed, in the late army? Is it not by that principle is present rank to be ascertained? — what time will be allowed me, in case of acceptance, for the arrangement of my private & domestic concerns; & in the last place what is the probability of permanence?

Under the first article I conceive there can be no question, but between Gen<sup>l</sup> Willett & myself. As it strikes my mind priority of rank was, in the late army, in my favor.

Under the second, such is the state of my books, that is, so numerous are my existing accounts, that a considerable time will be wanting for me to bring them to a close.

The business of the last may be perhaps only conjectural; but a degree of evidence is necessary to form an opinion of probabilities.

From this sketch you will discern my views. You may rely that so soon as I am favored with a line from you, my ultimate determination shall be forwarded. With every sentiment of respect & esteem, I am, Dear Sir
Your most obed<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

J. Brooks.

Medford April 24<sup>th</sup> 1792.

The Hon<sup>ble</sup> Henry Knox Esq<sup>r</sup>

42835:

[1792]

[Chapin]

Special Instructions to Israel Chapin Esquire
Deputy temporary Agent to the Five Nations of
Indians, the Stockbridge Indians included

1<sup>st</sup> By the stipulation recited in your General
Instructions, and the annexed Speech delivered
to the said nations of Indians, at Philadel-
=phia the 25<sup>th</sup> day of April 1792, will be seen
the appropriation of Fifteen hundred dollars
annually, and the general mode of applying
that bounty of the United States to the use of
those nations in connection with which the
following instructions are to be attended to.
If however, in carrying the plan into execution
any material alterations should be thought ex-
-pedient, you are to represent the same. —

2<sup>d</sup> The choice of Schoolmasters, blacksmiths
and Carpenters, is left with you, but as the suc-
cess of the plan will depend on the selection of
proper characters for those employments, you
are to use all possible care to choose such only
as sustain fair reputations; men of perfect
temperance, of unblemished integrity, and unaf-
-fected reverence for Religion,— Profane and
vicious persons would do more hurt by their
examples, than all their Instructions would do
good.

3<sup>d</sup> If you can find men practically acquainted
with husbandry, who have competent abilities
and learning to be Schoolmasters, such are to be
preferred. But however this may happen, the
Schoolmaster's attention will be so much occupied
with their schools, that occasional help, and per-
haps the constant assistance of a sober young
man may be necessary in the management of
their farms.—

4<sup>th</sup> If blacksmiths can be found, who
are competent to the repairs of the Indians Guns,
such one to be preferred: otherwise they must
each procure a sober Gunsmith for the purpose.

5. The Carpenters ought to be Wheelwrights,
or at least capable of repairing Wheels.

6. The Schoolmasters, blacksmiths and Carpen-
-ters should in preference be married men; and
must each be provided with a yoak of Oxen
and a cow or two, and the implements of Hus-
-bandry: one Bull at each establishment, will
answer for all of them. The blacksmith and
Carpenter must have the requisite tools of their
trades. The persons you may find most ready
to engage in this undertaking, will perhaps —
need assistance in providing all those things, which
assistance you will furnish, with the money
which shall be sent you for that purpose.—

An estimate of the expence of these articles and
other parts of the Institution is annexed. It is
supposed to be liberal: if you can provide them
at less expence, you will do it. In all cases
you are to study the strictest œconomy.—

7. The wives of the persons you engage
are to teach the Indian girls to spin, Sew, knit
and do all sorts of business proper for farmers
wives to be acquainted with. If either of them
is a weaver, She is also to teach some of the In-
-dian girls to weave. But they should be imme-
-diately taught to spin: for which purpose wheels
and Flax should be provided as soon as the
establishments are formed.

8. The farms of the Schoolmaster, blacksmith
and Carpenter should lie together and the School-
house erected near them. The farms will then
be easily fenced: the three Families will form
a little society, and their Children will be near
the School. The Indian children also, who go to
school, will be at hand to work on the Farms, more
or less daily, and some of them with the blacksmith
and Carpenter. —

9. To learn to milk Cows and do household
work, the girls may be divided into classes, and
attend in the white families weekly in succession,
at the same time going to School certain Hours
every day.

10. Not only children, but young men and
young women desirous to learn any of the arts
proposed, should be admitted freely to all the advant-
-ages the institution can afford. And it may not
be adviseable at first to attempt the instruction
of any children under ten years old. —

11. On Sundays the Schoolmaster should give
his Scholars information of [underline: the works of creation,]
in order to lead them up to [underline: the Creator;] and thence
deduce their obligations to him. He should instruct
them in the duties they owe to each other as mem-
-bers of Society, and to all people, of whatever colour
as children of the great Spirit, whose parental
kindness extends to all. But he should, for some
time make no attempt to teach them the peculiar
doctrines of Revealed Religion; excepting those
Indians to whom any of its mysteries have
been already unfolded.

12. The government to which the Indians have
been accustomed is so gentle, every thing bearing
the semblance of [underline: severity] must be avoided: not a
blow must be struck, nor any reproof given but
with mildness and in the form of [underline: advice:] neither
must it be attempted to employ them in any
Services in which the white people and their chil-
-dren do not Participate. This shows how necessa-
-ry it will be for the persons you engage to possess
good dispositions with the other qualifications
which have been mentioned. —

13. As these establishments are intended for the
benefit of the Indians nothing must be per-
-mitted which will in any measure defeat
their design, or lessen the good effects expected
from them; The Schoolmasters therefore are to
instruct none but Indians; excepting the
children of the deputy Agent and the persons
employed as members of the Institution. Nor
are the blacksmith, and Carpenter to do any
work, except for the Indians and the White
People so employed.

14. You are to keep a regular account of all
expenditures of public money and take proper
vouchers, and from time to time to report your
Proceedings to me as often as once a quarter of
course and oftner if required. —

The following encouragements to be pro-
-posed to the Indians to engage them in these
improvements.

1. During the first year, some of the
young men may learn to mow and make hay,
to drive a team and to plough. To every nation
in which such young men shall be found
there may be given at least one yoak of Oxen
a Chain, a Plough and Cart.

2. After the second year, when more of the young
men become acquainted with Farming and make
Hay and Fodder enough to keep more Cattle over
winter, more may from time to time be furnished:
observing in these gifts a convenient proportion to
the number and wants of each Nation. Until they
can make hay it will be a mere waste to give
them Cattle;—

3. Any young men who shall be thus fur-
-nished with Oxen who will take proper care of them
and assist the people of their Villages in the use
of them, especially in ploughing the Fields of the
poor women who have no men to help them, and
continue to give this assistance during three
years, shall afterwards have the oxen for their
own, exclusively to use in the cultivation of
their own Fields, or in working for their neigh-
-bours, for such hire as they can agree on; until
the oxen shall be of an age requiring them to be
fattened, when the deputy Agent shall receive
them, giving to each of the owners a young pair
of equal value.

4. As blacksmiths will be very useful
to the Indians — to encourage some young men to
learn the art, there shall be given to each one a
set of tools as soon as he becomes master of the
Art, until the smallest Nation has one blacksmith
so furnished with [strikethrough: tools,] and the largest with one or two

5. In like manner such as learn the Carpenters
trade shall be furnished with Carpenters tools.

6. Every boy and girl using for one year, reason-
-able diligence in learning the arts prescribed, shall
receive a blanket and breech-clout, and a shirt
or shift.

7. At the close of the second year, every
boy who has learned to read without Spelling
to write Joining hand, and to perform the first
plain operations in arithmetic, and who at the
same time has made a reasonable progress in the
practice of Husbandry, shall receive a suit
of Cloaths, consisting of a plain cloth Coat, waist
coat, over alls, shirt and woolen Hatt. —

8. Every girl who in two years, shall have
acquired equal Skill in reading, and learned
to spin well, to sew, knit, milk cows, and perform
the other common business suitable for Farmers
wives, shall receive a suit of cloaths, consisting
of a short gown, woolen waist coat, a petticoat
and woolen Hatt.

9. In addition to the foregoing encourage-
-ments, at the end of three years, as many as [underline: two]
and not exceeding [underline: six] of the most meritorious
young men in each Nation, who shall have
attained to twenty years of age, or upwards, and
shall by the course of Instruction proposed, have
become good Farmers and are temperate and
Industrious — and who are married to as many
sober and industrious young women, who can
card, spin, knit, sew, milk cows, and manage
houshold affairs in the manner of Farmers
wives among white people — shall be presented
each couple, with a cow, a pig, an axe, a hoe,
a Spinning wheel and Reel. —

10. As the success of this plan of improve-
-ment may be promoted by the good dispositions
and advice of the chiefs; and because the United
States will take pleasure in contributing to their
comfort and convenience — The deputy Agent
is to give to the Head Chief of each village, con-
-taining at least thirty Families, one good milk
cow, as soon as such chief shall have provided
a shelter of good Fodder, sufficient for her wintering;
Some breeding Sows and boars may be distributed
in the principal villages. —

The whole encouragement to be effected
out of the annual bounty of Fifteen hundred
dollars.— This the Indians were expressly told; the
progress is to be very gradual, in order to confine
the expenditures within the limits of the bounty.

in the City of Philadelphia, this twenty eighth

War department

April 28. 1792

Gentlemen

You are hereby appointed to conduct the Seneka Indians now in this city, and those of the other tribes who accompany them, to the Genesee Country —

Your route will be hence to Bethlehem, thence to Wyoming — Newton point Flanandagwe igenisee — where I suppose the Indians will disperse.

Waggons are furnished in order to carry their bagage to the Wind Gap.

You will use your highest exertions to keep the Indians sober on the route by representing to them the disgrace and pernicious consequences of a contrary conduct.

Indeed it will be much in your power to effect this object as they will be unable to obtain liquor but through you —

I have directed to be placed in the hands of M<sup>r</sup> Joseph Smith in order to defray the expenses of this journey the Sum of Five hundred and thirty three Dollars and one third —

He must keep a daily account of his expenditures always taking receipts for every payment, and upon his arrival at General Chapin's he must render the account and pay into his hands any balance which may remain.

As you value your reputation you must regulate your expenditures by œconomy taking care however that the Indians are comfortably accomodated on the Road.

I am
Gentlemen
Your obed<sup>t</sup> Servant
signed
H Knox

[Mess<sup>rs</sup> Jones and Smith
Interpreters to the five Nations
in behalf of the United States.]

Departamento de la Guerra. 20 de Abril de 1792—Muy S.<sup>or</sup> mio he recibido con mucho gusto el regreso de Vm a esta tailapia —

Aunque es satisfactorio tener noticias de Vm. por medio de un tercio si, sin embargo desearía mas que con pecuenacia, y ampliamente me escribiere x [undecipherable] en tiempo.

El trabajo hecho en Nueva York entre los criados unidos con Vm y los otros Jefes catabuches añade mucho de echoles fundamentos a una nueva felicidad para esa Nacion, si de él se hace el uso propio, y conveniente. El fuego entonces encendido se que se le suministre a tiempo en tiempo pabulo, para que sea perpetuo

La presencia del Impostor Bowles, y la aventura de Vm (supongo en consecuencia de aquellas) ha ocasionado alguna incomodidad, pero felizmente el amor a este oficio ha dirigido al Gobio.

Espero sinceramente que Vm. arregle inmediatamente sus cosas con M.<sup>r</sup> Seagrove para fixar las lindeas de los limites conforme al tratado de Nueva York. Un señorío demasiado de la naturaleza humana para no permitir que qualquiera de

no necesaria demora producirá una comodidad en timientes, viendo por tanto al interes de todos se moven, y prevenir todo motivo de mala inteligencia.

El sistema que el Presidente de los Estados Unidos, y el Gobierno general han adoptado con respecto a los negocios de los Indios esta tan lleno se atenciones a ellos, que todo hombre de bien debe deleitarse en promover sus miras.

No se piden riquezas a los Indios, nadie mar se solicita ellos que lo que puede contribuir a su felicidad, y propia dicha. M.<sup>r</sup> Seagrove a quien tengo exante exteriormente, explicara a Vm. todos, y cada una de las disposiciones del Gobierno para su satisfaccion.

Se estan poniendo en execucion todos los medios, que se han juzgado conducentes a inducir los Indios al Norueste del Ohio a que hagan las paz, y deseamos con ansia que produzcan efecto.

Pero si los dichos Indios despues de estar plenamente convencidos de las humanas intenciones de los Estados unidos continuaren a sus depredaciones sobre los indefensos frontera

aquellos, la misma humanidad deberia un verso contigo.

En este, y único conocimiento unas cientos, o docientos guerreros de esa Nacion a lo mas se emplearian ventajosamente con nuestro Ejercito.

Tenga Vm. la complacencia de observar ante esto: pronto que si esos Indios no se unen con nosotros, se juntaran con los Indios enemigos; pero ruego a Dios que ni se uno, ni esto Lado sea necesario.

M.<sup>r</sup> Seagrove manifestara a Vm. las particulares instrucciones que tiene sobre el asunto.

Tengo la satisfaccion de informar a Vm. que su sobrino esta bueno, que crece mucho; que aprende con la expedicion que puede Severse, que esta con unido; y que su conducta es irreprehensible, prueba y su aprovechamiento: escribo al Vm. la incluira.

Soy a Vm Señor, con la mayor atencion, y estima su mas humilde servidor, y amigo. [undecipherable]

The Secretary for the Department of War, to whom was referred the Petition of Samuel B. Turner, late an Ensign of the Maryland Battalion of Levies, on the expedition under Major General St. Clair—

Respectfully Reports.

That the petitioner was taken prisoner by the Indians, who defeated the troops under Major General St. Clair on the fourth of November, one thousand seven hundred and ninety one.

That after some short residence at the Indian towns, he was at the instance of a French trader sent to Detroit.

That Major Smith, the commanding Officer of the said post, exhibited on this occasion as well as on many previous cases, the greatest humanity. He directed that the petitioner should be furnished with a credit by some of the traders, whereby he not only paid his ransom to the Indians, amounting to forty two dollars as the petitioner informed the subscriber, but he also cloathed himself, and obtained the means of subsistence to Niagara.

That at Niagara the petitioner was furnished with a sum of money by Colonel Gordon, commanding officer, to the amount of thirty seven dollars and fifty cents.

That the object of the petitioner is to obtain from the public, in whose service he was captured, the expences attending his captivity, amounting to two hundred and sixty four dollars, forty five cents.

That the petitioner is equitably entitled to his pay and subsistence from the fourth of November, the time of his captivity, until the time of his arrival at his own home, amounting probably to about one hundred and thirty dollars, which he has received in part, some vouchers being wanting in order to ascertain the precise amount.

That it was a custom during the late war, that officers who were taken prisoners, continued to receive their pay and subsistence during the time they remained prisoners; but it does not appear to have been the practice that any extra expences were paid, excepting for medical assistance, and the additional price of one third of the price of the rations allowed to Officers not in captivity.

The question which appears to arise on the application of the petitioner is, how far the nature of the service on which he was employed, ought to create a deviation from the former practice?

In considering the question, the difference of treatment to prisoners taken by a civilized or savage enemy, presents itself— in the former case the lives of prisoners are generally spared; in the latter they are generally sacrificed.

If the Indians were certain of prompt payment of the ransom, they would probably be induced to spare the lives of their prisoners. If the Officers and Soldiers were certain that in cases of captivity, their ransom and all other expences would be paid by the public, it would probably stimulate to the highest discharge of duty, at very personal risque.

But an objection arises from the probable irregularities of the ransoms which may be stipulated. A person about to be sacrificed to savage fury would be apt to stipulate a pretty high ransom, which if not complied with, the effects might fall heavily on subsequent prisoners.

Besides, if all expences of captivity should be stipulated to be paid, some very exorbitant charges may be made, either from indiscretion or other improper conduct.

Although the impulse of a generous mind may be highly in favor of the petitioner's claim, yet it is to be regretted that its feelings are in a degree restrained by considerations of a general nature.

To grant the prayer of the petitioner in the extent claimed, would be to establish a new principle unsupported by the practice of the late war.

But if a general principle should be fixed, that ransoms and all expences attending captivity shall be paid by the United States, while at the same time the prisoners should receive their full [underline: pay and emoluments], yet certain regulations would necessarily be involved as to the rates which should be allowed for ransoms and expences.

That the ransom the petitioner paid of forty two dollars, appears a reasonable charge and would seem to claim an allowance, if upon mature consideration it should not as a precedent involve disagreeable consequences.

All which is humbly submitted to the Senate of the United States.
H. Knox.
Sec<sup>y</sup>. of War.

War Department,
1<sup>st</sup> May 1792.

Recruiting Instructions
For Captain Jedediah Rodgers appointed
to command a Troop of light dragoons
in the Service of the United States.

SIR,

You are immediately to commence the recruiting service in the States of New York & Connecticut. The principal rendezvous will be at West-Point.

You will recruit for the service of the Cavalry only. No foreigners not to be inlisted — None but white, healthy young men of good character, however, to be raised —

Your recruits will be furnished by The Contractor at West-Point — with rations, barracks, barrack utensils, straw and fuel; and also with such necessary medicinal assistance as they may require.

The recruiting service is sometimes abused, both as it respects the individuals recruited and the public at large,—that is, recruits are unwarily and unworthily entangled, contrary to their intentions: Such men generally desert the Service, at some critical moment, or serve grudgingly, and set bad examples to others; or, unsuitable persons are engaged, who are constitutionally defective and unfit for the hardships incident to a military life.

Although a recruiting officer may require peculiar talents to obtain uncommon success, yet it is in the power of every officer to conduct himself with candor, integrity and industry.

In order therefore to avoid the errors of this business, the following instructions are to serve as the general rules and principles, of your conduct:

1<sup>st</sup>. The recruits are to be inlisted for three years, unless sooner discharged.

2<sup>d</sup>. Each recruit is to receive a bounty of Eight Dollars;—but no part of this sum is to be advanced until the recruit shall have been fairly inlisted and sworn before a Magistrate, according to the form herein prescribed, and then only the said sum is to be advanced in such proportions as the judgment of the recruiting officer shall dictate, until experience shall in some degree have ascertained the fidelity of the recruit. Any money advanced contrary to this direction, will be at the risque of the recruiting officer.

3<sup>d</sup>. Every recruiting officer will be allowed the sum of Two Dollars, for the trouble and expense of inlisting each recruit—provided however that this allowance will not be made for any recruit who shall desert before he shall march from the rendezvous of the troops in the State where he shall have been recruited.

4<sup>th</sup>. The utmost fairness is to be used by the recruiting officers, in engaging their recruits; no individual therefore is to be inlisted in a state of intoxication, or be sworn until after he shall have been inlisted for the space of twenty-four hours.

5<sup>th</sup>. Each recruit (musicians excepted) must be five feet and five inches in height, without shoes—he must also be healthy, robust, and sound in his limbs and body, in all respects; and to ascertain which he must be thoroughly examined, previously to inlistment; by a Physician or Surgeon—but if, notwithstanding this direction, a recruit should have any secret disease at the time of his Inlistment, the expense of his cure, if retained in service, shall be deducted from his pay.

6<sup>th</sup>. Each recruit, before he is sworn, is to have distinctly read to him the rules and articles of war against mutiny and desertion; and relative to the administration of justice; and also the Act of Congrefs of the 30<sup>th</sup> of April 1790, establishing the rations, clothing, and compensation in cases of disability; and the Act of the 5<sup>th</sup> March 1792, establishing the pay; after which he is to take the following oath, before a Magistrate, to wit:

"I A.B. do solemnly swear (or affirm, as the case may be) to bear true allegiance to the United States of America, and to serve them honestly and faithfully against all their enemies or opposers whatsoever, and to observe and to obey the orders of the President of the United States of America, and the orders of the officers appointed over me according to the articles of war."

7<sup>th</sup>. Each recruit (musicians excepted) must be above eighteen and under forty five years of age.

8<sup>th</sup>. No negro, mulatto, or Indian, to be recruited.

9<sup>th</sup>. [undecipherable: All the recruits?], if possible, to be natives of the country, or persons of good character for fidelity and faithfulness who have been some time settled [strikethrough: who shall [undecipherable] before marching from the place [undecipherable] [undecipherable] [undecipherable] [undecipherable]]
[strikethrough: [undecipherable] [undecipherable] [undecipherable] [undecipherable] [undecipherable]]

10<sup>th</sup>. As soon as the recruits shall be assembled at the rendezvous, they are to be taught, by gentle methods, regularity of conduct, as it shall respect cleanliness of their persons, diet and rooms, and due subordination, and they are to be exercised at least four hours in every day, in the attitudes and other first principles of a soldier.

11<sup>th</sup>. The commanding officer at each place of rendezvous must make out, on every Saturday, a return of the number of recruits under his command, and of the number joined during the course of the week, and transmit the same to the War-Office by the next post; and also such information as he may possefs, of any officer under his command out on the recruiting service.

12<sup>th</sup>. You, or the commanding officer at rendezvous are to sign returns for the issues of all rations, and other necessary supplies for the troops, and on each Saturday, the daily returns made in the week are to be taken up, and one general return to be made out and signed for the rations received in the course of the week, noticing the daily issues.

13<sup>th</sup>. No allowance is to be made for the expenses of a recruit, until he shall join at the rendezvous, the bounty being considered as adequate for that object.

These instructions are to regulate the conduct of the field officers and all others therein concerned, but they are more particularly given to you as captain or commanding officer of the company to be raised in the States of New York & Connecticut, and you are to give copies hereof to your officers, and all others under your orders.

The recruits will be mustered and critically inspected as soon as possible after the company shall be completed, and any deviation from these instructions will be noticed.

The clothing, arms and accoutrements for your recruits will be furnished at West-Point.

It is expected that you will exert yourself in the highest degree in obtaining your proportion of the company about to be raised.—Any remarkable deficiency arising from want of due industry, on your part, will be reported to the President of the United States, and such conduct may be considered by him as a just cause for withholding your commission, in pursuance of the power vested in him by law.

N

Instructions to Captain Hendrick Aupaumut Chief of the Stockbridge Indians.—

You having agreed to repair to the great Council of Indians soon to be held at the Miami River of Lake Erie in order to convince them of the moderation Justice and desire of the United States for peace, and to regard this letter as the general rule of your conduct.

You will immediately repair to General Isaac Chapin in the Genesee Country having the charge of Indian Affairs in that district. He will accompany you to Buffaloe Creek or such other place upon Lake Erie as shall be agreed upon and make arrangements for your immediate departure for the Miami River.—

Upon your arrival at the Assembled Council, you will in the manner you shall judge best, inform the said Indians of the desire of the United States for peace. That they claim no Indian Lands but those purchased at a fair Treaty. That all the stories they have heard to the Contrary must be disbelieved. You having been informed upon this Subject, and being furnished with

with a Map of our Claims will be able to be precise upon this Subject.—

They must be sensible if they will reflect that our desires of peace do not arise from any fear of a War, but for the sake of humanity.

Inform them that we have also dispatched officers from the Ohio to them in order to give to them the same information, and that they must treat those officers kindly.—

You will also inform them that General Putnam will be sent by the President of the United States to conclude a treaty, and that in order to this end he will be at Fort Jefferson, our advanced Post, to which place they must send an escort to receive him, which escort you will accompany.

That if they are desirous of peace they must instantly dispatch summons to call in all their war parties, and that until the issue of these offers are made known, they may not be apprehensive of our striking their Towns.—

As General Putnam will be waiting at Fort Jefferson, it will be absolutely necessary that you should go personally and inform him of the dispositions of the Council of Indians whether favorable, or otherwise.— The

The business on which you are employed is of high importance to the United States, and honorable to yourself. In order to execute it properly will well deserve your highest exertions and perseverance. Let nothing therefore be wanting on your part, but push forward with all your might.—

Given under my hand in the City of Philadelphia this 8<sup>th</sup> day of May 1792.—

H. Knox

We find by yours of the 9<sup>th</sup> Inst. that we are directed to furnish supplies at posts not mentioned in yours of the 7<sup>th</sup> Inst. It may sufficed to say that we engage in the whole business at twelve Cents ration for all those places put at that rate in yours of the 7<sup>th</sup> and also for Chester Town Maryland; and at ten Cents for all other posts not comprehended in our Contract made with the Secretary of the Treasury on the 27<sup>th</sup> September 1791.

We thank you for your intimations respecting the supplies may probably be [strikethrough: needed] required this the summer as we shall thereupon make such deposits as will prepare us for all cases of emergency, and our utmost endeavours shall not be wanting to meet the wishes of the Commanding Officer in every thing dependant on us.

We have the honor to inform you that we have in store at Forts Washington, Hamilton & Jefferson.    300 thousand rations of flour
250 thousand of meat
An adequate quantity of Whiskey for the issues
In Kentucky about 150 head of fat Cattle
On the Monongahela 2000 Barrels of flour and a large quantity of Whiskey.
The other posts have at least three months supplies for the present Garrisons.

Our supplies are principally at Fort Washington and the interior posts North of it, our meat is nearly all obtained from Kentucky, and the difficulty of transporting it to the falls of Muskingum would be immense; under those considerations we pray that in case of a treaty the Miami may have the preference, provided there shall be no material objection on the part of the Indians.  When the price of the ration at the two places is compared it may readily be conceived that the fear of difficulty and disappointment and not mere motives of advantage, has induced us to take the liberty of making this request.

We have the honor to be

Upper Creeks Little Tallasie 18 May 1792.

Dear Sir.

I received your letter of 7 Instant. You have no doubt been expecting me some time. I had been waiting this Month past to get our Lower Gentry into humour of attending to national matters, and to recover from the confusion they had been thrown into by the Talks of the lying Chaplain — after he was seized by the Spaniards I had some hopes of their soon forgetting him and his British Pills. When to my surprise some Indians from Orleans have given and spread reports that has made matters worse than ever, and a Spanish Officer has actually arrived and tells the Indians that he has orders to prevent them from running the line or doing any other business with the Americans. And invites to a Meeting in September next at Pensacola. This last stroke is too much — The Indians at least a good many are as mad as ever and Bowles's partisans again getting loud about giving away land. Its no wonder that the Indians are distracted when they are tampered with on

every

conferate — and now engraft in the character of a Keeper of Bedlam and nearly fit for an Inhabitant.

Finding that the Bufistah Chiefs are still at home I cannot carry a Talk drawing them in more pressing language to go directly and have the honour, but since Bowles has given hope of British aid a Majority of the Towns would agree to cede no more than the East Side of Oconnee — and some they are told to give none at all and I seek that more may not be insisted upon, to prevent a worse dispute which must conse quence a [strikethrough: state of] war, in which they will be supported and in which I will not have my hand.

I am hastening to go and get an explanation from the higher powers and the reasons for their interference. As yet I cannot guess at their motives — You are no stranger to Mississipí politics.

The Indians will keep off these Spanish talks of themselves —

Dear General

from a Conversation we had whilst I was at Philadelphia you had reason to presume that the appointment which you have since offered me, would have been accepted without hesitation — Indeed I should then have gave little doubt on the subject —

To the Wyandott and Ottawa Nations of Indians, and all the red people living on Sandusky River & the Lakes in the Neighbourhood.

Sachems, Chiefs & Warriors.

Listen to the Voice of reason, it as with willing Ears: see with Open Eyes, and incline your Hearts to Peace; The Chief who addresses you, Respects you because you are true Men, and loves you because you are Good Warriors. He is now growing old, but is desirous to take the Hatchet, take you by the Hand and call you Brothers.

By order of General Washington, the Head Chief of the United States of America; I sent three young men, in the beginning of last month, with a talk, directed to all the Nations now at war, a copy of which talk I herewith send you: My young men were directed to Keep the big road, by which the Army Marched to Kaskinga, this fall before last, and they have now been absent forty four days since the departure of these young men, a big [undecipherable] has arrived here with a quiet talk from

our Father Washington and to morrow he will proceed with it towards the Ohio River.

Chiefs and Warriors.

This is the reason why I send this short talk to you, particularly at this time, is: because I have confidence in your Skills, and your wisdom, and that I wish you to repair immediately with the Bearer to [undecipherable], there to hear the talk of our Father General Washington, to have your Eyes Opened, and your Hearts, but at least, but if this should be disagreeable to you, it is my wish that all your Chiefs, should come immediately to this place up to Pittsburg for, and from thence to Philadelphia, where our Father waits to take you by the hand of friendship, and to convince you that bad and wicked men have been the cause of the War between us, and the Blood we have spilt.

Gen<sup>l</sup>. Hull —]

Newton 20<sup>th</sup> May 1792.

Dear Sir,

I have received your letter of the 20<sup>th</sup> inst. Before the recept of this you will doubtless receive mine of the 17<sup>th</sup> & 20<sup>th</sup> inst.

By that of the 20<sup>th</sup> you will find, I have declined the appointment, which was profferd by your goodness. I will recollect the conversations we had on the subject.

The one was previous to any appointment being made. The other, near the morning I left Philadelphia. In the first instance I felt a wish for an appointment and very candidly expressed it to you. Had it been made at that time it was my intention to have accepted. It was however not a disappointment or mortification to me that Gen<sup>l</sup> Brooks was preferred.

From my own knowledge of his talents and our relative rank during the war, had it been left to my determination, I should have said he ought to have the preference.

In the other conference, you observed, that if General Brooks should not accept, it was probable the appointment would be offered to me — If I rightly remember, my only reply was, "that Gen<sup>t</sup> Brooks would doubtless accept". I am willing however freely

to acknowledge, that even at that time, my feelings were in favor of the appointment. Otherwise I should very explicitly have desired you not to make any contract in my favor.

When I received your letter at the 6<sup>th</sup> of May, it became necessary for me to make a determination, which was not of much importance, except as it respected myself and family.

On my arrival home, I found my Father in law Judge Fuller in a very ill State of health. He has no expectation of living but a short time. For a country gentleman, he posesses a very independent property. Mrs Hull is his only Child. When I communicated to him, the contents of your letter, no arguments which I could make use of, would reconcile him to the measure. He considered that I had an intention, not only of abandoning him, but my family, which consists of five Children, the eldest of which is only nine years of age, and five of which are daughters.

A variety of other reasons have been [undecipherable] this Scale, which it is unnecessary to trouble you with, which have had an [undecipherable] other determinations.

I should not have said so much on the subject, had it not been that it is one of the first wishes of my heart to preserve with you a character of consistency and propriety of conduct.

I am with every sentiment of respect and esteem, yours very affectionate

Friend
William Hull.

Han<sup>ble</sup> M<sup>r</sup> Gen<sup>l</sup>. Knox.

To all the Sachems and Warriors of the Tribes inhabiting the Miamis of Jawa River and the Waters of the Wabash River The Wyandots Delawares, Chippawas Ottawas, Pottawatamies, Shawanoes Sweetkitous and all other Indian Nations residing Southward of the Lakes, East of the Missis sippi and Northward of the River Ohio.

Brothers

The Great Council of the United States having taken into consideration the present troubles subsisting between them and their Brothers of different Indian Tribes, have reason to believe in some measure, that these troubles have arisen from mis understandings between the Parties concerned, and being desirous to remove every just ground of complaint, the Great chief General Washington, more than two moons past sent a speech to you by Captain Freeman on the subject of Peace. with you on the purest principle of justice and humanity.

A String of three Branches

A String of two Branches

Brothers You have now heard what I have to say, at present fill your pipes with this Tobacco when you deliberate on this My Speech And above all let the great and good Spirit above guide you in your Councils and you will find that you will be blessed with peace and happiness

June 29, 1792

Sir —

I have received your letter of the 2<sup>d</sup> instant by your Son who with Doctor Allen and Cap<sup>t</sup> Joseph Brant arrived in this City on the 20 instant.

Cap<sup>t</sup> Brant's visit will I flatter myself be productive of great satisfaction to himself, by being made acquainted with the humane views of the President of the United States.

It was well judged to deliver Cap<sup>t</sup> Brants Son the horse you mention —

Doctor Allens account will be settled and paid here — for the sums you advanced him you will be credited —

No Horses have been purchased on the way to this City as the Journey was mostly performed by Water.

For the sums your Son expended down here you will be credited two hundred dollars the has been paid here for his services from the time of his setting out untill his return at the rate of two dollars

p day — And he has advanced to him on your account the further Sum of Six hundred dollars for which you will be held accountable — about two hundred dollars of this sum at the excess, may be expended in order to defray the expences back, which will leave the Sum of four hundred dollars in your hands to be appropriated as the public interests may require.

I am sorry you did not find it convenient to repair to this City, as certain sentiments of oeconomy and modes of management of the Indians might have been more successfully impressed than may be done by letter.

But I beg leave to observe strongly that the system of Indian expences and allowances are by no means to be measured by the helter skelter conduct which was observed under the late management which on several instances was unjustifiably expensive.

None but discreet men having a proper regard to their own characters and who will be content with reasonable compensations, are to be employed in the Indian department under your direction.

As you at present are regarded favorably, as well for your zeal as your oeconomy, it will be important to you that these principles be

manifest in all your future conduct; and while you consider the public good the rule of your actions, you may proceed with a confidence may depend upon support.

As to you being allowed a Clerk, there is no such [undecipherable] — you may however be allowed occasional assistance at a reasonable compensation, but at present, no fixed assistance can be allowed.

Mess<sup>rs</sup> Pierce and Danforth have no exclusive right to trade with the Indians — If they assert any such thing they do no honor to their recommendations and exhibit themselves in the first instance as unworthy of confidence.

This will be manifest when the enclosed copies of the permission be examined and when you are informed that Governor Clinton has also recommended for the same trade Abraham Fowler and John [undecipherable] to whom permissions are also given.

I am Sir
with great regard,
Your humble Servant

My dear Sir,

O'Hara, she is very comfortably accommodated with a decent [underline: Coachee], belonging to M<sup>rs</sup>. O'Hara, and a pair of excellent Horses of my own, with a careful driver accustomed to the road; in addition to which they have three Saddle Horses, one for herself, another for one of her little boys & one for Harrison to ride occasionally: thus appointed, they took their departure on the 4<sup>th</sup>; I had the pleasure with some other Gentlemen & a party of Dragoons, to accompany them seven miles on their way, and am happy to inform

you that M<sup>rs</sup> Wilkinson & her boys, were in high health & Spirits; & felt a confidence of a safe & pleasant journey to the Grand Emporium of America.

Inclosed are duplicates of my Letters of the 16<sup>th</sup> and 26 ult<sup>o</sup>.; perhaps you have not heard the fate of your first messengers named [underline: Freeman], and [underline: Gerrard] — it is said they have been killed by a party of Indians, near the miami villages: Gen<sup>t</sup>. Knox writes me "it would appear that they were taken prisoners, but in the first instance were spared, on asserting they were a flag to the Indian council. they had proceeded some distance, on their way to auglaize as prisoners, but they made so many enquiries of the Indians, relative to the distance of Indian towns, & the names of the water they crossed, that their conductors concluded they were Spies & killed them; which was very disagreeable to the chiefs at Au Glaize."

I hope that your other messengers of peace may meet a better fate; we are very anxious to hear the result of the Indian Council; & have some friendly Indians at it, from whom we expect the earliest intelligence: Every thing is quiet here: several detachments

of troops are on their march; but none yet arrived —

The President has not Determined upon the Companies that are to compose the Sub-Legions.

I have directed the purchase of a quantity of very fine grained powder, which with a little alteration in the touchhole of the Musket, in an oblique, in place of a right-angular direction with the caliber, will preclude the necessity of priming; as the concussion of the air, in forcing down the cartridge will cause each Musket to prime itself with more certainty than the common mode; the Eye of the Soldier, will therefore, be perpetually upon his Enemy, and he can load in a full [underline: trot] without danger of losing any part of his powder; ashe will have no other motion, but biting off the top & introducing the cartridge into the piece, and much quicker, than he could load standing in the usual way — This is a manoeuvre that must be practised, it will accustom the recruit

to the report of his own Musket, so as not to be alarmed at his own fire, which in addition to a powerful & well appointed Cavalry, I trust we shall produce a conviction, not only to the Indians, but to the world, that the United States of America are not to be insulted with impunity. —

I am with sincere Esteem your assured friend
& most ob<sup>t</sup>. Hum<sup>d</sup>. Serv<sup>t</sup>.

Anty Wayne

Bell informs me (corroborated by the report from Vincence) that the Shawanese met a Flag on the main trace — five or six days travel from Fort Washington, fired on them, Killed three dead on the spot, the Person who carried the Flag, leapt his ground. The Indians came up & took him, kept him a few minutes & killed him. They took all their Papers & a commission back to their town — examination by some Person who understood English they were found to be great Talks from the White Chief & were very wrong for what they had done —

Adieu my dear Sir, I believe that I am

War department
July 12. 1792

Sir

Captain Mills is instructed to muster and inspect your recruits and to place in your hands one Months pay for them. He will also deliver you four Months pay and three Months subsistence and forage for yourself — and four Months pay and three Months subsistence and forage for Cornet Van Rensselaer — and a further sum of fifty dollars for the contingent expences of your march.

As soon as the clothing arrives and which is now on the road to New Brunswick, I request that after clothing your men, you will immediately commence your march, agreeably to the orders which are enclosed.

You will apply to M<sup>r</sup> Bray to furnish you a waggon to transport the baggage of your detachment from Brunswick to Trenton — where M<sup>r</sup> Hunt will accomodate you in the same manner to Reading in Pennsylvania — At Reading James Collins Esq<sup>r</sup> will procure you the means of transportation to Pittsburg —

Let me hear from you by every opportunity while on the march —

I am
Sir
Your humble Servant —

43231:
Captain Jedediah Rodgers of the Cavalry in the Service of the United States.

SIR,

Your detachment having been mustered and inspected, and being prepared for marching for the frontiers, you are to commence your march accordingly for Pittsburg.

Your route will be from New Brunswick to Trenton in New Jersey- from thence to Reading in Pennsylvania- Harris's ferry- Carlile- Shippensburg- Bedford to Pittsburg.

you will draw provisions at New Brunswick- Trenton- Reading- Carlile- Bedford- and Pittsburg, from the Contractors.

You will pursue your march with all diligence consistently with the health of your men.

You will keep a regular journal, noticing the weather and distances of each day's march; a copy of which you are to transmit to the War Office; and also of the time of your arrival

On your arrival at that place you will receive further orders from Major General Wayne.

The expences incident to the march, such as straw, ferriages and fuel, are to be paid for, and regular accounts and vouchers are to be obtained for every payment. You have furnished you on this account, the sum of [strikethrough: ——] Fifty dollars, for which you are held accountable.

Every officer commanding a detachment of the troops of the United States, while on the march to the frontiers, will be held responsible, that the conduct of his detachment shall be conformably to the most perfect good order and discipline.

The civil authority is to be held in the highest respect. The inhabitants on the route are to be treated with civility and decency: any offence against this order, is to be punished on the spot.

No property of any sort is to be taken without a fair purchase and payment.

The troops are to be encamped every evening, and the officers are always to encamp with their companies.

War Department,
July 19 1792

Sir

I have the honor to congratulate you upon the organization of the government of Kentucky and upon your elevation to the office of Chief Magistrate.

I embrace by order of the President of the United States, this early occasion to assure you, that he shall hold the protection of Kentucky against the depredations of the Indians as a primary object of his attention.

That very considerable levies have been made of troops for three years in order to be in a situation by the force of discipline and good order, to take all measures which shall be deemed proper and necessary —

That an Indian War however is considered by the great mass of the citizens of the United States as an event, to be avoided if possible.

That this disposition, combined with principles of just policy have induced the attempt to explain to the Indians the moderate and humane views of the United States, in order that such explanations may lead to the conclusion of a peace upon proper terms,

That as it is probable these negotiations may occupy a considerable portion of time, the President of the United States requests that you would be pleased to issue the most peremptory orders, that no in roads by the Militia of Kentucky be made into the Indian Country until the effects of a pacific overtures be known.

That it is however to be explicitly understood, that this restriction is not to extend to any depredatory parties of Indians, whom it is to be desired, may be punished in an exemplary manner,

The President of the United States expresses his confidence that in case the pacific offers should fail of producing the desired effect, and it should result that force is to decide the contest, that you and the State of Kentucky will exhibit, a lively zeal in co-operating with the army in the manner which may be regulated by the Commanding General, agreeably to the law of the United States.

The commanding Officer of the troops of the United States at Fort Washington had orders in March last to make an effective arrangement for the defensive protection of Kentucky, by calling into Service at the expence of the United States, such scouts or rangers as should upon consultation with Brigadier General Scott be considered as necessary.

Information has accordingly been received that certain Scouts have been ordered into Service, but no rangers.

If it should be your judgment that small parties of rangers should be added to the Scouts to make the defensive protection more perfect, you are hereby authorized to do so at the expence of the Union, and upon the pay and rations established for the troops,

In this case it will be necessary that such parties of rangers should be mustered, upon Oath, at the commencement and termination of their service, and that triplicate copies of these musters should be made out, one to be retained by the officer commanding the party, one to be transmitted to this Office and one to the Paymaster of the troops at Fort Washington.

That upon these rolls being examined and approved, by the Paymaster, Pay abstracts will be formed and certified [undecipherable] who will issue his orders upon the said Paymaster for payment.—

43238:
[No 6]
[From Gen'l Knox, Sec'y of War]

War department
. July 13<sup>th</sup> 1792 —

Sir,

I have had the honor this morning to receive your favor of the 6<sup>th</sup> instant.

The season of the year seems very improper to make any general inoculation of the troops — the precautions which you therefore have taken upon this subject are judicious — that is to obtain a return of the persons who have not had the Disorder, and post them in a situation where they will not probably take it.

Hereafter, when in winter quarters, you could order, if then the measure should appear expedient, all persons who have not had it to receive it by inoculation

You will please to take effective measures to arm, equip & clothe the companies of rifle men stated to you in my letter of the 15<sup>th</sup> ultimo — the rifles accoutrements and clothing have been forwarded to Pittsburgh

I shall immediately direct Thomas Lewis, Howell Lewis and W<sup>m</sup> Preston, or such proportion of them as are raised, to repair to the mouth of the great Kenhawa in order to be armed, equipped & clothed. you will please to order these articles from Fort Pitt under such effectual protection, as shall leave nothing to chance.

Captain Guion has arrived at Brunswick with a full company of ninety five — Cap<sup>t</sup> Rodgers of the Cavalry is expected there hourly — they will both march from that place probably by the 18<sup>th</sup> at furthest.

Lieutenant Davidson, who belongs to Rodgers, will join him at Bedford, with his recruits now at Hagerstown — this troop will be full and you will as soon as they shall arrive at Pittsburgh order them on to Fort Washington in order to be mounted. —

The detachments of Carberry's and W<sup>m</sup> Lewis's companies, amounting to one hundred men marched from Hagers-town on the eighth instant. —

A detachment of fifty recruits from Jersey under Ensign Hunter, will march from Carlisle on, or about the seventeenth.

I have ordered a detachment of Cap<sup>t</sup> Cooke's company of Riflemen, amounting to forty two, who are at Carlile, under Ensign Lee, to either join Hunter's detachment or to march by itself, as Major Thomas Butler shall direct.

Captain Ballard Smith has been exceedingly tardy in moving with his recruits from Richmond. He was sometime detained on account of the non arrival of his tents & camp equipage. but after he had received all these articles, he writes me word he shall still stay at Richmond, until he receives my Orders, whether M<sup>r</sup> — Balfour a Surgeons mate is to march with him — I have ordered this measure, I presume he is on his way, but the detention is very improper on his part.

Lieut. His Campbell of Stakes troop has complained of the Saddles as being defective. If I am to pay credit — first to the workmen who made the Saddles — Secondly — To a Sadler who had no agency in the contract and who was the sworn inspector of them — thirdly to the report of Major Rudulph — the Saddles are perfect — It is true the stuffings may not have been fitted to the horses — but this was the business of the Officer, who ought to have attended to this matter.

I hope the troop has arrived, or will arrive before you receive this letter.

The Detachments of Captains Hannah, Brock & Stevenson will be accelerated by Major Rudulph who has gone forward for that purpose.

I will examine into the arrangements you mention, relative to the Quarter Masters department; and if there are any regulations requisite they shall be forwarded — I do not conceive, how there can be any clashing, between the old and new Quarter Masters — the former has nothing to do with the service but to settle his accounts. —

You have placed the request of Cap<sup>t</sup> Case in its proper point of view.

I enclose you the arrangement of the officers to the four Sub Legions — the principles of which were approved by the President of the United States.

You will therefore, plans to direct this to be carried into execution, and as the troops arrive they will fall into their respective corps.

The President of the United States has directed Major Gaither to repair to Georgia, to take the command of the troops there — Major Call will be ordered to join you.

Major Burbeck, the commanding officer of the artillery, has been sick in this city — he is on the recovery, and will as soon as he is able repair to Head Quarters.

I have ordered Dunlap's daily paper to be forwarded to you, from the first instant — it will be seen there the Disorders which subsist in the troops on the frontiers of France.

The clothing for the old troops, will be in motion for Pittsburgh in the course of ten days.

Our recruits by returns amount to about Sixteen hundred, to which probably may be added by estimate about one hundred and fifty — the success is by no means equal to my expectation & almost precludes the hope of an active campaign this year, even if the conduct of the Indians will require it. —

I have the honor to enclose you the copy of a letter to the Governor of Kentucky.

It will be necessary that you should send an Express to Nashville to prevent the Chickasaws from joining at Fort Washington: to have them repair to that post & to keep them in idleness would be a monstrous evil.

It will however be necessary that some discretion should be vested in this messenger, who therefore ought to be an Officer of Judgment — his conduct to be regulated by circumstances — for if the Indians should refuse our offers and fall upon the frontiers, then you would require the assistance of the Chickasaws, but certainly they would be an embarrassment to you if the negotiations should continue much longer.

If the hostile Indians can be brought to understand us, it is difficult to conceive of the impediments to a peace — but if they will not listen it will be unfortunate for them.

I have not written to General

43243:
N° 6/ To Major Gen<sup>l</sup> Knox — [undecipherable]

Pittsburgh 13<sup>th</sup> July 1792

Dear Sir,

There are no traces of hostile Indians to be discovered upon the borders of the frontiers; all is quiet & the farmers are assiduously employed in harvesting their hay & grain, which I hope they will effect, & secure in safety.

I have directed Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson [undecipherable] to improve the present opportunity (i.e. this temporary suspension of hostilities) to throw as large a supply of provision & forage into Fort Jefferson, and the intermediate posts as circumstances will admit of — no troops have yet arrived — the first & second Regiments are almost destitute of clothing; in fact the language of the commanding officers at the respective posts generally is "that the situation of the troops with respect to clothing is a disgrace to the Service"; for god's sake send it forward (if not already done) that I may have it in my power to shut their clamorous mouths.

I have made a small experiment of the Idea I mentioned to you, respecting the improvement of the Musket, by an alteration in the touch hole i.e. by filling up the [undecipherable], and drilling a new one pretty large in an oblique in place of a right-angular direction with the Caliber; which with a very fine grained powder will most certainly preclude the necessity of priming: the concussion of the air, in forcing down the charge will cause each musket to prime itself with more certainty, in action than the common mode; the eye of the Soldier will therefore be constantly upon his enemy; & he can pursue & load in full trot without danger of losing any part of his powder, as he will have nothing to do, but to bite off the top of the cartridge, & introduce it into the piece, and, much quicker than he could load standing in the ranks in the usual way; this is a measure that must be practised by the light troops — it will accustom them to the report of their own muskets, so as not to be alarmed at their own fire; and with the Aid of a powerful and well appointed Cavalry (should the Indians prefer the Hatchet to the olive branch) I trust will produce a conviction, not only to the savages, but to the world, that the U.S. of America are not to be insulted with impunity — the fire in this way is as three to two standing & as two to one running — and may yet be improved by an equal ramrod. —

I herewith send you a sample of the powder I wish for, pray forward it, with all possible dispatch, if it can be met with or purchased at Double price, for if the present overtures of peace are treated with contempt or neglect, we must not suffer another defeat.

I have the honor to be with sincere esteem and friendship, Sir, y<sup>r</sup> most obed<sup>t</sup> and very hum<sup>ble</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup> —

Anty Wayne.

Treasury Department,
COMPTROLLER's OFFICE,
26th July, 1792.

SIR,

YOU having been appointed Pay-Master of the Troops of the United States, it has become my duty to transmit to you instructions in respect to the forms for keeping and rendering the accounts of your office.

By the act under which you have been appointed, the following duties are assigned to the Pay-Master of the troops of the United States.

*Firstly,* To receive the Pay Abstracts of the Pay-Masters of the several regiments or corps, and compare the same with the Returns or Muster Rolls which shall accompany the said Pay Abstracts.

*Secondly,* To certify accurately to the commanding officer the sums due to the respective corps which shall have been examined as aforesaid.

*Thirdly,* To transmit to the Accountant of the War Department, copies of all reports to the commanding officer, and of the warrants issued thereon.

The monies necessary to enable you to discharge such warrants as may be drawn on you by the commanding officers, will be placed in your hands, in consequence of warrants to be drawn by the Secretary of War on the Treasurer of the United States.

It has been determined by the Secretary at War, that the troops shall hereafter be paid monthly; but as the arrangements for effecting this object in a regular manner will necessarily consume some considerable time, it is proposed, that in the first instance one settlement shall be made to include all the pay which shall be due to the last day of August ensuing.

For this purpose you will cause the Pay-Masters of the different regiments and corps, and the commanding officers of detached garrisons and posts, to be notified that triplicate Muster Rolls will be expected of the state of each company or independent corps, on the said last day of August ensuing; to be made out according to the form herewith transmitted, marked (A.)

In case an inspector shall be present, the Muster Rolls are to be certified by him according to the form prescribed: but in case no inspector shall be present, the Muster Rolls are to be certified by the two senior officers of the company or corps, in case so many shall be present.

Two of the Muster Rolls are forthwith to be transmitted to you, and the third to the Pay-Master of the regiment, corps or detachment.

As an auxiliary check upon the Muster Rolls of companies, you will require from such garrisons and posts as shall be designated to be *paid by detachment,* triplicate Muster Rolls, two of which are to be transmitted to you, and the third to be lodged in the hands of the agent. The form of a Muster Roll for a detachment is herewith transmitted, and is marked (E.) In examining these rolls, it will be necessary, that you refer to the Pay Rolls of the companies or corps from which the men were detached, for the purpose of correcting erroneous entries. The certificate which you are to give on the several rolls, and the manner of proceeding for obtaining a warrant and making payment, will be the same as in the case already stated.

The entries to be made in your books will be few, and it is expected that they will be clear and explicit. For monies which shall be remitted to you by warrants of the Secretary at War on the Treasurer of the United States, you will credit the Treasurer of the United States, and debit an account to be opened under the head of *Cash.* If you shall receive monies from any other quarter you are to debit *Cash,* and credit the person on whose account it was received. For all warrants paid by you the accountable officer named in the warrant is to be charged, and cash credited: and all these accounts are to be balanced by means of a general account to be opened under the head of *Department of War.*

I am, Sir, very respectfully,
Your obedient servant,
OLIVER WOLCOTT, Comp'r.

CALEB SWAN, Esquire,
*Pay-Master of the Troops of
the United States.*
