The pay of the troops is to be made monthly through the hands of the Regimental paymasters, excepting only at such ports and Garrisons as on account of their distance from the Head Quarters of the Army shall be exempted from this regulation by the Secretary of War, or commanding Officer.

The persons who are to act as Agents at detached Garrisons or posts will be designated by the Secretary of War, or commanding Officer, and [strikethrough: will] be considered as Subject in all respects to the same regulations, as Regimental Paymasters, and will therefore exhibit to you monthly Pay rolls and Muster rolls for their respective Garrisons and detachments.

At the end of each month triplicate muster rolls are to be exhibited which are to be framed according to the form (A) and certified either by an Inspector, or in Case there is no Inspector, by the two Senior Officers in Case two shall be present, of the respective companies or Corps — In these muster Rolls are to be included all the persons belonging to the respective companies or Corps, whether present, absent, on Command or on detachment. The Muster Rolls Certified in one of the modes prescribed are to be considered, as indispensible vouchers to the Pay Rolls, and without them, no roll is to be received for examination — triplicate Pay Rolls are also to be exhibited monthly, for each Company according to the form Marked (C) the aggregate amount of which for each regiment, will be entered in the Regimental Pay roll, to be also rendered monthly according to the form D.

The Services which are to be charged in the monthly regimental rolls, will be taken from the muster rolls and will include the whole pay due to the Regiments respectively, except the pay of such troops as shall be mustered as on Service at those Garrisons and posts, where a Special agent shall have been designated by the Secretary of War, or commanding Officer.

After being possessed of the documents before described it will be your duty to compare the said Pay rolls with the musters, and to ascertain the Sums which shall be due thereon — When this is done, you will certify on each Sett of the Pay Rolls the Sums to be paid agreeably to the form annexed to the roll Marked D. One Sett of the pay rolls will then be transmitted to the Commanding Officer, who will grant his warrant on you for the amount, agreeably to the form thereof, on the said Roll D. When a warrant has been obtained, payment is to be made and duplicate receipts taken on the Pay rolls; one of which is to be on the roll to which the warrant is annexed — at the time of payment you will deliver to the Paymaster one Sett of the pay rolls certified as before directed by which he is to be regulated in the distribution of the money.

It will be necessary that you Notify the Several Paymasters by Letter, that no assignments of the pay of a Non Commissioned Officer or private after the first day of June last, are to be considered as valid — and that it is expected of the Paymasters, that they will produce Separate receipts for the Sums advanced on each Pay Roll on the Settlement of their accounts with the accountant of the department of War — In cases where the men are unable to sign their names to receipts for their pay, the Signature of one Commissioned or two Non Commissioned Officers as Witnesses to the payments, will deemed necessary vouchers.

It has been already intimated that on account of the dispersed situation of the Troops in the Western country it has been judged advisable, that certain Garrisons and posts should be paid by detachment — the Stations at which this regulation will be adopted, and the persons who will officiate as Agents, will be designated by the Secretary of War, or Commanding Officer — As this part of the proposed arrangement appears to be most liable to difficulties in the execution, a Strict attention to order will be expected on your part.

You are to observe, that the Muster rolls of each Company, or independant Corps to be rendered according to the form A are to exhibit the names of all persons whether present or absent on Command or on detachment. — And that the pay rolls which are to accompany the said musters are to include all the pay which may be due except the pay of such troops as shall be mustered on Service at those Garrisons & posts for which a Special Agent shall have been designated by the Secretary of War or Commanding Officer. The most pointed attention to this instruction will be requisite to prevent pay being drawn on two Pay Rolls for the Service of the same persons. As an Auxiliary check upon the Muster rolls of Companies you will require from such garrisons and posts, as shall be designated to be paid by detachment, triplicate muster rolls, two of which are to be transmitted to you, and the third to be lodged in the hands of the agent. The form of a Muster Roll for a detachment is herewith transmitted and is Marked (E.) — The muster rolls are to be accompanied with duplicate pay rolls which are to be rendered according to the form Marked F. In examining these rolls, it will be necessary that you refer to the Pay rolls of the Companies or Corps from which the men were detached, for the purpose of correcting erroneous entries. The certificate which you are to give on the Several rolls, and the manner of proceeding for obtaining a Warrant, and making payment, will be the same as in the case already stated.

It may happen, in adjusting pay rolls, where monies have been advanced on account, that balances will appear in favor of the United States; if it shall be in your power to recover any such balances, you will pass duplicate receipts therefor to the party intitled thereto, and credit the amount in your account with the department of War.

The entries to be made in your Books will be few, and it is expected that they will be clear and explicit. For monies which shall be remitted to you by Warrants of the Secretary at War, on the Treasurer of the United States, you will Credit the said Treasurer, and debit an account to be opened under the head of Cash; if you shall receive monies from any other quarter you are to debit Cash, and credit the person on whose account it was received. For all Warrants paid by you the accountable officer named in the warrant is to be charged, & Cash credited — and all these accounts are to be balanced by means of a General account to be opened under the head of Department of War.

You will from time to time, but, at least once in each quarter, make up and transmit your accounts to the accountant for the department of War, for Settlement. The charges to be made in your accounts will in all cases be supported by one Sett of the original Muster rolls, and also by that Sett of the Pay Rolls to which the warrants of the commanding Officer shall be annexed, with proper discharges from the persons or their assigns in whose favor said Warrants shall be drawn — The credits will consist of monies which shall be remitted to you by the Treasurer of the United States, on account of Warrants to be drawn by the Secretary of War in your favor, and of such monies (if any) as shall be received by you on account of balances apparently due to the United States —

In passing receipts for monies which may be received of individuals, you will take care to specify that Such monies are received on account; as Settlements made by you cannot be considered as definitively binding on the Public —

The Accountant of the War department will transmit to you a list of advances to Officers for the recruiting Service — You will apply to such Officers for their accounts, and will receive any balances which shall appear to be in their hands, for which, as also for the Accounts which they shall deliver to you, you will pass receipts.

For the monies you will pass credits in your Books, and the accounts you will forthwith transmit to the accountant of the War department for Settlement.

As no legislative arrangement has until lately been made for the payment of the Troops, it is possible that difficulties which have not been foreseen may occur in the execution of this System; if this should be the case, you will state them, as also such measures as shall appear to you adviseable to be adopted; but ruled by the instructions shall be received, you will govern yourself by the forms now transmitted subject to the limitations herein contained.

[address:] Irwin Esq.
Pay Master to the Troops of the United States

Sir,                                                                     War department.
                                                                          27 July 1792.—

I have the honor to enclose duplicates of my letters to you of the 20<sup>th</sup> & 25 instant, and to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 20<sup>th</sup> instant.

The spirit of desertion manifested in Asheton's detachment is an unpleasant event— the cause I know not excepting it being a depravity of mind disgraceful to human nature. I shall hope for the descriptive list you have mentioned— Asheton ought to have sent it on to this office weekly while on [underline: his long march].

It is a matter of serious consideration how this infamous conduct is to be checked— it is concluded by all men who have examined the question, that severity is not so efficacious as certainty of punishment for crimes— How far hard labour generally adopted instead of death, which the laws allow, and direct, would effect a reformation is to be determined.

An unfavorable position for desertion would be a desireable circumstance, and it is to be hoped your Cavalry will be able to apprehend generally all deserters, which with such other regulations you should adopt may terminate this propensity.

Major Ridoulph will put in motion from Baltimore, Alexandria, Winchester & Shepherds town and Hagerstown about two hundred and fifty recruits, so they may arrive somewhere about the twentieth of next month.

The rifle clothing to complete the companies at the great Kenhawa and the Companies to be clothed at Pittsburgh will be sent off instantly.

Six hundred suits of clothing for the old first regiment is on the way to Pittsburgh— as soon as it arrives you will be pleased to forward it to Fort Washington as all the troops for which it is designed are at & below that Post.

The clothing for the 2d second regiment will be on the road in a few days— some of those troops are on the upper parts of the Ohio, the clothing will be directed as nearly as possible for each company according to the arrangement of the twentieth instant transmitted to you.

Medicines will also be forwarded to Pittsburgh for the use of the troops there— there is an abundance at Fort Washington excepting some particular articles which are provided—

I have applied to the Governor of this State for permission for the rifle officers to recruit out of M'Culley's corps— but he declines it— It may be hoped that about the expiration of the times of the said companies, that you ride the officers of the rifle companies to be at the head of the said companies when they are discharged that they may have an opportunity of enlisting in Continental troops if they think proper. Cap't Butler, Cummons and Springer of the rifle companies of this State are greatly deficient.

The Season is so far advanced that it is not probable any very serious offensive operations can be undertaken before the cold weather sets in.

If this should be the case it will not be proper to endeavor to obtain a body of the Chickasaws to join our army, should they be brought to Fort Washington with the expectation of seeing a large Army ready for serious operations and find it otherwise despair would ensue.

But perhaps they would like to make a stroke the negotiations should be at an end and it shall be Discovered that it was much regret.

The Saddles were all inspected by a sworn inspector who had nothing to do with the contract also with major Ridoulph upon their excellency, but it can easily be conceived that the stuffing would not suit every horse.

The recruits enlisted at all the rendezvous marched & a march may be estimated at about one thousand eight hundred, but from the number, he must be deducted the deserters on the march— I will have an estimate transmitted you from the returns.

Captain Eaton of the fourth Sub Legion recruiting in Vermont will be nearly completed. I have ordered them forward. The regulations for the payment of the troops & the distribution of the Stores, will I hope be ready to be forwarded by the next post.

You will see by the enclosed letter from M'r Halle to M'r O'Hara the prospect of open shores in Kentucky.

Brigadier General Wilkinson will have a large quantity of hay cut for forage in the vicinity of Fort Hamilton.

By a letter from Gen'l Wilkinson received two days ago & dated the 5 and 31 may & 8<sup>th</sup> June it appears that M'r Harmar and Major Prueman left Fort Washington on the 25<sup>th</sup> of May— the former to repair to Sandusky, and the latter to the Glaise on the Maumee river of Lake Erie— It is high time to hear of their fate— it may be momentarily expected— if they shall be received kindly— I think peace will probably be the consequence.

In the dispersed manner in which the troops have been moved, it was impracticable until the troops should be assembled to give the respective Sub Legions distinctive marks.

It is conceived the following will be sufficient.
The First Sub Legion— White binding on the hats & white plumes.
The Second Sub Legion— Red binding to the hats & red plumes.
The Third Sub Legion— Yellow binding & yellow plumes.
The Fourth Sub Legion— No binding— black plumes.
The Officers plain hats with the plumes of their respective Sub Legions.

But when the troops take the field it is conceived that any plumes would not only be unnecessary but improper.

I will order the binding for the men's hats to be forwarded.

By one of your enclosures dated at Clarks Station crooked creek on the 14 instant I regard John Princy Col. I show he estimates the desire of a volunteer expedition against the Indians— it would be difficult for him to find an object within the reach of Volunteers— If Brant's information is to be credited the Wyandots & Delawares have removed from Sandusky to the west side of the Maumee river of Lake Erie— Three hundred or seven hundred volunteers would be utterly inadequate in the present state of things to cross the said Miami— any Volunteer without object would be fruitless to the public & therefore ought not to be undertaken, but while the negotiations are pending, it would be very highly disgraceful & ruinous.

As persons may be wounded or disabled, it is necessary the evidences requisite to entitle them to receive the pensions should be regulated— the following is therefore prescribed, the substance of which was contained in my letter to Brigadier General Wilkinson of the 17<sup>th</sup> instant a copy of which has been transmitted to you.

All Officers and Soldiers entitled by their wounds or other casualty to be placed on the pension list of the United States, must be examined by the principal Surgeon, and the two next seniors present in the medical department, these must certify the nature and degree of the disability— whether it will incapacitate the invalid entirely from labor, or, in what proportion, and whether the disability is probably temporary or permanent.

The officer commanding the Corps to which the invalid belonged, or the post which he is at, must also certify the time and place at which the invalid was disabled, & the circumstances thereof, whether by wounds or other casualties.

These certificates are to be transmitted to the war office through the Commander in chief together with the state in which the invalid chuses to draw his pension.

If the certificates are satisfactory, the invalid will be placed upon the list & he will receive a pension in half yearly payments in proportion to his disability according to law.

All the officers, making the certificates aforesaid will be responsible for the entire truth & propriety thereof.

way from Philadelphia — as soon as it arrives it shall be forwarded under a proper Escort, so as to be delivered as nearly as may be at the same time, in order that we may judge of the comparative [underline: attention] of the company Officers, to the [underline: clothing] of the Soldiers. —

The Secretary of War has received information that a considerable number of Chickasaw Indians, are about to assemble at [underline: Nashville], in order to proceed to Fort Washington to act against the hostile Indians in concert with our army; it will therefore be necessary that you should send an express to [underline: Nashville] to prevent them from advancing to Fort Washington for the present; to have them repair to that post & to keep them idle might be attended with very evil consequences: it will also be proper that some discretional should be vested in the messenger, who ought to be an officer of Judgment — his conduct to be regulated by circumstances — for if the Indians should refuse our offers of peace and fall upon our frontiers — then we shall require the assistance of the Chickasaws — but certainly they would be an embarrassment to us at Fort Washington, if the negotiations should continue much longer —

therefore they must be detained & supported at Nashville, until further orders. —

Three small parties of Indians struck at the frontiers of Ohio County ten days since and killed seven men & wounded a few more — we have a rumour that a Serjeant, Corporal and twelve men were lately killed near Fort Jefferson — by a party of Eighty Indians: it is also reported that Col<sup>o</sup>. Harding and Major Trueman are murdered; I hope it is nothing but rumour I report — however that may be, this kind of anxious suspence — is far more intolerable, than a certain & vigilant war, which if the Savages provoke — by Heavens! they shall feel its keenest effects; nor is a single moment lost in preparing for that event: In the interim, it is of the utmost consequence, that you keep me duly informed of the State of affairs in your quarter, by as constant a correspondence as circumstances will admit of. the last & only letter I have received from you was dated the 12<sup>th</sup> of June & Ensign Harrison. —

You will herewith receive an

Extract from Gen<sup>t</sup>. orders approving the sentence of the general Court Martial on Cap<sup>t</sup>. John Platt, who is dismissed the Service, & Sercombe Howe appointed to the command of the Company late Platts: I sincerely hope that we shall have but few occasions to make like examples, for crimes so Disgraceful to the Service, and to the character of an officer; but I am Determined whenever they appear, that they shall not pass with impunity. —

I send you some of the latest Philadelphia papers, by which you will see the fatal effects of want of Discipline, & due Subordination in the armies of France — we must prevent the most Distant Appearance of that worst of all evils, in the American Legion. —

I am Sir, with very Sincere esteem & friendship your most obed<sup>t</sup>.
& very
hum<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>.
Anty Wayne.

The Hon<sup>bl</sup>.
Brig<sup>t</sup>. Gen<sup>t</sup>. James Wilkinson. —

N°.10.     War department
                August 3. 1792
Sir,

I have received your favor of the 28 ultimo dated at 9 o'clock A.M. — In this you refer for intelligence to a letter written the day before which I have not received — The letter you mention as inclosed for D. Smith was not received.

I am glad to have so good accounts as you give of Gibbons Custons and Springers companies —

In order that there should be neither difficulty or delay in marching Gibbons, Custons, Thomas Sevier and Howell Sevier's recruits, and the recruits under the immediate direction of Captain Henry Royeger of the Cavalry, I have sent Lieutenant Melcher from this [City?] to muster, inspect, accelerate and pay the men one Months pay and three Months pay for the officers of the said companies — They will rendezvous at Queen Briar burnt House and thence proceed to Point Pleasant, to the mouth of the great Kenhawa under the 6 front of Gibbons company which I have reason to believe is complete as to its numbers and which has had [sent?] to it, Arms, Accoutrements Clothing tents &c

Bouyers Recruits will also be completely clothed and furnished with tents and camp equipage —

An Invoice of Clothing for Custons, Thomas Sevier and Howell Sevier companies is enclosed and the clothing will probably be at Pittsburgh in ten days after you receive this letter — Over besides the trifles and equipments thereto belonging and tents for the said three companies which Major Craig must forward he must also send three hundred Canteens, three hundred Knapsacks and three hundred pairs of Shoes.

That half of Flattons company under Dacharros and [undecipherable] must be deducted by Major Craig from the quantity for Flattons company.

I have also sent an invoice of six hundred and sixty suits of clothing for the first Regiment, but Blankets and shoes are wanting to complete them — These articles will be immediately forwarded — the contractors have been [pushed?] accordingly to find suitable Blankets, and the shoes have been manufactured at Morristown in Jersey and with the blankets have been detained by contrary winds.

I have also enclosed an Invoice of two hundred and sixteen suits of Rifle clothing, Hats and blankets excepted which are also on the road — these are together with the two hundred suits before forwarded to Pittsburg for clothing the companies raised in the upper parts of this State and in—

Ohio County, two hundred suits more will soon be in motion.

The clothing for the late Second Regiment on the Ohio is nearly [packed?] and will soon be on its way to Pittsburg

All the saddles and cavalry equipments of every sort which have been or shall be forwarded to Pittsburg for Dragoon, Rangers and [Wintens?] to Pittsburgh which are to be mounted at Fort Washington will within be delivered to such parts of the said troops as may arrive at Pittsburg or they will be forwarded altogether to Fort Washington under the care of the garrison troops as you shall judge proper —

Perhaps they should be all put in the possession of Major Rudolph who will be responsible for the proper delivery of them.

I transmit you a copy of the instructions and regulations from the Comptroller to the Paymaster with the Army — the original was forwarded by the last post to the Paymaster — I submit to you the idea whether it may not be proper for you to direct immediately the troops [stationed?] on the upper parts of the Ohio to do those things required in the instructions and forms.

The directory parts of the instructions designed to produce an uniformity in the returns and forms prescribed should be as general as possible, promulgate [among?] the Officers and perhaps through the medium of general orders, but care should be taken to distinguish between directions to the Paymaster and directory and forms for the Officers and not to publish the forms

H

It is to be regretted that the Pay Master is not with you as it would be his duty to point out what should be published and what should be retained.

I also transmit you certain regulations prescribed for the orderly receiving, distributing, and accounting for all public property designed for the army — I pray for your attentive consideration thereof and after any alterations or additions you judge necessary for the public interests you will please to publish the same in orders and from time to time enforce the observance thereof.

If experience should point out any difficulties or changes I shall be obliged by a communication thereof.

And I also enclose certain regulations relatively to forage proper work. The observance of a proper economy of public property is an important principle of discipline — every particle of public property should be accounted for by some person.

I flatter myself that your command will be distinguished by the highest degree of discipline in all parts of the troops and in the highest attention to the public property.

In the first instance irregularities will be practised and waste [must?] by the carelessness of raw recruits — but I hope the regularity of payments, clothing and other public promises will be such as will afford you the best possible plea for enforcing a perfection of duty from the troops.

H

It is with deep regret I transmit you the enclosed paper marked A, the purport of which I received from M<sup>r</sup>. Robert Morris on the 31 Ultimo.

The number of persons with Major Trueman — the time — and the other circumstances would seem to render the account but too credible.

But on the other hand, there has been a gentleman in this town within a day or two past, but whom I did not see, who says he left Fort Washington after the return of General St. Clair's son, which must have been after the 28 of June, who says the accounts from the Indian Country were favorable by the return of some of the information via the Wabash — I hope and for the information of Trueman be not true — I have not divulged this report here and I request you would keep it to yourself for the present.

Since writing the foregoing I have received your favours of the 27 instant. I am persuaded that your arrangements of Service is formed on just principles.

I am glad to learn that Captain Hendricks had proceeded Westward. I sincerely hope the others will also go. But they are so slow and dilatory as to exhaust all patience. I believe Captain Knox will be at the Council at Au Glaize by the 28 of the present month at furthest.

General Israel Chapin is the Deputy Agent to the Six Nations. I believe that no attempts ought to be made to retain the Indians contrary to his request — Wellborn planter's judgment ought to be conclusive on this

Head — the sincerity of whose attachment cannot be doubted — but he has been too open in his powers to be well received at the Council of the hostile Indians indeed the attempt would be dangerous to him.

The letters communicated by you in confidence relative to the State troops shall be retained — the opinion of the person you mention is indeed extraordinary.

I should be glad was it practicable to receive Major St. Clair and his troops on the establishment — I have an high opinion of his worth and [conduct?] at the time the arrangements were making that he could not be appointed — The State troops Major Clarke and Major Butler who were of the times the last year and whose services merited a reappointment.

* I wrote you last post relative to the Uchee [Indians?] — I am inclin[ed?] to the opinion they ought not to be retained — the reason will be too far advanced to have particular action of them.

I am charmed at the idea of the commencement of discipline — The proof of the powder shall be sent you, it cannot be better — and I hope you will find the grain sufficiently fine — I am unwilling to put the public to the expence of other powder not better in its quality, than that which is on hand — at the same time I am desirous of complying with your wishes — when you receive the sample sent by the last post I will take

the necessary measures on receiving your communications.

I have complained to the Post Master General of the cider I requested him to provide another.

We have no essential information about Recruits since my last; I have written to all the recruiting Officers urging them in the highest degree to complete their complements.

Two of Ashtons deserters have been taken this day — indeed there are five apprehended and in Gaol — I will give the list you have sent to the Constables who for the sake of the reward like to hunt deserters — By the time of Eatons company arriving from Vermont, I expect at least twenty deserters will be apprehended — Major Butler has secured several at Carlisle.

The Sixteen legionary howitzers were forwarded on the 17 Ultimo — there has been a defect in the contractor for the Shells which will soon be remedied — Three pound Balls will suit them.

Three chests of medicines have also been forwarded for the troops on the upper part of the Ohio — the Invoices will be transmitted the next post —

I have the honor to be
with great esteem
your most obd: Servant

H Knox
Secy War

[Maj: Gen<sup>l</sup> Wayne.]

I have the honor of [underline: enclosing] copies of two letters from Mr Rosecrantz of the 19<sup>th</sup> ultimo, and one from Cap<sup>t</sup> Cas of the 27<sup>th</sup>; in addition to these accounts an express arrived last evening from Fort Washington, by which Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson informs me of the loss of a Sergeant, Corporal and fourteen men, who were cutting & curing hay, in the vicinity of Fort Jefferson, by a party of nearly one hundred Indians on the 25<sup>th</sup> of June: & also that on the 7<sup>th</sup> of July a canoe ascending the river, to the neighbouring Settlement of Columbia, was fired upon by a party of Savages within 3 miles of Fort Washington, by which one man was killed and another dangerously wounded & a boy, the only Son of Gen<sup>l</sup> Spencer taken prisoner: but of these affairs you must be fully in[undecipherable]med before this period, as Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson [strikethrough: informs] tells me, that he had dispatched an express by land, with letters to you dated the 6 & 9<sup>th</sup> of July, copies of which he transmitted me on the 12<sup>th</sup> at

at which time no new occurrence had happen'd.

The account from S<sup>t</sup> Vincents, by Mr Vigo of the murder of our flag, is but too well corroborated by that mentioned in Rosecrantz's Letter, brought by an Indian from Detroit— the officer in all probability was Major Trueman; Col<sup>o</sup> Harding as I am informed wore a plain coat or rather hunting Shirt.—

The idea mentioned by Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson in his letter of the 6<sup>th</sup> of July "that a new tribe had engaged in the war, & that they had recently been supplied with clothing from the whiteness of their Shirts"; is also corroborated by a man who was taken prisoner by the Indians, in the course of last summer from the County of Washington, & was lately liberated at Detroit, which place he left some time in June, & arrived in Washington on Monday last, where he was examined by the Lieut. of the County & says that about seven weeks since - or early in June upwards of one hundred Canoes, came by the way of Lake Huron to Detroit (now head quarters) in which were about 800 Indians i.e. eight to a canoe; that the Indians were supply'd at Detroit with clothing, Arms, ammunition & provision in abundance, and immediately proceeded to join the hostile Indians, at the mouth of

of the Miamis or Aumi river, and Lake Erie.— I have not seen this man as yet, but I am informed by a Gentleman of veracity who was present at his examination, that he told his story very short & very particular.—

The report of the massacre of Col<sup>o</sup> Harding and Major Trueman, so recently after that of Trueman & the Frenchman, if true & I really [strikethrough: believe] fear it is true indicates a very vindictive Spirit in the savages, who generally revere a [underline: flag].— can these things be passed by? would it not stamp disgrace upon the american character, in the eye of the world, were such enormities permitted with impunity?— these reports — and they bear but too strong marks of authenticity, leaves little ground to hope for an [underline: honorable] or [underline: lasting peace], should the event be war,— by heaven's the Savages shall experience its keenest effects!

Inclosed is a general monthly return of all the troops at this place; together with copies of General Orders upon the Courts martial of Cap<sup>tn</sup> Shaylor and Cap<sup>tn</sup> John Platt— I have information of two small parties of recruits being near— we have not more than

than twelve complete suits of clothing at this place; nor have we any information of any being actually on the road:— independent of the two hundred & eighty five suits for Cap<sup>t</sup> Tho. Lewis's, Howell Lewis's and W<sup>m</sup> [Prestons] companies— nearly Sixty of Shrimgers and ninety five of Sparks's are yet to be clothed— Cap<sup>t</sup> Sparks was here yesterday and says that he is nearly complete— I have ordered Maj<sup>r</sup> Clark, to muster & march these men to this post the soonest possible & expect them in the course of ten Days, so that there will be four hundred and forty suits wanting for those five companies: I really feel uneasy upon this business— as the troops ordered to point pleasant will probably be obliged to wait there, for some time, in a very [underline: unpleasant] situation; in addition to this it is necessary from present appearances to reinforce Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson with those very riflemen, in order to enable him to procure forage at Fort Jefferson, which is an object of the first consequence as the dismounted Dragoons arrive, I will immediately forward them to him, & direct him to order the Horse to some convenient & safe place on the Kentucky side of the river, ready for mounting; I hope that the arms, & Horse equipments to me forward [undecipherable]

There is however some very reprehensible conduct respecting the transportation of Stores &c: many of the essential articles mentioned in the invoice from the 1<sup>st</sup> of January, until the 30<sup>th</sup> of June 1792 have not yet arrived; & not one single article contained in that from the 1<sup>st</sup> to the 17<sup>th</sup> of July— what can be the cause?

Whilst I am writing I am honor'd with yours of the 27<sup>th</sup> ult<sup>o</sup> with the enclosures— among which is a copy of yours of the 23 No 8 the original has not yet arrived.—

As you do not mention the letters & Express from Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson of the 6<sup>th</sup> & 9<sup>th</sup> with interesting intelligence from Major Hamtramck, I take the liberty to inclose you the Copies sent me by Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson, lest some accident may have happened the express; and as it will be impracticable for me to have them copied in time for the post— I pray you to return the same or Copies, when convenient.

We have a number of sick in our hospital; the last Detachment brought with them another malady, besides the small pox many of the men are afflicted with a virulent Veneri— every precaution

is taken to prevent its spreading; & I mean to levy the men under moderate stoppages who have contracted this malady, to be appropriated for the support & comfort of the children of the army— the duty is too severe for one Physician— Doctor Carmichael is the only Surgeon belonging to the army now at this post— nor has a single one come forward, out of all the late appointments— do, be so good as to order on a [underline: Dozen] of them— Medicine & Medicinal Stores are & will be much wanting at this post.— The cloathing for the rifle men being only now ordered on from Phil<sup>a</sup>— I am almost tempted to direct one hundred more mounted rifle volunteers from Kentucky, in order to insure the cutting & securing forage at Fort Jefferson— should the next information from Mr Rosecrantz be unfavorable, I shall adopt the measure.—

I have the honor to be
Sir,
your most obed<sup>t</sup> & very
hum Serv<sup>t</sup>

Hon. Maj<sup>r</sup> Gen<sup>l</sup> Knox                    Anty Wayne.
Sec<sup>y</sup> of War.—

Pittsburgh 5<sup>th</sup> august 179[2]

Sir,

Since writing you on the 31. ultimo I have been honoured with yours of the 12<sup>th</sup> of July inclosing copies of letters to the Secretary of War, and other papers; I am much obliged by your ideas, [underline: respecting] the Enemy we have to contend with, which perfectly coincide with my own, but I fear that the season will pass over, previously to our knowing the ultimate intentions of the hostile Indians, with respect to peace or war.— nor can we attempt any thing until that event is known, altho from present appearances there can be but little expectation of an honorable [and lasting] peace, with a victorious, [underline: haughty], and insidious enemy— Stimulated by British Emissaries to a continuance of the War— or to dictate terms of peace, perhaps disgraceful to the American character:— but such was the prevailing disposition of a decided majority in Congress— that

that Government, was compelled to adopt the measure of attempting every possible means of procuring peace previously to any hostile [strikethrough: operations].—

I fear that Major Trueman & Col<sup>o</sup> Harding have been martyrs to this State policy— the account brought by Mr Vigo from S<sup>t</sup> Vincents, of their murder is too strongly corroborated by recent intelligence by way of Detroit & Niagara— a Mr Rosecrantz, who is on a mission to and with the Five nations, writes on the 19 ult that a vessel had just arrived from Detroit, in which was an Indian from the mouth of the Miami of Lake Erie, who says that an officer and one man bearing a [underline: flag], were killed on their way to the council of hostile Indians, but that the interpreter— who spoke the Delaware Language very well, was saved and carried on as a prisoner— should this be really the case it will soon be authenticated, as the five nations have sent Cap<sup>ton</sup> Henry, a famous chief of the Onondago nation, with a message from themselves a talk from the president of the U.S. to the hostile Indians, and from whom they expect to hear every hour— Rosecrantz waits his return, notwithstanding all this, I have very little expectation of any real intention of the hostile Indians for a permanent peace and therefore wish it were possible to secure a very large quantity of hay at Fort Jefferson.—

My intention was to reinforce you with the three companies of riflemen mentioned in my last immediately— but unfortunately their clothing is not yet arrived at this place, owing to some unaccountable neglect— I expect the Dragoons for two troops of Cavalry at this place in the course of a few Days; they marched from Trenton & Frederick town between the 20<sup>th</sup> & 24<sup>th</sup> ulto. the moment they arrive I will arm them with Muskets & bayonets, and order them to descend the river for Fort Washington, carrying with them the arms & accoutrements for the Cavalry— You will therefore please to give the necessary orders for the horse upon which they are to be mounted— that have been purchased by the deputy Q.<sup>r</sup> M<sup>r</sup> Gen<sup>l</sup> in Kentucky, to be collected at some safe & convenient place for the purpose— you may certainly expect them to join you within two weeks after the receipt of this; and probably the rifle corps about the same time, or within twenty days at furthest, which I presume would be as early as you could possibly obtain a volunteer rifle corps from Kentucky.

But as the timely arrival of these troops is eventual; you are hereby authorised to retain the hundred mounted volunteers from Kentucky until joined by the troops beforementioned: and if you can do the business without risking too much, do, exert every nerve to secure as great a quantity of hay as [undecipherable: possible] [rifle] at Fort Jefferson.—

August 2<sup>d</sup> 179[2]

Regulations for the receiving distributing and accounting for all Military Stores designated for the Army of the United States

All public Stores destined for the Army of the United States on the Ohio [River] to first [pass and be received] by the [Commissary] of Military Stores or his Deputy at Philadelphia to the Quarter Master General or his Deputy at Pittsburg, who shall transport them to the Detachments to which they belong, or to the Garrisons or detachments for which they are designed, and to take duplicate receipts of the several commanders; [which] shall be transmitted to the Commissary of Military Stores in Philadelphia — The packages or parcels shall be marked or labeled for the Department to which they belong —

The Stores which shall be so provided shall be charged to the respective Departments —

The Ordnance Department comprehends Ordnance and arms and Ordnance and Military Stores of all sorts belonging to arming and accoutering of a Soldier, and all Armourers and Artillery Artificers — The

The Quartermasters Department comprehends all things relative to the transportation of the tools and tents, boxes &c and Accounts and Quartermasters baggage, Camp equipage, Barrack Stores and equipments, Forage, and such other duties as shall be directed by the commanding Officer —

The Hospital Department comprehends the Medicines, Instruments, Hospital Stores and Furniture and all things relative to the sick or wounded of the Army —

The Clothing Department comprehends the clothing for the troops — The' suit taken in Requisitions to be the Agents by which the Clothing shall be received, distributed, and accounted for —

The Indian Department comprehends articles provided by the United States for the use of said Department —

The Quarter Master General, or his Deputies will receive and distribute any thing in his own Department and be accountable for the same —

He will also receive all Indian Goods and [issue] them on the Requisitions of the Superintendent or his Deputy or the Commanding General as the case may be — keeping [separate] accounts of all Issues and deliveries —

The Conductor of Military Stores at [Head] Quarters will receive all Articles in the [Ordnance] Department [except] for the main body of the troops — But articles [designated] for any detachment or garrison on the Ohio will be [transported] directly for such detachment or garrison, and receipts for [it] to the commanding Officer thereof —

The Director of Military Stores shall [have charge of] the Ordnance, Arms, Ammunition and Stores near the [Posts] for the Commanding Officer of Artillery, and the Armourers and Artillery Artificers shall be under the direction of the commanding Officer

of Artillery —

The Medical Instruments and all things belonging to the Hospital Department to be received for by an Hospital Store Keeper, to be appointed and his pay fixed by the commanding General —

The Quarter Master General and his Deputies, the Director of Military Stores and the Hospital Stores Keeper shall keep an account with each and every Battalion, Company, Patrol, Detachment, and Garrison to whom they shall be ordered to deliver Stores, always taking duplicate receipts for the articles delivered —

The commanding Officers of Companies, Troops and Detachments shall account for the inspection returns for all public Articles [named] with the Stores under their orders. And the Sublegionary and battalion Quarter masters, where there are no Staff Officers, and commanding Officers of detached Garrisons, shall account monthly for all public property in their possession —

The Surgeons and Surgeons mates to whom Medicines, Instruments or Hospital Stores shall have been delivered shall account monthly for the same to the Chief Surgeon of the Army —

It is always to be understood that the presence of the commanding General or [to have] every Department [conducted] — the Indian Department where the [frontier] of the Western [territory] or his Deputy shall be present; but for the sake of regularity it would be better that his orders in all practicable cases be addressed to the Heads of Departments —

And whereas the public Service may from time to time require separate Posts and Garrisons and may [at] first [need such] magazines and posts the appointment of subordinate branches of the several Staff Departments — in all such cases the Commandants of those said garrisons are to make returns and issue orders on the several Departments for such articles as shall be delivered to the public — and the said Commandants shall be responsible — as well to the propriety of their returns and orders as for rendering a just account monthly to the Commanding General of all Stores [received, delivered, and on hand]

and an estimate of articles requisite for public Service —

The Quarter Master General, the commanding Officer of Artillery, and one senior Surgeon shall on the 1<sup>st</sup> first day of January, the first day of April, the first day of July and the first day of October, or as often as the nature may require, make out exact quarterly returns in their respective Departments received, [taken] kind on hand, since the last return — noting the serviceable from the unserviceable articles and also estimates of the articles wanted for public service —

Sir,

I have the honor to enclose you a copy of Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson's letter to you of the 9<sup>th</sup> ult<sup>o</sup> which was mentioned in my last of the 3. instant.

I am sorry to inform you, that the report of the murder of Col<sup>s</sup> Harding & Major Trueman by the indians appears to be reduced to a certainty.—

I have this moment examined two men just from Detroit, by the way of Niagara who were taken prisoners by the indians— one of them near Fort Jefferson in the 27<sup>th</sup> of october; and the other M<sup>r</sup> John Cleghorn, near the falls of ohio in april last, who was carried to Michilimackinac, & from thence to Detroit, where he arrived on the 24<sup>th</sup> of June, and says, that whilst he was at Michilimackinac accounts were received that a Captain Harding and one or two others were killed by the indians, and the papers that were found upon them, were sent or given to Capt. M'Kee. he was also informed at Detroit (when the report was common) that a Captain Trueman, & another man were killed, near the miamis towns, by two indians who were in company with them on the Evening— that the indians affected to be very uneasy, upon which Capt. Trueman & tomahawked the man that was] tied— that the interpreter made his escape into a swamp or wood— that the indians called to him & promised not to hurt him— upon which he came to them & they carried him to the Council as a prisoner and reprobated the foolish conduct of Captain Trueman (as they termed it) for suffering the man to be tied— that those papers were also given up to M'Kee, and said this was a fifth flag they had killed, nor had they any intention or wish to make peace with us, as the Americans has already deceived them, both last Summer & before.

Sir,

I am sorry to inform you that the report of the murder of Col<sup>o</sup> Harding & Major Trueman by the indians appears to be but too well founded.

I have this moment examined two men just from Detroit, by the way of Niagara, who were taken prisoners by the indians, one of them near Fort Jefferson on the 27<sup>th</sup> of october, and the other, a M<sup>r</sup> Cleghorn near the falls of Ohio, in april last, who was carried to Michilimackinac, & from thence to Detroit, where he arrived on the 24<sup>th</sup> of June, & says that whilst he was at Michilimackinac, accounts were received that a Capt. Harding & one or two others had been killed by the indians, and the papers that were found on them sent to Capt. McKee— he was also informed at Detroit (where the report was common) that a Capt. Trueman and another man, were killed near the miami towns, by two indians, who were in company with them in the evening; that the indians affected to be very uneasy— upon which Captain Trueman told them they might tie the other man, so, that their numbers should be equal, which was accordingly done— that they then shot Trueman, and tomahawked the man that was tied— that the interpreter made his escape into a swamp or wood— that the indians called to him & promised not to hurt him— upon which he delivered himself up, & they carried him to the Council as a prisoner: and reprobated, the foolish conduct of Trueman, (as they termed it) for suffering the man to be tied: that their papers were also given to McKee— and said this was a fifth flag they had murdered; nor had they any wish or intention to make peace, as they had already been deceived by the Americans, last Summer & before:— He further says that a certain Simon Girty, with Four hundred indians, had left Detroit, some days before he arrived, say about the 15<sup>th</sup> of June; and swore that he would make a stroke upon the americans immediately, & either kill or be killed in the attempt—

Query,— may not this be the person in scarlet, who was seen with the indians, in the attack upon the Serjeants party near Fort Jefferson on the 25<sup>th</sup> of June.— however this Man, Cleghorn, goes with this conveyance to Fort Washington, where you can have an opportunity of examining him more minutely; upon the whole I believe, that the Death of those two unfortunate Gentlemen, is reduced to a certainty.—

You'l please to make Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson acquainted with this information— your letter of the 16<sup>th</sup> ultimo came safe to hand.

I have the honor to be, with Sincere esteem
your most obed<sup>t</sup> & very hum. Serv<sup>t</sup>.

Anty Wayne.

Brig<sup>d</sup> Gen<sup>l</sup>
Rufus Putnam.

[Nº 11  From Gen<sup>l</sup> Knox Sec<sup>t</sup>. of war.]

War department
August 7<sup>th</sup> 1792.

Sir,

Having received by the way of Kentucky, the dispatches herein enumerated from Fort Washington, and perceiving that the lowness of the waters in the Ohio, mentioned in yours of the 28<sup>th</sup> ultimo, may have prevented you from receiving similar intelligence, I have thought proper to forward copies for your information & consideration by Express.

Comparing the information now transmitted with that from Norton contained in my last, but little doubt can remain that poor Truemans fate is sealed— but I hope Col<sup>o</sup>. Hardin may have escaped.

Although two sets of messengers (Hardin perhaps excepted) have thus been destroyed, the hostile indians may be possessed of the desires of the United States for peace— unless Girtty and such wretches dependant on the traders under the British auspices, may have concealed them.

If Hardin should also be murdered our remaining hope for the hostile tribes to be acquainted with our pacific overtures must rest upon the Senecas, Captain Hendricks, Colonel Louis and Captain Brant, the indians who were in this City for that purpose.

I estimate that some of the above indians are at Buffaloe at present & perhaps most of them will be there in a few days— I should hope that considerable dependence may be placed on Captain Brant— He is well acquainted with the subject, and if his faithfulness in the cause be equal to his intelligence, he will probably effect a treaty.

Time will shortly disclose whether the murder of our messengers has been the premeditated act of the council of the council of the hostile tribes— the act of the Shawanese & other opposers of peace, or the effect of blood thirsty disposition of individuals.

I have enclosed you Brigadier Gen<sup>l</sup>. Putnams plan for carrying on the war— I feel exceedingly obliged to him or any other person for any plans Ideas or even hints which they may think proper to offer, but every Idea which he has brought forward has been weighed maturely by the President of the United States previously to the present arrangement. The result was that the Wabash and Amies river of lake Erie should be the boundaries in case of progressing hostilities.

If the propositions made by Gen<sup>l</sup>. Putnam are then relinquished for the present plan, reasons for perseverance therein multiplied greatly. I shall therefore attempt to point out the [strikethrough: objections] exceptions to the big Beaver & Cuyahoga route which occur to my mind.

First, reasons of national policy will restrain (during disputes & negotiations relative to the Posts) all arrangements on the Lakes, which might occasion collisions with the British inferior agents. this is a Delicate point & is not therefore to be undertaken.

Secondly— that in case of offensive operations a division of the probable efficient force would be such as to render the success problematical.

Thirdly the immediate object could be followed for the operation of the said force moving by the way of Cuyahoga— provided the information given by Captain Brant could be depended upon, to wit, that the Wyandots & Delawares have left Sandusky.

Fourthly— that even if the foregoing reason did not exist so strongly the [undecipherable] season would prevent the measure, this year, unless the motives were so powerful as to be a reason for the Troops encountering all the hardships and dangers of the late season as in the last Campaign.

Fifthly— A post or posts established at & below the Miami village towards Lake Erie would it is presumed have the direct effect to make all the hostile Indians, hitherto resident to the Eastward of the said Omee river, as at Sandusky & other places remove to the westward of the said river, provided they have not already removed, which is highly probable.

The above objections together with others arising from the necessity & propriety of continuing our advance from Fort Jefferson to the Miami village are offered on Brig<sup>t</sup>. Gen<sup>l</sup>. Putnams proposition for your consideration & remarks.

The season of the year is too far advanced, the number of recruits too few and the undisciplined state of the army such as to preclude any great expectation of all forward important movements this season.

If the war is to progress the number of recruits authorised by law must be completed during the autumn & winter and every preparation by discipline and otherwise be made for the most active & forward operations as early in the ensuing spring as the waters & herbage will allow.

Another conflict with the savages with raw recruits is to be avoided by all means.

I shall transmit these remarks to the president of the United States & his observations on the proposition of Brigadier Putnam, & the objections herein stated shall be transmitted to you. You will judge from Brigadier Gen<sup>l</sup>. Wilkinsons letter of the propriety of forwarding him a respectable detachment of five or six hundred troops— The men designed for the Cavalry will of course be forwarded, as they must be mounted there— but I beg you to give the proper orders that they be not prematurely hazarded.

More volunteers from Kentucky would be too expensive.

In order that you may have all the information I possess on the subject of the navigation of the Big Beaver Creek and the route thence over to Cuyahoga. I enclose you the late major Hearts report upon that subject on consequence of instructions from me in the year 1790.

The Letter of Brigadier Gen<sup>l</sup> Putnam of the 9<sup>th</sup> of July, relative to the Establishment of a post on the Muskingum is referred to your judgment. If the maps are to be depended upon, a post at the place where Fort Lawrence stood which was built in the year 1764 would appear to have a good effect to protect Ohio & Washington Counties— but whether it would be [undecipherable] of itself, unless the Garrison was very large, and whether it could be easily supplied so as to be enquired into, and above all whether the division of force and the expense would be amply repaid by the benefits.

I enclose you copies of the letters written to Brigadier General Putnam & Wilkinson.

It would be a species of injustice were it concealed that Brigadier General Wilkinson has afforded the greatest satisfaction by his conduct which has evinced the most indefatigable [undecipherable] zeal to promote the good of the Service. I have this moment received the enclosed letter from Israel Chapin the agent to the Five nations— I transmit it to you as a new light upon the pacific overtures, and the expectation which we may entertain of the agency of the indians, independent of Captain Brant, who I think will be at the Amie river of Lake Erie, rather previous to the 20 instant.

I am still of opinion, and the more confirmed in it from Chapins letter, that the Seneka's with Captain Jeffers party ought not to be pressed to stay in service— their continuance may have bad effects.

I shall from time to time communicate to you all the information which I shall receive relative to the objects of your command, in order that you may be enabled to take a comprehensive view of the subject and decide accordingly as the public interests shall direct.

The President of the United States in a letter received from him this day mentions "Reiterate in your letters to General Wayne the necessity of employing the present calm in disciplining and training the troops under his command for the peculiar service for which they are destined— He is not to be sparing of powder & lead (in proper & reasonable quantities) to make the Mens marksmen.

So long as the vice of drunkeness exists in the army, so long I hope [undecipherable] of those officers who are found guilty of it will continue; for [underline: that], and [underline: gaming] will debilitate & render unfit for active service any army whatever.

I have the honor to be with great respect
your most obed<sup>t</sup>. Serv<sup>t</sup>

Knox    P.S—

Maj. Gen<sup>l</sup>. Wayne.

August 10<sup>th</sup> 1792.

Sir,

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 3 instant containing enclosures from Brig<sup>r</sup> General Wilkinson, Captain Cafs, and Mr Rosecrantz— I thank you for your early attention in making this communication, which with additional letters from General Putnam and Israel Chapin I thought of Sufficient consequence to justify the expense of an express to transmit the same to you on the eighth instant P.M.

Let the event of the council at Au Glaise, be what it may, Peace or War, it is pretty evident for the three following reasons, that we shall not be able this year to make any very important offensive operations.

First— Because the final and explicit result of the council at Au Glaise, will not probably be known until deep in October, if they wait for the advice of the six nations & the Canada Indians.

Secondly Because our recruits will not be assembled in Sufficient numbers.

Thirdly Because our army will not be Sufficiently disciplined according to the nature of the warfare in which it is to be engaged to justify our risking a general engagement far Advanced on the But—
Indian Country.

But if war must finally be the result, notwithstanding all overtures, most certainly, the great mass of the citizens of the United States, must cordially & vigourously support a war, which cannot be terminated but by a manifestation of our Superiority, or a base abandonment of our frontiers to Savage cruelty, and the culpable intrigues and support of an an improper interference on the part of a people who ought to act otherwise.

If force must decide the contest I join heartily with you, that the parties & tribes who have committed the greatest barbarities ought if possible to be punished with such exemplary severity, as to deter in future other tribes from a repetition of similar crimes against the United States.

You mention that many essential articles mentioned in the invoice from the 1<sup>st</sup> of January to the 30 of June, have not yet arrived and not a single article contained in that from the first to the Seventeenth of July.

I wish you had men[tio]ned the articles which had not arrived of those sent before the 30<sup>th</sup> of June in order that a strict scrutiny might be made after the delinquents.

I expect that most of them are found, by a detachment of Dragoons under Cornet Taylor, who I sent in pursuit of them — he had found their trail, & was not far on their rear yesterday noon. his orders are if they attempt resistance, to put them to instantaneous death. —

By the enclosed paper you will see the measures I have adopted to prevent desertion in future — two Deserters were brought in yesterday by two Countrymen, for which they received ten Dollars each —

The written descriptive list of Deserters are those who deserted from their posts at the alarm, and who I expect to see in the course of the day. It however may be possible, notwithstanding the near approach of the Dragoons that they may escape, it will therefore not be amiss to have the whole inserted & republished in the Philadelphia papers.

I have in contemplation a brand with the word [underline: Coward], to stamp upon the forehead of one or two of the most alert Cullies, & to divest them of every military insignia, & cause them to be constantly employ'd in the most menial services about camp.

You'll please to observe that there has scarcely been any desertions from this place, except those occasioned by the alarm; they have generally taken place on their march, from the respective rendezvous. Whether would it not be adviseable to furnish the officers marching Detachments with printed blank descriptions by way of advertisement.

Eight howitzers have arrived but without wheels or carriages — no account of clothing — permit me again to reiterate my request for a quantity of fine grained powder of equal [undecipherable] & quality with the [undecipherable] sent [undecipherable] [undecipherable] —

War department

August 13. 1792

Sir

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your favor of the 8<sup>th</sup> instant, enclosing copies of a letter from Arthur Campbell Esq<sup>r</sup> Lieutenant of Washington County dated July 19<sup>th</sup>, and from [undecipherable] Wilson commanding the Harrison Militia dated 19 July; also informing of the departure of His Excellency Governor Lee for the South Western Frontier.

My last letter from Governor Blount was dated on the 11 of July. He mentioned that he had then called into service a troop of Horse, without specifying the numbers which would serve as an escort for him and General Pickens to Nashville for which place they Should set the next day.

As the horses were to be accompanied by some respectable chiefs of the Cherokees down the Tennessee together with proper crews and Guards Governor Blount did not seem to be apprehensive of danger.

It is to be greatly desired that Governor Blount should terminate all the disputes with the neighbouring Indians and find some other way than actual force to keep the refractory part of the Chiccamagas quiet — if War shall once commence with the Cherokees it will be difficult to prevent its spreading generally throughout the Southern tribes.

The result of the grand national Council of the Cherokees held at Estanaula from the 26 of June to the first of July appeared to be favorable to a general pacification — This Council granted the escort of the chiefs to the goods — after which it is not probable that any individuals would attempt violence thereon.

Had any injury been attempted either upon the party with the Goods, or the Governor it is most likely that we should have been informed thereof before the present time.

It is therefore much to be hoped that the information given by the chief mentioned by Col. Campbell of the bad designs of the Cherokees was not well founded —

I have the honor to be

Sir

Your most obed. Servant

[signature]

The Honorable
James Wood Esq<sup>r</sup>

August 13<sup>th</sup> 1792

Sir

Your favor of the 15<sup>th</sup> May was received on the 28<sup>th</sup> of June, and submitted to the President of the United States.

Your ideas of the difficulty of establishing a peace with the hostile Indians without [strikethrough: further] conflict it is to be apprehended are too well founded. But it is an object of too high importance to make every reasonable effort for that purpose, in order to convince a considerable proportion of the Citizens of the United States that the thing is impracticable.

The cordial zeal with which you have left your private affairs in order to endeavour to benefit the public, is highly satisfactory and gratifying to the President of the United States.

It is probable that the service of the Indians may not be required this year, owing to the long protracted Council of the Northern Indians, who are to repair to the assembled hostile Indians in order to endeavour to make a peace. As the time that the result of these peace overtures shall [strikethrough: be] be known, it will probably be too late to undertake any offensive operations of importance, and more particularly to engage any Indians for the purpose of their rendering it the —

But if one practicable, the war will probably be pushed with great vigor early in the Spring, when our troops will be completed and disciplined for the nature of the service. In this event, auxiliary Indians may be required and I am persuaded that taking a considerable command of them and other light troops would be particularly acceptable to the President of the United States. Will you have the goodness to impart to me your dispositions on the case herein stated in order to be submitted to the President.

I have the honor to be
with great respect
Your humble Servant

Brig Gen<sup>l</sup> Pickens                    H Knox

Pittsburgh 17<sup>th</sup> Aug 1792

Sir

I am honored with yours of the 7. instant [undecipherable], inclosing copies of Letters & communications from Generals Putnam, Wilkinson, & from Gen'l Israel Chapin, also Capt Hearts reports & sketch of the big beaver &c— I had the honor to inclose copies of Gen'l Wilkinsons letters & Major Hamtramck's communications to you on the 8 inst. in which I took the liberty to request them to be returned, as I would not have time to take copies without detaining the post, these you have now honored me with [undecipherable] the necessity of those.— By the many corroborating accounts from every quarter, I believe there can be little doubt the fate of our three [underline: flags], & that both Col. Harding and Major Trueman have been victims of savage ferocity. It is also probable that the first embassy, if not the second, from the five nations to the hostile Indians (mentioned in the enclosed copy of a letter from Capt [undecipherable]) have experienced the fate of our [underline: flags], the first has been absent two moons; the other one, when the complanter was at Fort Franklin, on the 29 ultmo. had any material intelligence been received at the mouth of Buffalo as late as the 7 inst. I should have been made acquainted with it by this time.

The alarm of two large parties of Indians being in the vicinity of this place, turned out to be a party of about [underline: six], who finding themselves discovered, went off without doing any damage. they were followed about sixty miles.— another small party made their appearance near Wheelen about fifty miles below this place on the Ohio, the beginning of this week, and fired upon three or four people, who returned it, by which fire one Indian fell, and one of our people was shot thro the Shoulder.

I have in some measure anticipated the presidents orders, on firing at marks— by permitting the Rifle men to practice to shot a man every fair day, and by Directing the Guards relieved from duty, to discharge at marks, waistband high, as mentioned in my letter of the 16—

On Wednesday we had a sharp engagement— the rifle Corps, by reiterated attacks & highly painted, acted with the part of Savages— which required all the skill & fortitude of our little Legion to sustain, until by a combined manoeuvre of the reserve composed of cavalry and infantry— they were outflanked and charged in front & rear, at the same instant, (by actual surprise) part of the cavalry having crossed and recrossed the Alleghany, for that purpose, during the action. this little representation of an action, has had a good effect, by animating the respective corps with a Spirit of Emulation— but it will not do to repeat it— at least for some time— I had no Idea, that the mind could be so diffusively inflamed by imagination only— fortunately no material accident has happened, some have had their faces a little burnt with powder— and two or three slightly wounded with wadding— but in a manner that caused more anger than hurt.

I am much obliged by Gen'l Putnam's plan of carrying on the war against the Indians, & for your observations thereon, and will give them a full consideration— I had projected in my own mind, a plan of operation something Different from that of Gen'l Putnams, and am decidedly of opinion that the plan he proposes for operations, is very improper, for raw & undisciplined troops— who have not yet learned to live upon their rations. I will not enter into a discussion at present, as I mean to submit my Ideas, fully & freely to you, upon this Subject by the next post.

The Indians, that were attached to Capt Jeffers corps have been dismissed & sent home, ever since the beginning of July— except two or three, who don't show a disposition to leave this place— in fact Jeffers, whole corps of rangers has been disbanded near two months, as I found the soldiers were much averse to that kind of service, which has caused many Desertions.—

Captain Mills did not march from Carlisle, until the 10<sup>th</sup>, nor do I hear of any other detachment being near— I expect him here about the 24.<sup>th</sup>

Whilst I am writing I am honored with yours of the 10<sup>th</sup> with inclosures, and shall direct [undecipherable] Craig, to make out a list of the articles that have not yet arrived, mentioned in the invoices from the 1<sup>st</sup> of January, to the 30<sup>th</sup> of June, & from the 1<sup>st</sup>, until the 1<sup>st</sup> of July—

It is indispensibly necessary, that some effectual mode of transportation of stores should be adopted— probably, if the owners of waggons were obliged to deliver the stores committed to their charge at Pittsburgh within 25 days it might have a good effect— Capt Porter, of the artillery, who arrived yesterday, says that he has seen considerable quantities of public Stores left at several taverns, along the road

Pittsburgh 31 August 1792.

Sir,

I have the honor to enclose a copy of Captain Haskell's letter to me of the 21 instant — in addition to which Capt. Wm. Mills, brother to our Capt. John Mills, by whom the letter came, says, that in conversation with the British Officers he mentioned that whilst he was with the Indians they expressed an anxiety for a Hostile interview, that nothing prevented them from committing depredations but a full expectation of our advance into their country, that they affect to hold us in the utmost contempt for offering to treat of peace, with a people who neither want or wish for it. Be that as it may I am decidedly of opinion that we ought immediately to establish our magazines of forage & provision. [undecipherable] I now have directed the Quarter Master General to contract for Fifty thousand bushels of grain — chiefly Indian Corn & five hundred tons of hay — at present nothing can be done by water — the Ohio has never been so low in the memory of the oldest inhabitants.

The Copy of a letter to the Q. M. G. will give you some idea. But at the time the Boats went from this place there was a smart fresh on the Monongahela, but it was evaporated before it reached Marietta.

The Clothing for the late first Regiment has [undecipherable: just] arrived, as well as that for the Rifle Corps except Hats & Blankets & part for the second, not a single moment shall be lost in forwarding it, when the state of the water will admit, in order to stop the mouths of Haskell & others.

I enclose a copy of Gov. Mifflin's letter to the Lieutenant of Alleghany County — I shall forbear to comment upon it. I however informed Col. Procter that at present I did not think myself justifiable in calling out any Militia or in [undecipherable: resorting] to the measure; that when there was necessity, I would do it with ample reliance upon their turning out with alacrity.

We are in want of many articles in the Hospital department, of which the enclosed letter of invoice from Doctor Carmichael will inform you.

By this morning's post you will receive the numbers & condition of our force at this Post — the men in confinement have all been tried by a General Court Martial — some are condemned to death, some to Corporal punishment — others are acquitted, or ordered to do the drudgery of the camp for a given time, the whole of which sentences will take place tomorrow & many save, I trust, it will break the neck of desertion. You'll please to observe that the principal part of these Criminals were lately brought here on by the several detachments as prisoners.

to present my best Compliments to Major Stagg & inform him that I have been honored with his letter of the 25 instant, with invoices of Clothing & so forwarded between the 25 & 23 of this month, a duplicate of yours of the 17<sup>th</sup> instant. I have the honor to be with true esteem

Your most obed.
& very hum. Serv.

43515:
[N<sup>o</sup> 15]     From Gen<sup>l</sup> Knox Sep<sup>t</sup> for war

War department
September 1<sup>st</sup> 1792.

Sir

Your favors of the 17 and 20 ult: have been received.

I have directed a person to be sent to examine the road from hence to Pittsburgh to see whether there any stores lingering upon the road, and if so, to accelerate them & report the delay greatest — but Major Craig writes on the 20<sup>th</sup> that several waggon loads of stores had just arrived.

I submitted your letter of the 17 instant and shall duly submit that of the 20 instant to the President of the United States.

I have not yet had time to consider of your propositions for carrying on the war, in case pacific overtures should fail — in general they when first sight appear judicious and do have been well weighed by you, and an explicit answer shall be transmitted thereon upon the receipt of the Presidents opinion.

I wish you have been pleased to transmit the information which gives you the belief that Sandusky is not mostly abandoned by the women and children — The indians may be raising some corn there but I believe no more — I am apprehensive that any expedition against that place without further information would be pushing against a cloud.

No doubt however can be entertained of the propriety of accumulating the magazines of forage & provisions you propose at Fort Washington and the posts advanced there — and you will please explicitly to understand that if you

you had not the authority before — that it is hereby fully vested in you.

As this is the season for laying up salt provisions the Contractors will take your orders upon that head — they are bound by the contract to lay up three months for the Garrisons, but you will require at your advanced posts a far greater quantity of which you will please maturely to consider & order accordingly.

The fine grained powder has been forwarded to the amount of forty small casks — all the clothing has been forwarded excepting for Fords company of artillery, which will be forwarded immediately.

I do not estimate that the Virginia Rifle Companies will be at the mouth of the Great Kenhawa before the 15<sup>th</sup> of this month — Stephenons, Breckinens Hannahs attachments will be soon with you.

Eatons company has not yet arrived from the Eastward — when it does — I hope from Jersey & New York to make it a detachment of one hundred and fifty men.

The recruiting service has been almost at a Stand — I know not how it can be stimulated, only by an additional sum to their pay for which no authority exists — perhaps in the autumn and winter we may complete the numbers authorized.

Have you ordered your paymaster up from Fort Washington? I have been waiting for Eatons company to send on money to complete the pay to the first of august and also ten thousand Dollars for the Quarter master which his agent has drawn from the Treasury — but I believe some other

the opportunity must be sought.

I have the honor to be
with great respect
your obedient Servant

Knox Sep<sup>t</sup> for war

Major Gen<sup>l</sup> Wayne

East Windsor, Sep<sup>tr</sup> 3. 1792.

My dear Sir,

I write you again and sh[oul]d write to you oftener, if you were more at leisure. Your thoughts and time I am sensible must have been very busily engaged in the great and arduous affairs which are intrusted to you. I have no doubt of your ability and integrity in the management of them. I have felt with you for the unfortunate events, relative to our common defence against a Savage enemy:
"'Tis not in mortals to command Success."

Pacifick measures which I wished ardently at first, are now probably too late.

When I wrote you, I knew not that so many attempts had been made to conciliate the hostile tribes, as I find by your public declaration, had been made.

It affords the mind some consolation when we can deduce good out of evil. The calamity of the Indian war, is I think productive of one great good of the negative kind, which is the prevention of a too extensive and emigration over the western Territory. Now this embankment removed, thousands would [undecipherable] themselves, over that boundless region from the Lakes to the Missisipe & I have no doubt would gradually & speedily lose the habits of Subordination in Society, the restraints of law & government & the means of education & religion & adopt the habits of Savages & possibly in the course of half a century, would be harder to civilize than the present inhabitants & more formidable foes to the [undecipherable] of our national government. But now they [undecipherable] proceed no faster than they can carry the arts [undecipherable] civilization along with them. And the present evil is a wise ordering of providence to prevent a greater. The frontier people of the Southern States, now experience those calamities that the first Settlers of New England felt. The foundations of all new empires are laid in blood.

Since I wrote you my younger brother James, who lost a leg in the war, died in Dublin in Ireland. He was master of a Ship from Exeter. You have likewise lost a Son, one of three promising boys that I saw with you at Hartford. Our changes in this mutable world are many and frequent. Let us live for a better.

I inclose two Discourses on the death of two worthy friends, of which I beg your acceptance, as a pledge of affectionate remembrance, from Dear Sir,

Your Sincere friend &
very Oble Servant
David McClure
